standard.description: The passport is folded from plain paper. Thank-you tokens are torn paper strips.
items: Index cards — 100, for skill cards
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for passports and thank-you strips
Pencils — 20
Crayons — 4 boxes, shared

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: The passport is folded from plain paper already in the room.
items: Index cards — 100, for skill cards

focus: Name one thing you are good at
Make a skill card (draw it)
Show your skill to a partner
Words: skill, good, teach, learn
Describe your skill in a sentence
Teach your skill step by step to a partner
Notice a skill you learned from someone
Vocabulary: skill, practice, teach, talent
Break your skill into clear steps to teach it
Give and get feedback at the fair
Explain how skills have value to others
Vocabulary: expertise, feedback, value, demonstrate
Plan a mini-lesson and teach it effectively
Evaluate which skills are most useful and why
Reflect on how skills can be traded or hired
Vocabulary: proficiency, specialization, market value, mentor

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Let students show their skill with their hands first and add words after.
Give the frames "My skill is ___." and "First you ___. Then you ___."
Pair students with a partner who speaks their language for the first teaching round.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Offer a short list of skills to pick from (tying shoes, drawing a cat, folding paper) with a picture for each.
Let students draw the skill card and tell the teacher the words.
Let a student watch the first teaching round before they teach.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Write the skill as three numbered steps a stranger could follow.
Teach a harder version of the skill to a second partner and note what they had to explain differently.
Explain what they would charge to teach the skill for an hour, and why.

description.en: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.
description.es: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

description.en: "The friends found $4.73 in one week just by looking. Today you're going to count a jar of coins and figure out the total."
description.es: "The friends found $4.73 in one week just by looking. Today you're going to count a jar of coins and figure out the total."

sayThis.en: "The friends found four dollars and seventy-three cents in one week, just by looking. Your group gets a pile of coins. Let's find out how much it is."
sayThis.es: "The friends found four dollars and seventy-three cents in one week, just by looking. Your group gets a pile of coins. Let's find out how much it is."

watchFor.en: Kids who can't tell the coins apart. Hold up each coin once and say its name and value.
watchFor.es: Kids who can't tell the coins apart. Hold up each coin once and say its name and value.

doneWhen.en: The class has named all four coins with you.
doneWhen.es: The class has named all four coins with you.

description.en: Each group gets a pile of mixed coins. Sort into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.
description.es: Each group gets a pile of mixed coins. Sort into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.

sayThis.en: "Make four piles. Pennies. Nickels. Dimes. Quarters. Read the number on each coin."
sayThis.es: "Make four piles. Pennies. Nickels. Dimes. Quarters. Read the number on each coin."

watchFor.en: One child doing all the sorting. Give each person in the group one kind of coin to collect.
watchFor.es: One child doing all the sorting. Give each person in the group one kind of coin to collect.

doneWhen.en: Every group has four piles with no mixed coins.
doneWhen.es: Every group has four piles with no mixed coins.

description.en: Count each pile. Record how many of each. "We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."
description.es: Count each pile. Record how many of each. "We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."

sayThis.en: "Count each pile. Touch each coin as you count. Fill in: We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."
sayThis.es: "Count each pile. Touch each coin as you count. Fill in: We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."

watchFor.en: Kids counting money instead of coins. Say, "How many coins, not how much money. That comes next."
watchFor.es: Kids counting money instead of coins. Say, "How many coins, not how much money. That comes next."

doneWhen.en: Every group has four numbers written down.
doneWhen.es: Every group has four numbers written down.

description.en: Add up the total. Teacher checks with the class. Correct if needed. Tier 1 (K-1): count the pennies only, then watch the teacher count the rest out loud to get the total.
description.es: Add up the total. Teacher checks with the class. Correct if needed. Tier 1 (K-1): count the pennies only, then watch the teacher count the rest out loud to get the total.

sayThis.en: "Now how much money? Count the quarters by 25s, the dimes by 10s, the nickels by 5s, then add the pennies."
sayThis.es: "Now how much money? Count the quarters by 25s, the dimes by 10s, the nickels by 5s, then add the pennies."

watchFor.en: Groups stuck when time runs out. Do one group's total on the board, counting out loud together.
watchFor.es: Groups stuck when time runs out. Do one group's total on the board, counting out loud together.

doneWhen.en: Each group's total has been checked against your list.
doneWhen.es: Each group's total has been checked against your list.

discussionQuestions: Did the total surprise you? Were there more pennies or more dimes?
If you found 1 coin every day for a year, how much would you have?
What would you do with $4.73 — spend it, split it, save it, or buy something for the group?

beforeClass.en: Cut paper coins and write 1¢, 5¢, 10¢ or 25¢ on each one. Make one mixed pile per group, and write down how many of each coin you put in so you can check their counts.
beforeClass.es: Cut paper coins and write 1¢, 5¢, 10¢ or 25¢ on each one. Make one mixed pile per group, and write down how many of each coin you put in so you can check their counts.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Count Each Pile, count only pennies and dimes, and do Calculate Total together on the board. Short: in Calculate Total, have groups trade piles and check each other's total.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Count Each Pile, count only pennies and dimes, and do Calculate Total together on the board. Short: in Calculate Total, have groups trade piles and check each other's total.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

description.en: Each student draws or receives a savings jar tracker. Explain: "Each day this week, you'll save a different amount. Today is Day 1 — save 25 cents." Students draw a quarter in Row 1 and write $0.25.
description.es: Each student draws or receives a savings jar tracker. Explain: "Each day this week, you'll save a different amount. Today is Day 1 — save 25 cents." Students draw a quarter in Row 1 and write $0.25.

sayThis.en: "This is your savings jar tracker. Seven rows, one for each day. Day 1: you found a quarter. Draw it in Row 1 and write $0.25."
sayThis.es: "This is your savings jar tracker. Seven rows, one for each day. Day 1: you found a quarter. Draw it in Row 1 and write $0.25."

watchFor.en: Rows too small to draw coins in. Tell them to make each row about two fingers tall.
watchFor.es: Rows too small to draw coins in. Tell them to make each row about two fingers tall.

doneWhen.en: Every tracker has seven rows and a quarter with $0.25 in Row 1.
doneWhen.es: Every tracker has seven rows and a quarter with $0.25 in Row 1.

description.en: Run all 7 days in 8 minutes. Teacher calls out each day's "find": - Day 1: 25¢ (quarter near the vending machine) - Day 2: 10¢ (dime at the park bench) - Day 3: 3¢ (three pennies near the fountain) - Day 4: 5¢ (nickel outside the corner store) - Day 5: 50¢ (found in the wash at home) - Day 6: 35¢ (three dimes and a nickel) - Day 7: $3.45 (found a whole collection — big find!) Students record each day and draw the coins.
description.es: Run all 7 days in 8 minutes. Teacher calls out each day's "find": - Day 1: 25¢ (quarter near the vending machine) - Day 2: 10¢ (dime at the park bench) - Day 3: 3¢ (three pennies near the fountain) - Day 4: 5¢ (nickel outside the corner store) - Day 5: 50¢ (found in the wash at home) - Day 6: 35¢ (three dimes and a nickel) - Day 7: $3.45 (found a whole collection — big find!) Students record each day and draw the coins.

sayThis.en: "Day 2: a dime at the park bench. Draw it and write ten cents." Keep going, one day at a time.
sayThis.es: "Day 2: a dime at the park bench. Draw it and write ten cents." Keep going, one day at a time.

watchFor.en: Kids falling behind while drawing. Tell them to write the amount first and draw only if there's time.
watchFor.es: Kids falling behind while drawing. Tell them to write the amount first and draw only if there's time.

doneWhen.en: Every tracker has all seven days written in.
doneWhen.es: Every tracker has all seven days written in.

description.en: Students add up all 7 days. Compare with a partner. Correct answer: $4.73. Tier 1 (K-1): count how many coins you drew this week, and the teacher shows the $4.73 total on the board.
description.es: Students add up all 7 days. Compare with a partner. Correct answer: $4.73. Tier 1 (K-1): count how many coins you drew this week, and the teacher shows the $4.73 total on the board.

sayThis.en: "Add up all seven days. Then check with your partner. Do you match?"
sayThis.es: "Add up all seven days. Then check with your partner. Do you match?"

watchFor.en: The $3.45 lined up wrong with the small amounts. Have them add Days 1 to 6 first ($1.28), then add $3.45.
watchFor.es: The $3.45 lined up wrong with the small amounts. Have them add Days 1 to 6 first ($1.28), then add $3.45.

doneWhen.en: Every pair agrees on $4.73.
doneWhen.es: Every pair agrees on $4.73.

description.en: Read aloud the three options from the story: "Benny said SPLIT IT. Ellis said SAVE IT. Layla said BUY SOMETHING WE ALL SHARE." Class vote. Discuss why people chose differently.
description.es: Read aloud the three options from the story: "Benny said SPLIT IT. Ellis said SAVE IT. Layla said BUY SOMETHING WE ALL SHARE." Class vote. Discuss why people chose differently.

sayThis.en: "Benny said split it. Ellis said save it. Layla said buy something we all share. Which would you pick? Hands up for each one."
sayThis.es: "Benny said split it. Ellis said save it. Layla said buy something we all share. Which would you pick? Hands up for each one."

watchFor.en: Kids voting with their best friend. Before the vote, have each student tell a partner one reason for their pick.
watchFor.es: Kids voting with their best friend. Before the vote, have each student tell a partner one reason for their pick.

doneWhen.en: The vote count is on the board and two students have explained different choices.
doneWhen.es: The vote count is on the board and two students have explained different choices.

discussionQuestions: Did Day 7's big find change things? What if you'd spent the first $1.28 before Day 7?
Ellis wrote everything in his notebook. Why was that helpful?
Why did Mr. Mason's penny jar story change how the friends thought about their money?
If you save $4.73 per week, how much do you have in a month? ($18.92) Tier 1 (K-1): if you save $1 a week, how much do you have after 4 weeks?

beforeClass.en: Draw a tracker with seven rows, Day 1 to Day 7, on the board for kids to copy, or give each student one already drawn. Keep the list of daily finds in your hand so you can call them out fast.
beforeClass.es: Draw a tracker with seven rows, Day 1 to Day 7, on the board for kids to copy, or give each student one already drawn. Keep the list of daily finds in your hand so you can call them out fast.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in the Week Simulation, have students write the amounts and skip drawing the coins. Short: in The Group Decision, ask one student from each side to explain their vote.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in the Week Simulation, have students write the amounts and skip drawing the coins. Short: in The Group Decision, ask one student from each side to explain their vote.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

sayThis.en: "Four columns. Date. Amount. Running total. Where you found it. Ellis kept records — that's the only reason he knew there was four dollars and seventy-three cents."
sayThis.es: "Four columns. Date. Amount. Running total. Where you found it. Ellis kept records — that's the only reason he knew there was four dollars and seventy-three cents."

doneWhen.en: Every ledger has four labeled columns.
doneWhen.es: Every ledger has four labeled columns.

watchFor.en: Students who skip the running total. Without it the next step doesn't work.
watchFor.es: Students who skip the running total. Without it the next step doesn't work.

description.en: Students set up a personal ledger: Date | Amount Found | Running Total | How Found. Teacher explains: "Ellis kept records. That's how he knew you're not going to believe this — we have $4.73!"
description.es: Students set up a personal ledger: Date | Amount Found | Running Total | How Found. Teacher explains: "Ellis kept records. That's how he knew you're not going to believe this — we have $4.73!"

sayThis.en: "Thirty coins are hidden in this room. When you find one, write it down before you go looking for the next one. If it isn't in your ledger, it doesn't count."
sayThis.es: "Thirty coins are hidden in this room. When you find one, write it down before you go looking for the next one. If it isn't in your ledger, it doesn't count."

doneWhen.en: All thirty coins are found and every one is written in somebody's ledger.
doneWhen.es: All thirty coins are found and every one is written in somebody's ledger.

watchFor.en: Pocketing coins and recording later. Say the rule again mid-round. Also the student who finds nothing — steer them toward an untouched corner.
watchFor.es: Pocketing coins and recording later. Say the rule again mid-round. Also the student who finds nothing — steer them toward an untouched corner.

description.en: Teacher has hidden 30 "coins" (paper or play) around the classroom in advance. Students hunt for them. Every coin found gets recorded in the ledger immediately: where found, denomination, running total updated. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each coin you find in your ledger, and the class counts the total together in the next step.
description.es: Teacher has hidden 30 "coins" (paper or play) around the classroom in advance. Students hunt for them. Every coin found gets recorded in the ledger immediately: where found, denomination, running total updated. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each coin you find in your ledger, and the class counts the total together in the next step.

sayThis.en: "Pool everything. Sort by type. Count each pile. One person writes the totals. Then we check it — because a total nobody checked is just a guess."
sayThis.es: "Pool everything. Sort by type. Count each pile. One person writes the totals. Then we check it — because a total nobody checked is just a guess."

doneWhen.en: One agreed grand total is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: One agreed grand total is written on the board.

watchFor.en: Two different totals. Good. Make them find the error rather than telling them.
watchFor.es: Two different totals. Good. Make them find the error rather than telling them.

description.en: Class pools all found coins. Pairs sort by denomination and count. One recorder writes the totals on the board. Class verifies the grand total.
description.es: Class pools all found coins. Pairs sort by denomination and count. One recorder writes the totals on the board. Class verifies the grand total.

sayThis.en: "Three proposals. Split it equally. Save it four more weeks. Spend it on something everyone gets. Thirty seconds each. Then we vote."
sayThis.es: "Three proposals. Split it equally. Save it four more weeks. Spend it on something everyone gets. Thirty seconds each. Then we vote."

doneWhen.en: All three proposals have been heard and every ballot is in.
doneWhen.es: All three proposals have been heard and every ballot is in.

watchFor.en: Proposals with no detail. Split it how? Save it for what? Make them finish the sentence.
watchFor.es: Proposals with no detail. Split it how? Save it for what? Make them finish the sentence.

description.en: Teacher facilitates a formal "financial meeting" — three students make proposals (assign roles in advance or take volunteers): - "I move that we split the money equally." (Propose how.) - "I move that we save it for 4 more weeks and then decide." (Propose what goal.) - "I move that we spend it on something the whole class can enjoy." (Name what.) Class discusses pros and cons. Vote by written ballot (secret vote adds engagement).
description.es: Teacher facilitates a formal "financial meeting" — three students make proposals (assign roles in advance or take volunteers): - "I move that we split the money equally." (Propose how.) - "I move that we save it for 4 more weeks and then decide." (Propose what goal.) - "I move that we spend it on something the whole class can enjoy." (Name what.) Class discusses pros and cons. Vote by written ballot (secret vote adds engagement).

sayThis.en: "The winning plan gets a budget. Here's the exact total. Spend it down on paper — item, cost, what's left. You can't go over, and you can't leave more than a dollar sitting there."
sayThis.es: "The winning plan gets a budget. Here's the exact total. Spend it down on paper — item, cost, what's left. You can't go over, and you can't leave more than a dollar sitting there."

doneWhen.en: Two teams have read a complete budget out loud.
doneWhen.es: Two teams have read a complete budget out loud.

watchFor.en: Rounded numbers that don't add up. Make them show the running balance line by line.
watchFor.es: Rounded numbers that don't add up. Make them show the running balance line by line.

description.en: The winning proposal now gets a budget. Teams take the exact total the class counted and plan how to spend it down to the last cent on a scrap-paper budget sheet — item, cost, running balance. They may not go over and they may not leave more than a dollar unspent. Two teams read their budgets out. Ask which plan the class would actually vote for now that the money has real things attached to it. Tier 1 (K-1): draw two or three things to buy with whole-dollar prices, and the teacher keeps the running balance on the board.
description.es: The winning proposal now gets a budget. Teams take the exact total the class counted and plan how to spend it down to the last cent on a scrap-paper budget sheet — item, cost, running balance. They may not go over and they may not leave more than a dollar unspent. Two teams read their budgets out. Ask which plan the class would actually vote for now that the money has real things attached to it. Tier 1 (K-1): draw two or three things to buy with whole-dollar prices, and the teacher keeps the running balance on the board.

sayThis.en: "Write the decision in the class ledger. Now — did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds once real things had prices on them?"
sayThis.es: "Write the decision in the class ledger. Now — did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds once real things had prices on them?"

doneWhen.en: The decision is written in the ledger and two students have said what changed their thinking.
doneWhen.es: The decision is written in the ledger and two students have said what changed their thinking.

watchFor.en: Sore losers. Name it: the vote was close, and the other plan wasn't stupid.
watchFor.es: Sore losers. Name it: the vote was close, and the other plan wasn't stupid.

description.en: Record the winning decision in the class savings ledger. Ask: "Did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds?"
description.es: Record the winning decision in the class savings ledger. Ask: "Did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds?"

discussionQuestions: Ellis said 'we need to record this.' Why does writing down what you have matter?
What would have happened if the friends spent their first $1 before they found the rest?
Mr. Mason saved for a whole year. What does that take? What gets in the way?
You voted to ___. Does everyone feel good about the decision? What did you give up?
How is a savings jar different from a savings account? What's the same?
extensionIdeas: Run the class savings simulation for a real week — each day a student "deposits" a token (a real penny or a paper one) and the class tracks the running total
Research: what is a savings account? What is interest? How does a bank use your money while it's saving?
Calculate: if you save $4.73 per week for 52 weeks, what do you have? What could you buy?

beforeClass.en: Hide the thirty paper coins before students arrive and write down where, or you'll lose some for good. Decide whether the vote is secret ballot or hands — secret works better.
beforeClass.es: Hide the thirty paper coins before students arrive and write down where, or you'll lose some for good. Decide whether the vote is secret ballot or hands — secret works better.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the coin hunt to six minutes; the counting and the meeting matter more. Short: run a second hunt with fewer coins and a time limit.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the coin hunt to six minutes; the counting and the meeting matter more. Short: run a second hunt with fewer coins and a time limit.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: All coins are paper. The teacher pre-cuts them or students cut their own.
items: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
Scissors — 10, shared in pairs
Pencils — 20
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room
Scrap paper — 20 pieces, for ballots and budget sheets
Chart paper — 1 sheet, for the class savings ledger

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: All coins are paper. Scissors, paper and pencils are already in the room.
items: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room
Chart paper — 1 sheet, for the class savings ledger

focus: Add a coin to the jar each day
Count the coins with the class
Draw how full the jar is getting
Words: save, coin, count, more
Record the daily total on a chart
Predict tomorrow's total
Decide as a group what to save for
Vocabulary: savings, daily, total, goal
Track the running total and the days remaining
Calculate how many more days to reach a goal
Explain why saving steadily works
Vocabulary: balance, goal, estimate, progress
Model the savings plan and project the end total
Compare saving fast vs. slow to the same goal
Defend a savings strategy with your data
Vocabulary: projection, interval, target, strategy

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Post a coin chart with a picture, the name and the value of each coin.
Count out loud together, pointing to each coin as you say the number.
Give the frames "I found ___ cents." and "I want to ___ because ___."

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Use large paper coins with the value written big on each one.
Give a tracker or ledger with the rows and columns already drawn.
Keep a coin value card on the desk the whole time.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Work out what $4.73 a week adds up to after a month and after a year.
Write a coin story problem for a partner to solve.
Find two different sets of coins that make the same total.

description.en: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?
description.es: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

description.en: Students draw a plan for their tower on one sheet of paper BEFORE touching the other materials. "What shape? How tall? How does it stand up?" Teacher models drawing a quick box-with-layers plan.
description.es: Students draw a plan for their tower on one sheet of paper BEFORE touching the other materials. "What shape? How tall? How does it stand up?" Teacher models drawing a quick box-with-layers plan.

sayThis.en: "Draw your tower first. Don't touch the other paper yet. What shape is it? How tall? How will it stand up?"
sayThis.es: "Draw your tower first. Don't touch the other paper yet. What shape is it? How tall? How will it stand up?"

watchFor.en: Students folding the building paper while they draw. Move the two blank sheets to the corner of the desk until the plan is done.
watchFor.es: Students folding the building paper while they draw. Move the two blank sheets to the corner of the desk until the plan is done.

doneWhen.en: Every student has a drawing on one sheet and two blank sheets still flat.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a drawing on one sheet and two blank sheets still flat.

description.en: Using only the remaining 2 sheets of paper and 1 strip of tape, build the tallest freestanding structure possible. No scissors. Structure must stand on its own for 10 seconds.
description.es: Using only the remaining 2 sheets of paper and 1 strip of tape, build the tallest freestanding structure possible. No scissors. Structure must stand on its own for 10 seconds.

sayThis.en: "Now build. Two sheets and one piece of tape. No scissors. It has to stand up by itself while I count to ten."
sayThis.es: "Now build. Two sheets and one piece of tape. No scissors. It has to stand up by itself while I count to ten."

watchFor.en: Flat sheets that flop over. Show once how rolling or folding a sheet makes it stiff.
watchFor.es: Flat sheets that flop over. Show once how rolling or folding a sheet makes it stiff.

doneWhen.en: Every student has a tower standing, or has tried and is ready to measure.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a tower standing, or has tried and is ready to measure.

description.en: Teacher measures each structure with a ruler or hand-widths. Tallest wins. Show blueprints: "Did your plan match what you built?"
description.es: Teacher measures each structure with a ruler or hand-widths. Tallest wins. Show blueprints: "Did your plan match what you built?"

sayThis.en: "Hands off. I'll measure. Now hold up your plan. Does your tower look like your drawing?"
sayThis.es: "Hands off. I'll measure. Now hold up your plan. Does your tower look like your drawing?"

watchFor.en: Students whose tower fell feeling they lost. Ask what they would change on their plan.
watchFor.es: Students whose tower fell feeling they lost. Ask what they would change on their plan.

doneWhen.en: Every tower is measured and the tallest one is named.
doneWhen.es: Every tower is measured and the tallest one is named.

discussionQuestions: Did your blueprint help you build faster or slower?
Mr. Mason said 'before you build, you need a plan.' Were the friends glad he said that?
What would you do differently if you had one more piece of paper?

beforeClass.en: Give each student 3 sheets of plain paper, 1 pre-cut strip of masking tape and a pencil. Keep a ruler handy. Clear a flat spot where towers can stand on their own.
beforeClass.es: Give each student 3 sheets of plain paper, 1 pre-cut strip of masking tape and a pencil. Keep a ruler handy. Clear a flat spot where towers can stand on their own.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: skip showing blueprints in Measure & Share and just measure. Short: after measuring, let anyone whose tower fell rebuild it with the same paper and measure again.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: skip showing blueprints in Measure & Share and just measure. Short: after measuring, let anyone whose tower fell rebuild it with the same paper and measure again.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

description.en: Teams of 2-3. Draw a blueprint together — must agree before touching materials. Assign roles: one person is the "builder," one is the "holder," one is the "checker" (does it match the plan?).
description.es: Teams of 2-3. Draw a blueprint together — must agree before touching materials. Assign roles: one person is the "builder," one is the "holder," one is the "checker" (does it match the plan?).

sayThis.en: "Draw one plan together. Everybody has to agree before anyone touches the tray. Pick a builder, a holder and a checker. In a team of two, the holder is also the checker."
sayThis.es: "Draw one plan together. Everybody has to agree before anyone touches the tray. Pick a builder, a holder and a checker. In a team of two, the holder is also the checker."

watchFor.en: One child drawing while the others watch. Ask the quiet one to add one part to the plan.
watchFor.es: One child drawing while the others watch. Ask the quiet one to add one part to the plan.

doneWhen.en: Every team has one blueprint and each person can say their job.
doneWhen.es: Every team has one blueprint and each person can say their job.

description.en: "Look at what you have. Can you build your plan with exactly these materials? You may NOT get more. This is your budget."
description.es: "Look at what you have. Can you build your plan with exactly these materials? You may NOT get more. This is your budget."

sayThis.en: "Look in your tray. That is all you get. No more. Can you build your plan with just this?"
sayThis.es: "Look in your tray. That is all you get. No more. Can you build your plan with just this?"

watchFor.en: Hands going up for more tape. The answer is no, every time.
watchFor.es: Hands going up for more tape. The answer is no, every time.

doneWhen.en: Every team has checked its tray against its budget card.
doneWhen.es: Every team has checked its tray against its budget card.

description.en: Build the structure using only the materials listed on the budget card. The budget card is an index card listing what is in the team's tray.
description.es: Build the structure using only the materials listed on the budget card. The budget card is an index card listing what is in the team's tray.

sayThis.en: "Build your plan. Builder builds. Holder holds. Checker looks at the plan. Only what is in your tray."
sayThis.es: "Build your plan. Builder builds. Holder holds. Checker looks at the plan. Only what is in your tray."

watchFor.en: Checkers going quiet. Walk by each team once and ask the checker, "Does it match?"
watchFor.es: Checkers going quiet. Walk by each team once and ask the checker, "Does it match?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has a structure standing or is on its last fix.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a structure standing or is on its last fix.

description.en: Structure must: (a) stand on its own, (b) be taller than 6 inches, (c) have a "roof" (something covering the top).
description.es: Structure must: (a) stand on its own, (b) be taller than 6 inches, (c) have a "roof" (something covering the top).

sayThis.en: "Three tests. Does it stand by itself? Is it taller than six inches? Does it have a roof?"
sayThis.es: "Three tests. Does it stand by itself? Is it taller than six inches? Does it have a roof?"

watchFor.en: Hands steadying the build. Hands off, or it doesn't count.
watchFor.es: Hands steadying the build. Hands off, or it doesn't count.

doneWhen.en: Every structure has been checked on all three tests.
doneWhen.es: Every structure has been checked on all three tests.

description.en: Each team shows their blueprint and their structure side by side. "What changed? What did you discover?"
description.es: Each team shows their blueprint and their structure side by side. "What changed? What did you discover?"

sayThis.en: "Put your plan next to your build. What changed? What did you find out?"
sayThis.es: "Put your plan next to your build. What changed? What did you find out?"

watchFor.en: Teams saying nothing changed. Point to one difference you can see.
watchFor.es: Teams saying nothing changed. Point to one difference you can see.

doneWhen.en: Every team has named one change from plan to build.
doneWhen.es: Every team has named one change from plan to build.

discussionQuestions: Were you ever tempted to grab extra materials? What stopped you?
The friends used an old blanket they found — they didn't plan for that. Did you find any 'surprise' resources?
Mr. Mason said they built the fort 'using only things you found.' How is your structure similar?
What was the most resourceful thing your team did?

beforeClass.en: Put a tray on each team's table with craft sticks, index cards, string, paper clips, binder clips, rubber bands and a few tape strips. Write what is in the tray on an index card; that is the budget card. Have a ruler ready for the test.
beforeClass.es: Put a tray on each team's table with craft sticks, index cards, string, paper clips, binder clips, rubber bands and a few tape strips. Write what is in the tray on an index card; that is the budget card. Have a ruler ready for the test.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Test Phase, check only standing and height, and skip the roof. Short: in Debrief, give each team two minutes to change one thing so the build matches the blueprint better.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Test Phase, check only standing and height, and skip the roof. Short: in Debrief, give each team two minutes to change one thing so the build matches the blueprint better.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

sayThis.en: "Four jobs, and they're real. Architect decides. Builder builds. Inspector checks the build against the plan. Materials Manager tracks what gets used. If you're not the Builder, you're not touching the materials."
sayThis.es: "Four jobs, and they're real. Architect decides. Builder builds. Inspector checks the build against the plan. Materials Manager tracks what gets used. If you're not the Builder, you're not touching the materials."

doneWhen.en: Every team member is holding a role card and one member of each team has said their job out loud.
doneWhen.es: Every team member is holding a role card and one member of each team has said their job out loud.

watchFor.en: Everyone wanting Builder. Assign rather than let them choose, and say why.
watchFor.es: Everyone wanting Builder. Assign rather than let them choose, and say why.

description.en: Distribute role cards (one index card per role, written ahead). Each person reads their role: - **Architect:** draws the blueprint, makes final decisions on design - **Builder:** main hands on materials - **Quality Inspector:** checks that the structure matches the blueprint; flags problems - **Materials Manager:** tracks what materials are used; ensures nothing is wasted
description.es: Distribute role cards (one index card per role, written ahead). Each person reads their role: - **Architect:** draws the blueprint, makes final decisions on design - **Builder:** main hands on materials - **Quality Inspector:** checks that the structure matches the blueprint; flags problems - **Materials Manager:** tracks what materials are used; ensures nothing is wasted

sayThis.en: "Draw it before you build it. Materials Manager, list exactly what goes where. Nobody touches a thing until every name is on that blueprint."
sayThis.es: "Draw it before you build it. Materials Manager, list exactly what goes where. Nobody touches a thing until every name is on that blueprint."

doneWhen.en: Every blueprint is drawn, listed and signed by all four.
doneWhen.es: Every blueprint is drawn, listed and signed by all four.

watchFor.en: Teams building while drawing. Stop them. This rule is the whole lesson.
watchFor.es: Teams building while drawing. Stop them. This rule is the whole lesson.

description.en: Architect draws blueprint with team input. Materials Manager lists exactly which materials will be used for which part. Blueprint must be signed by all team members before building begins.
description.es: Architect draws blueprint with team input. Materials Manager lists exactly which materials will be used for which part. Blueprint must be signed by all team members before building begins.

sayThis.en: "Build the plan. Inspector — if it stops matching, call a deviation check. Then your team decides. Change the build, or change the plan. Either one's fine. Doing neither isn't."
sayThis.es: "Build the plan. Inspector — if it stops matching, call a deviation check. Then your team decides. Change the build, or change the plan. Either one's fine. Doing neither isn't."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a standing structure and a deviation check marked on their blueprint.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a standing structure and a deviation check marked on their blueprint.

watchFor.en: Inspectors going quiet because calling it feels like telling tales. Back them publicly the first time it happens.
watchFor.es: Inspectors going quiet because calling it feels like telling tales. Back them publicly the first time it happens.

description.en: Build according to blueprint. Quality Inspector calls "deviation check" if the build strays from the plan — team must discuss whether to change the plan or change the build.
description.es: Build according to blueprint. Quality Inspector calls "deviation check" if the build strays from the plan — team must discuss whether to change the plan or change the build.

sayThis.en: "Mr. Mason's rule. If you spot something in this room that isn't in your tray, you can use it — but only if you can tell me why it's better than what you've already got."
sayThis.es: "Mr. Mason's rule. If you spot something in this room that isn't in your tray, you can use it — but only if you can tell me why it's better than what you've already got."

doneWhen.en: At least one team has justified a found item to you.
doneWhen.es: At least one team has justified a found item to you.

watchFor.en: Grabbing first, justifying after. Make them say it out loud before it goes near the build.
watchFor.es: Grabbing first, justifying after. Make them say it out loud before it goes near the build.

description.en: At the midpoint, teacher introduces: "Mr. Mason's Rule — if you find something in the room that isn't on your materials budget, you may use it IF you can justify why it's a better choice than something you have." Teams look around — what do they see? (Rubber bands? Paper clips? A book as a weight?)
description.es: At the midpoint, teacher introduces: "Mr. Mason's Rule — if you find something in the room that isn't on your materials budget, you may use it IF you can justify why it's a better choice than something you have." Teams look around — what do they see? (Rubber bands? Paper clips? A book as a weight?)

sayThis.en: "Three tests. Stands for fifteen seconds. Has a roof. Taller than eight inches. I'm counting out loud, and it goes on the chart either way."
sayThis.es: "Three tests. Stands for fifteen seconds. Has a roof. Taller than eight inches. I'm counting out loud, and it goes on the chart either way."

doneWhen.en: Every structure is tested and every result is on the chart.
doneWhen.es: Every structure is tested and every result is on the chart.

watchFor.en: Hands hovering to steady it. Hands off, or it doesn't count.
watchFor.es: Hands hovering to steady it. Hands off, or it doesn't count.

description.en: All structures tested: must stand 15 seconds, must have a roof element, must be taller than 8 inches. Measure. Record on class chart.
description.es: All structures tested: must stand 15 seconds, must have a roof element, must be taller than 8 inches. Measure. Record on class chart.

sayThis.en: "Move one seat over. Inspect their fort against their blueprint — not against what you would have done. Two things on the slip. One place it matches, one place it doesn't." Then: "Four minutes. Fix the build or change the plan. Tell me which one you picked."
sayThis.es: "Move one seat over. Inspect their fort against their blueprint — not against what you would have done. Two things on the slip. One place it matches, one place it doesn't." Then: "Four minutes. Fix the build or change the plan. Tell me which one you picked."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a slip and has written which they chose on their blueprint.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a slip and has written which they chose on their blueprint.

watchFor.en: Inspections turning into criticism of the build quality. Pull it back to the blueprint every time.
watchFor.es: Inspections turning into criticism of the build quality. Pull it back to the blueprint every time.

description.en: Teams rotate one seat over and inspect another team's fort against that team's own blueprint. The visiting Quality Inspector writes two findings on a scrap-paper inspection slip: one place the build matches the plan, one place it does not. Slips go back to the owners. Each team then gets four minutes to either fix the build or amend the blueprint — and must say which they chose and why. Ask whether changing the plan is cheating. Tier 1 (K-1): the inspector says the two findings out loud instead of writing them.
description.es: Teams rotate one seat over and inspect another team's fort against that team's own blueprint. The visiting Quality Inspector writes two findings on a scrap-paper inspection slip: one place the build matches the plan, one place it does not. Slips go back to the owners. Each team then gets four minutes to either fix the build or amend the blueprint — and must say which they chose and why. Ask whether changing the plan is cheating. Tier 1 (K-1): the inspector says the two findings out loud instead of writing them.

sayThis.en: "Did you use everything in your tray? Did anybody find something they never planned for? And the real one — is changing your plan cheating?"
sayThis.es: "Did you use everything in your tray? Did anybody find something they never planned for? And the real one — is changing your plan cheating?"

doneWhen.en: At least two students have given a reason out loud.
doneWhen.es: At least two students have given a reason out loud.

watchFor.en: Everyone saying changing the plan is fine. Push the other way once: when would it be cheating?
watchFor.es: Everyone saying changing the plan is fine. Push the other way once: when would it be cheating?

description.en: "Did you use your full materials budget? Did anyone find something they didn't plan for? What was the most resourceful moment?"
description.es: "Did you use your full materials budget? Did anyone find something they didn't plan for? What was the most resourceful moment?"

discussionQuestions: Your blueprint was the plan. Your materials budget was your financial constraint. How did it feel to work within limits?
If you could have bought anything for $5 to improve your structure, what would you buy? Did you really need it?
Ellis figured out the best angles. Riley arranged branches in patterns. Layla directed. Benny carried. In your team, who did what naturally?
Layla found an old blanket — a found resource that wasn't in the plan. What found resource did you discover mid-build?
Mr. Mason didn't buy anything to help them build the fort. What did he bring? (Knowledge, rope, experience.) What's the value of that?
extensionIdeas: Upgrade challenge: teams must rebuild using ONLY found/recycled materials from home (no purchased supplies)
Design a blueprint for a space in school that needs improvement — present it to the principal or custodial staff
Research: famous struct

beforeClass.en: Sort materials into one tray per team before the lesson. Decide where structures will be tested and measured, and put the class chart up. Check you have something to measure with.
beforeClass.es: Sort materials into one tray per team before the lesson. Decide where structures will be tested and measured, and put the class chart up. Check you have something to measure with.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: drop the found-resource rule and keep the cross-inspection. Short: add a second build round where teams must make the structure two inches taller with nothing new.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: drop the found-resource rule and keep the cross-inspection. Short: add a second build round where teams must make the structure two inches taller with nothing new.

title.en: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge
title.es: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge

chapterTitle.es: La Caja de Recetas de Frances

description.en: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.
description.es: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

description.en: "Frances made bread for $2 that fed 12 people. A store muffin also costs $2 — but it feeds one person. Which is the better deal?" Establish: MORE food for the SAME price = better deal.
description.es: "Frances made bread for $2 that fed 12 people. A store muffin also costs $2 — but it feeds one person. Which is the better deal?" Establish: MORE food for the SAME price = better deal.

sayThis.en: "Frances's bread cost two dollars and fed twelve people. A muffin costs two dollars and feeds one. Same money. Which gives you more food?"
sayThis.es: "Frances's bread cost two dollars and fed twelve people. A muffin costs two dollars and feeds one. Same money. Which gives you more food?"

watchFor.en: Students picking the muffin because they like muffins. Ask which one feeds more people.
watchFor.es: Students picking the muffin because they like muffins. Ask which one feeds more people.

doneWhen.en: The class agrees that more food for the same price is the better deal.
doneWhen.es: The class agrees that more food for the same price is the better deal.

description.en: Teacher reads 3 scenarios; students circle "homemade" or "store-bought" as the better deal: - Homemade soup: $3 for 6 bowls = $0.50/bowl. Can soup: $1.50 per bowl. Which is cheaper? - Homemade cookies: $2 for 20 cookies. Store cookies: $4 for 20 cookies. Which costs less? - Homemade lemonade: 1 lemon ($0.50) + water + sugar ($0.25) = 4 glasses. Store lemonade: $1 per glass. Which costs less per glass? Tier 1 (K-1): do the cookie scenario with whole dollars; for soup and lemonade, just tell them the homemade price and ask which number is smaller.
description.es: Teacher reads 3 scenarios; students circle "homemade" or "store-bought" as the better deal: - Homemade soup: $3 for 6 bowls = $0.50/bowl. Can soup: $1.50 per bowl. Which is cheaper? - Homemade cookies: $2 for 20 cookies. Store cookies: $4 for 20 cookies. Which costs less? - Homemade lemonade: 1 lemon ($0.50) + water + sugar ($0.25) = 4 glasses. Store lemonade: $1 per glass. Which costs less per glass? Tier 1 (K-1): do the cookie scenario with whole dollars; for soup and lemonade, just tell them the homemade price and ask which number is smaller.

sayThis.en: "Listen to each one. Circle homemade or store — the one that costs less. Don't call it out."
sayThis.es: "Listen to each one. Circle homemade or store — the one that costs less. Don't call it out."

watchFor.en: Students circling the food they like, not the one that costs less. Read the two prices again, slowly.
watchFor.es: Students circling the food they like, not the one that costs less. Read the two prices again, slowly.

doneWhen.en: Every student has circled an answer in all three boxes.
doneWhen.es: Every student has circled an answer in all three boxes.

description.en: Go through answers. Discuss: "Was homemade always cheaper? Why might someone still buy from the store?"
description.es: Go through answers. Discuss: "Was homemade always cheaper? Why might someone still buy from the store?"

sayThis.en: "Hands up if you circled homemade. Now store. Was homemade cheaper every time? Why might someone still buy it at the store?"
sayThis.es: "Hands up if you circled homemade. Now store. Was homemade cheaper every time? Why might someone still buy it at the store?"

watchFor.en: Answers only about price. Ask what making it at home takes — time, dishes, knowing how.
watchFor.es: Answers only about price. Ask what making it at home takes — time, dishes, knowing how.

doneWhen.en: At least two reasons to buy from the store have been said out loud.
doneWhen.es: At least two reasons to buy from the store have been said out loud.

discussionQuestions: Frances's vegetables came from her garden — that made the bread cost less. What if you grew your own food?
"Even if homemade is cheaper, what does it cost that we didn't count?" (Time, effort)
Benny said this bread was better than store-bought AND cheaper. Do you think that's always true?

beforeClass.en: Have the three scenarios ready to read, with the prices written on the board. Each student folds a sheet of paper into three boxes and writes "homemade" and "store" in each box.
beforeClass.es: Have the three scenarios ready to read, with the prices written on the board. Each student folds a sheet of paper into three boxes and writes "homemade" and "store" in each box.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: read two scenarios instead of three and go straight to Reveal & Discussion. Short: in Reveal & Discussion, have students make up one more homemade-or-store question for the class.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: read two scenarios instead of three and go straight to Reveal & Discussion. Short: in Reveal & Discussion, have students make up one more homemade-or-store question for the class.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

description.en: Display the trail mix recipe. "Today you're Frances — figure out if homemade is worth it. First, estimate: do you think homemade trail mix costs MORE or LESS than $1.50 per serving?"
description.es: Display the trail mix recipe. "Today you're Frances — figure out if homemade is worth it. First, estimate: do you think homemade trail mix costs MORE or LESS than $1.50 per serving?"

sayThis.en: "Today you're Frances. Here's a trail mix recipe. At the store, one serving costs a dollar fifty. Guess: does homemade cost more or less? Write your guess."
sayThis.es: "Today you're Frances. Here's a trail mix recipe. At the store, one serving costs a dollar fifty. Guess: does homemade cost more or less? Write your guess."

watchFor.en: Students trying to add it all up now. Tell them it's only a guess; the math comes next.
watchFor.es: Students trying to add it all up now. Tell them it's only a guess; the math comes next.

doneWhen.en: Every student has written "more" or "less" on their sheet.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written "more" or "less" on their sheet.

description.en: Students fill in worksheet: write each ingredient, its cost, add them up for total batch cost. Tier 1 (K-1): count the ingredients and circle the one that costs the most.
description.es: Students fill in worksheet: write each ingredient, its cost, add them up for total batch cost. Tier 1 (K-1): count the ingredients and circle the one that costs the most.

sayThis.en: "Write each ingredient and its cost, one on each line. Then add them all up. That's what the whole batch costs."
sayThis.es: "Write each ingredient and its cost, one on each line. Then add them all up. That's what the whole batch costs."

watchFor.en: Adding 40 cents and 30 cents and getting 70 dollars. Have them line up the decimal points before adding.
watchFor.es: Adding 40 cents and 30 cents and getting 70 dollars. Have them line up the decimal points before adding.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows a batch total of $1.10.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows a batch total of $1.10.

description.en: "Our batch makes 4 servings. How much does each serving cost?" ($1.10 ÷ 4 = $0.275 ≈ $0.28 per serving.) Tier 1 (K-1): skip the division — tell them one serving costs about 28 cents and ask if that is more or less than a dollar.
description.es: "Our batch makes 4 servings. How much does each serving cost?" ($1.10 ÷ 4 = $0.275 ≈ $0.28 per serving.) Tier 1 (K-1): skip the division — tell them one serving costs about 28 cents and ask if that is more or less than a dollar.

sayThis.en: "The batch makes four servings. Split $1.10 into four equal parts. How much is one part?"
sayThis.es: "The batch makes four servings. Split $1.10 into four equal parts. How much is one part?"

watchFor.en: Students stuck at $0.275. Show them to round to the nearest cent: about 28 cents.
watchFor.es: Students stuck at $0.275. Show them to round to the nearest cent: about 28 cents.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows about $0.28 per serving.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows about $0.28 per serving.

description.en: Write: Homemade = $0.28/serving. Store-bought = $1.50/serving. "How much do you save per serving?" ($1.22) "If your family makes this once a week, how much do you save in a year?" Tier 1 (K-1): ask only which costs less, homemade or store-bought, and skip the yearly savings.
description.es: Write: Homemade = $0.28/serving. Store-bought = $1.50/serving. "How much do you save per serving?" ($1.22) "If your family makes this once a week, how much do you save in a year?" Tier 1 (K-1): ask only which costs less, homemade or store-bought, and skip the yearly savings.

sayThis.en: "Homemade is 28 cents. The store is a dollar fifty. How much do you save on one serving? Now — if your family makes it every week, how much is that in a year?"
sayThis.es: "Homemade is 28 cents. The store is a dollar fifty. How much do you save on one serving? Now — if your family makes it every week, how much is that in a year?"

watchFor.en: Students who don't know how many weeks are in a year. Write 52 on the board.
watchFor.es: Students who don't know how many weeks are in a year. Write 52 on the board.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows $1.22 saved per serving.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows $1.22 saved per serving.

description.en: "What does homemade cost that we didn't add up?" (Time, dishes, shopping for ingredients.)
description.es: "What does homemade cost that we didn't add up?" (Time, dishes, shopping for ingredients.)

sayThis.en: "Homemade saved money. What did it cost that we didn't add up?"
sayThis.es: "Homemade saved money. What did it cost that we didn't add up?"

watchFor.en: Silence. Ask who does the shopping and who washes the bowl.
watchFor.es: Silence. Ask who does the shopping and who washes the bowl.

doneWhen.en: Time and one other hidden cost have been named.
doneWhen.es: Time and one other hidden cost have been named.

discussionQuestions: Was your estimate right? Were you surprised by how much cheaper homemade is?
Riley asked Frances 'how much does this cost?' Why is that a smart question?
Is homemade always better? Can you think of when store-bought might actually be a better choice?
Frances's vegetables were free from the garden. What's something your family grows or gets for free that could lower a food cost?

beforeClass.en: Write the trail mix recipe on the board with prices: cereal $0.40, raisins $0.30, pretzels $0.25, sunflower seeds $0.15. That is $1.10 for 4 servings. Store-bought is $1.50 a serving.
beforeClass.es: Write the trail mix recipe on the board with prices: cereal $0.40, raisins $0.30, pretzels $0.25, sunflower seeds $0.15. That is $1.10 for 4 servings. Store-bought is $1.50 a serving.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Compare, skip the yearly savings question. Short: in Tradeoff Discussion, ask what would happen to the cost per serving if the batch made 8 servings instead of 4.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Compare, skip the yearly savings question. Short: in Tradeoff Discussion, ask what would happen to the cost per serving if the batch made 8 servings instead of 4.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

sayThis.en: "These are real grocery prices. You're going to design a recipe on paper — something a kid could actually make — and work out whether it's a good deal. Nothing gets cooked today. Circle three things on the list you'd use."
sayThis.es: "These are real grocery prices. You're going to design a recipe on paper — something a kid could actually make — and work out whether it's a good deal. Nothing gets cooked today. Circle three things on the list you'd use."

doneWhen.en: Every student has the price list with three items circled.
doneWhen.es: Every student has the price list with three items circled.

watchFor.en: Students expecting to eat. Say it once, clearly, at the start.
watchFor.es: Students expecting to eat. Say it once, clearly, at the start.

description.en: Review price list together. "These are real approximate grocery costs. You're going to design a simple recipe — something K-4 could actually make at home — and figure out whether it's a good deal."
description.es: Review price list together. "These are real approximate grocery costs. You're going to design a simple recipe — something K-4 could actually make at home — and figure out whether it's a good deal."

sayThis.en: "Three to six ingredients, all off the list. It has to be real — something you'd actually eat. Write the amounts, not just the names."
sayThis.es: "Three to six ingredients, all off the list. It has to be real — something you'd actually eat. Write the amounts, not just the names."

doneWhen.en: Every recipe has between three and six ingredients with amounts.
doneWhen.es: Every recipe has between three and six ingredients with amounts.

watchFor.en: Recipes with one ingredient, or twenty. Hold the range.
watchFor.es: Recipes with one ingredient, or twenty. Hold the range.

description.en: Each student designs a simple recipe (3-6 ingredients from the list). Must be something real (a snack, simple breakfast, lunch item). List all ingredients and amounts.
description.es: Each student designs a simple recipe (3-6 ingredients from the list). Must be something real (a snack, simple breakfast, lunch item). List all ingredients and amounts.

sayThis.en: "Cost for each line, then add it up. Now the harder bit — how many servings does that actually make? Guess honestly."
sayThis.es: "Cost for each line, then add it up. Now the harder bit — how many servings does that actually make? Guess honestly."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a batch total and a serving count.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a batch total and a serving count.

watchFor.en: Pricing a whole bag when the recipe uses a spoonful. Ask how much of it they actually used.
watchFor.es: Pricing a whole bag when the recipe uses a spoonful. Ask how much of it they actually used.

description.en: Fill in cost for each ingredient, add for batch total. Estimate how many servings the recipe makes. Tier 1 (K-1): count the ingredients and the servings, and add up the costs together as a class.
description.es: Fill in cost for each ingredient, add for batch total. Estimate how many servings the recipe makes. Tier 1 (K-1): count the ingredients and the servings, and add up the costs together as a class.

sayThis.en: "Total divided by servings. Write it big. That's the number that matters."
sayThis.es: "Total divided by servings. Write it big. That's the number that matters."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a cost per serving written clearly.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a cost per serving written clearly.

watchFor.en: Division errors that make snacks cost eleven dollars. Get a partner to check anything that looks strange.
watchFor.es: Division errors that make snacks cost eleven dollars. Get a partner to check anything that looks strange.

description.en: Divide total cost by number of servings. Write it clearly. Tier 1 (K-1): no division — work out the cost per serving together as a class.
description.es: Divide total cost by number of servings. Write it clearly. Tier 1 (K-1): no division — work out the cost per serving together as a class.

sayThis.en: "What does the store version cost? Work out what you save per serving. Then times it by fifty-two."
sayThis.es: "What does the store version cost? Work out what you save per serving. Then times it by fifty-two."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a saving per serving and a yearly figure.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a saving per serving and a yearly figure.

watchFor.en: Wild store prices. Anchor them with two real examples.
watchFor.es: Wild store prices. Anchor them with two real examples.

description.en: What would the store equivalent cost? (Teacher provides examples or students estimate.) Calculate the savings per serving. Calculate the annual savings if made weekly. Tier 1 (K-1): circle which costs less, homemade or store, and skip the yearly figure.
description.es: What would the store equivalent cost? (Teacher provides examples or students estimate.) Calculate the savings per serving. Calculate the annual savings if made weekly. Tier 1 (K-1): circle which costs less, homemade or store, and skip the yearly figure.

sayThis.en: "New rule. Your recipe has to come in under the target now. Swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings. Redo the math. Your partner checks it."
sayThis.es: "New rule. Your recipe has to come in under the target now. Swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings. Redo the math. Your partner checks it."

doneWhen.en: Every student is under the target and a partner has initialed the new math.
doneWhen.es: Every student is under the target and a partner has initialed the new math.

watchFor.en: Stretching servings to twenty to hit the number. Ask whether that serving is still a real portion.
watchFor.es: Stretching servings to twenty to hit the number. Ask whether that serving is still a real portion.

description.en: Teacher names a target: your recipe now has to come in under a set cost per serving. Students redesign on paper — swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings — and recalculate. Nothing is cooked or brought in; this is all arithmetic on the price list. Partners check each other's new math. Ask what the recipe lost when it got cheaper, and whether it was worth the saving. Tier 1 (K-1): swap one ingredient for a cheaper one on the list and say which recipe costs less now.
description.es: Teacher names a target: your recipe now has to come in under a set cost per serving. Students redesign on paper — swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings — and recalculate. Nothing is cooked or brought in; this is all arithmetic on the price list. Partners check each other's new math. Ask what the recipe lost when it got cheaper, and whether it was worth the saving. Tier 1 (K-1): swap one ingredient for a cheaper one on the list and say which recipe costs less now.

sayThis.en: "One sentence. Mine costs this per serving, the store costs that, I save this, and in a year that's this. Then tell us what your recipe lost when it got cheaper."
sayThis.es: "One sentence. Mine costs this per serving, the store costs that, I save this, and in a year that's this. Then tell us what your recipe lost when it got cheaper."

doneWhen.en: Every student has presented and their trade-off is written on their sheet.
doneWhen.es: Every student has presented and their trade-off is written on their sheet.

watchFor.en: Presentations that skip the last part. That's the interesting half.
watchFor.es: Presentations that skip the last part. That's the interesting half.

description.en: Each student (or pair) presents their recipe in one sentence: "My [recipe] costs $[X] per serving. The store version costs $[Y]. I save $[Z] per serving. In a year, that's $[A]."
description.es: Each student (or pair) presents their recipe in one sentence: "My [recipe] costs $[X] per serving. The store version costs $[Y]. I save $[Z] per serving. In a year, that's $[A]."

discussionQuestions: Did any recipe surprise you — either cheaper or more expensive than you expected?
Frances used vegetables from her garden (free). If you grew one ingredient, how does that change your math?
Benny said the bread was better than store-bought. Is 'better' part of the math? (Satisfaction has value too.)
What's the tradeoff for the recipe you made cheaper in the cut-the-cost round? Is it always worth it?
What's one thing your family makes at home that saves money? Do you know how much it saves?
extensionIdeas: Grocery store field trip or virtual grocery tour: find the cheapest version of 5 items on the price list
Create a "Class Cookbook" of the cheapest recipes designed in this activity
Research: what percentage of American food spending is on restaurants vs. groceries? What's the math behind eating at home?

beforeClass.en: Print the price list, or write it on the board and have students copy it onto their sheet before step 1; every student needs one in front of them. Pick your target cost per serving for step 6 now, based on what the list makes possible. No food is brought in or made — this is arithmetic.
beforeClass.es: Print the price list, or write it on the board and have students copy it onto their sheet before step 1; every student needs one in front of them. Pick your target cost per serving for step 6 now, based on what the list makes possible. No food is brought in or made — this is arithmetic.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the store comparison and go straight from cost-per-serving to the cut-the-cost round. Short: add a second target that's harder, and see what breaks.

description.en: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). They diagnose the problem, decide on a repair approach, fix it, and then calculate: what would it cost to replace this vs. repair it? The activity builds both hands-on competence and a repair-vs-replace decision-making habit.
description.es: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). materials: Plain paper — 60 sheets, teacher pre-tears the damaged items

description.es: Teacher holds up a new index card. "A pack of index cards costs $3 for 100 cards — about 3 cents each. How much did your repair cost?" (Almost nothing — just a piece of tape.) sayThis.es: "A new card costs about three cents. Your fix cost one piece of tape. Which cost less — fixing or buying new? What did you save?"

watchFor.en: Students saying fixing saved nothing because a card is cheap. Ask what they would save if it were a book.
watchFor.es: Students saying fixing saved nothing because a card is cheap. Ask what they would save if it were a book.

sayThis.es: "Four broken things. No tools yet. On the back of each one, write or draw what's wrong: torn, wrinkled, cut or bent."

doneWhen.es: Every student has tried a repair on all four items.

Tier 1 (K-1): for each item, circle whether fixing or replacing costs less instead of writing dollar amounts.
description.es: For each item, complete the chart: | Item | What I used to fix it | Cost to fix | Cost to replace | Money saved | Teacher provides replacement costs: index card = $0.03, book = $5-15, frame = $10-20. sayThis.es: "Fill in one row for each item. What did you use? What did the fix cost? What would a new one cost? How much did you save?"

watchFor.es: Leaving the cost to fix blank because tape feels free. Tell them to write a few cents.

watchFor.es: Running over. Take two quick answers and stop.

doneWhen.es: Two students have answered.

discussionQuestions: Mr. Mason fixed Ellis's torn book cover by showing Ellis how to tape it himself. Why did he teach Ellis instead of just doing it?

watchFor.es: Hands on the tape already. Take the tape off the desks for this step.

description.en: Before touching any tool, students must write a diagnosis for all 4 items: "What is broken? How did it break? What's the best tool to fix it?" Establish: Mr. Mason always diagnosed before reaching for a tool.
description.es: Before touching any tool, students must write a diagnosis for all 4 items: "What is broken? How did it break? What's the best tool to fix it?" Establish: Mr. Mason always diagnosed before reaching for a tool.

sayThis.en: "Your two easy ones first. Do it the way you wrote it down. If your diagnosis was wrong, cross it out and write what it actually was."
sayThis.es: "Your two easy ones first. Do it the way you wrote it down. If your diagnosis was wrong, cross it out and write what it actually was."

doneWhen.en: Every student has two items in front of them with a repair on each.
doneWhen.es: Every student has two items in front of them with a repair on each.

watchFor.es: Tape over everything. Inspectors should be saying things like "that overlap will make it worse".

description.es: Students fix their 2 easiest items. Two or three students picked as Quality Inspectors review 3-4 students' work mid-round and give one piece of feedback: "The tape is overlapping the edge — that would make it worse."

sayThis.en: "The two hard ones. You can combine tools now — glue and tape and a paper patch all together if that's what it takes."
sayThis.es: "The two hard ones. You can combine tools now — glue and tape and a paper patch all together if that's what it takes."

doneWhen.en: All four items are in front of every student with a repair attempted on each.
doneWhen.es: All four items are in front of every student with a repair attempted on each.

watchFor.en: Giving up early. Ask what they'd try if they had one more idea.
watchFor.es: Giving up early. Ask what they'd try if they had one more idea.

description.en: Fix the 2 more difficult items. Students may combine tools (glue + tape + scrap paper patch).
description.es: Fix the 2 more difficult items. Students may combine tools (glue + tape + scrap paper patch).

sayThis.en: "Fill in all four. Cost to fix. Cost to replace. What you saved. Even the ones that failed — a failed repair still cost you the tape."
sayThis.es: "Fill in all four. Cost to fix. Cost to replace. What you saved. Even the ones that failed — a failed repair still cost you the tape."

doneWhen.en: All four rows are filled for every student, failures included.
doneWhen.es: All four rows are filled for every student, failures included.

watchFor.en: Blank rows for failures. Those rows matter most.
watchFor.es: Blank rows for failures. Those rows matter most.

description.en: Fill in full worksheet for all 4 items. Calculate total cost to fix vs. total replacement cost vs. total savings. description.es: Fill in full worksheet for all 4 items. Calculate total cost to fix vs. total replacement cost vs. total savings. Students draw the report on plain paper and note about how many minutes each repair took. Tier 1 (K-1): for each item, circle fix or replace to show which costs less, and skip the totals.

sayThis.en: "Repairs cost time, not just tape. How long did each one take? Pick an hourly rate for yourself. Now work out what each repair really cost — materials plus your time. Circle every one that cost more than just buying a new one."
sayThis.es: "Repairs cost time, not just tape. How long did each one take? Pick an hourly rate for yourself. Now work out what each repair really cost — materials plus your time. Circle every one that cost more than just buying a new one."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a real cost per repair and at least one circle on their sheet.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a real cost per repair and at least one circle on their sheet.

watchFor.en: Rates of a hundred dollars an hour. Ask what somebody who does this all day would actually earn.
watchFor.es: Rates of a hundred dollars an hour. Ask what somebody who does this all day would actually earn.

description.en: Repairs cost time, not just tape. Students time-stamp each of their four repairs from their report, pick an hourly rate for their own labor, and work out what each repair really cost — materials plus time. Then compare that figure to the replacement cost they already wrote down. Circle every repair that cost more than replacing it. Ask why a real repair shop would still take that job. Tier 1 (K-1): skip the hourly rate — ask which repair took the longest and whether it was worth that time.
description.es: Repairs cost time, not just tape. Students time-stamp each of their four repairs from their report, pick an hourly rate for their own labor, and work out what each repair really cost — materials plus time. Tier 1 (K-1): skip the hourly rate — ask which repair took the longest and whether it was worth that time.

sayThis.es: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it, but it'll never be as strong. A new one is fifteen dollars, and you've got fifteen dollars. Fix it or replace it?"

doneWhen.es: Both sides have been argued by students, not by you.

watchFor.es: The room agreeing too fast. Take the unpopular side yourself.

description.es: Teacher poses: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it but it will never be as strong. A new one costs $15. You have $15 saved. Fix or replace? Why?" Class debates. No right answer — unpack reasoning.

sayThis.es: "Who fixed all four? Who's got one they couldn't save? Hold it up. What would Mr. Mason say about that one?"

doneWhen.es: The tally is on the board and at least one student has held up an item they couldn't fix.

watchFor.es: Embarrassment about failures. Name your own failed repair first.

discussionQuestions: Mr. Mason said 'rushing can ruin the fix.' Did you rush any repairs? What happened?
