description.es: Count resources on the "Free/Borrow" side. "If you used these instead of buying, how much money could you save in a week? A month?" Tier 1 (K-1): count the Free/Borrow cards and name one thing you would not have to buy.

sayThis.en: "Let's count the Free and Borrow cards. If you used these instead of buying, how much could you save in a week?"
sayThis.es: "Let's count the Free and Borrow cards. If you used these instead of buying, how much could you save in a week?"

watchFor.en: Guesses like a million dollars. Ask what one library book would cost at a store.
watchFor.es: Guesses like a million dollars. Ask what one library book would cost at a store.

doneWhen.en: The count is on the board and one savings guess has a reason.
doneWhen.es: The count is on the board and one savings guess has a reason.

discussionQuestions: Was there anything on the 'Must Buy' list that you could BORROW instead?
Miss Chen said you can borrow craft kits from the library. Did that surprise you? What else might the library have that you didn't know about?
Why do parks and libraries exist? Who decided to make them free?
If you had a library card and used it every week, how much could you save in a year?

beforeClass.en: Label three sheets of chart paper Free, Borrow and Must Buy, and tape them where students can reach. Draw the school in the middle of a fourth sheet for the map.
beforeClass.es: Label three sheets of chart paper Free, Borrow and Must Buy, and tape them where students can reach. Draw the school in the middle of a fourth sheet for the map.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Our Neighborhood Resource Map, add only the five resources the class named most. Short: in Reflection, have each student put a sticky note on the map by a place they want to visit.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Our Neighborhood Resource Map, add only the five resources the class named most. Short: in Reflection, have each student put a sticky note on the map by a place they want to visit.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance

sayThis.en: "Six categories on the board. Three minutes. Fill in as many as you can. It only counts if it's free, or almost free, to use."
sayThis.es: "Six categories on the board. Three minutes. Fill in as many as you can. It only counts if it's free, or almost free, to use."

doneWhen.en: Every category has at least two entries on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every category has at least two entries on the board.

watchFor.en: Teams stuck on the first category. Give them one example and move them on.
watchFor.es: Teams stuck on the first category. Give them one example and move them on.

description.en: Teacher writes categories on board. Teams fill in as many as they can in 3 minutes: - Learn: library, tutoring, YouTube, teacher's knowledge - Play: parks, playgrounds, community pools, school gym after hours - Create: art classes, library craft kits, school art supplies - Stay healthy: school nurse, community health events - Get food: school lunch program, community gardens, food banks - Connect: community centers, faith organizations, neighborhood apps (Buy Nothing groups)
description.es: Teacher writes categories on board. Teams fill in as many as they can in 3 minutes: - Learn: library, tutoring, YouTube, teacher's knowledge - Play: parks, playgrounds, community pools, school gym after hours - Create: art classes, library craft kits, school art supplies - Stay healthy: school nurse, community health events - Get food: school lunch program, community gardens, food banks - Connect: community centers, faith organizations, neighborhood apps (Buy Nothing groups)

sayThis.en: "Pick three. For each one — who can use it, what you get, and what it costs. And if it's free, say who's paying for it. Somebody is."
sayThis.es: "Pick three. For each one — who can use it, what you get, and what it costs. And if it's free, say who's paying for it. Somebody is."

doneWhen.en: Every student has three completed profiles.
doneWhen.es: Every student has three completed profiles.

watchFor.en: Three profiles of the same kind of place. Make them span categories.
watchFor.es: Three profiles of the same kind of place. Make them span categories.

description.en: Each student picks 3 resources from the brainstorm and completes a profile for each (one index card each). They must think about: who can use it, what it provides, what it costs (if anything). Tier 1 (K-1): draw one resource on the card and say who can use it.
description.es: Each student picks 3 resources from the brainstorm and completes a profile for each (one index card each). They must think about: who can use it, what it provides, what it costs (if anything). Tier 1 (K-1): draw one resource on the card and say who can use it.

sayThis.en: "Onto the map. Location, a symbol, and the saves-you line — what would you be spending if this wasn't free?"
sayThis.es: "Onto the map. Location, a symbol, and the saves-you line — what would you be spending if this wasn't free?"

doneWhen.en: Every profile is on the map with a saves-you figure.
doneWhen.es: Every profile is on the map with a saves-you figure.

watchFor.en: Crowding at the map. Send teams up one at a time and give the others a job while they wait.
watchFor.es: Crowding at the map. Send teams up one at a time and give the others a job while they wait.

description.en: Teams pool their profiles and add resources to the community map. Each resource gets a location mark, a symbol, and a "saves you ___" note (estimate how much you'd spend on this if it didn't exist for free). Tier 1 (K-1): for the saves-you note, say "a little" or "a lot" instead of a dollar amount.
description.es: Teams pool their profiles and add resources to the community map. Each resource gets a location mark, a symbol, and a "saves you ___" note (estimate how much you'd spend on this if it didn't exist for free). Tier 1 (K-1): for the saves-you note, say "a little" or "a lot" instead of a dollar amount.

steps.title: "I Didn't Know This Existed!" Sticky Notes

sayThis.en: "One or two notes. Something you found out today that you've never used but want to. They all go in this corner."
sayThis.es: "One or two notes. Something you found out today that you've never used but want to. They all go in this corner."

doneWhen.en: Every student has at least one note in the corner.
doneWhen.es: Every student has at least one note in the corner.

watchFor.en: Copying a neighbor's note. Ask what they personally want to try.
watchFor.es: Copying a neighbor's note. Ask what they personally want to try.

description.en: Students add 1-2 sticky notes to the map marking something they discovered today that they've never used but want to try. These go in a specific corner of the map.
description.es: Students add 1-2 sticky notes to the map marking something they discovered today that they've never used but want to try. These go in a specific corner of the map.

sayThis.en: "Pick the one thing on this map nobody uses enough. Ninety seconds to sell it. What it is, who it's for, what it saves you. Then the class answers one question with hands — would you actually go?"
sayThis.es: "Pick the one thing on this map nobody uses enough. Ninety seconds to sell it. What it is, who it's for, what it saves you. Then the class answers one question with hands — would you actually go?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has pitched and every score is tallied on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every team has pitched and every score is tallied on the board.

watchFor.en: Pitches that describe instead of persuade. Remind them the question is would you go, not what is it.
watchFor.es: Pitches that describe instead of persuade. Remind them the question is would you go, not what is it.

description.en: Each team picks the one resource on the map they think is most underused and gets ninety seconds to sell it to the class — what it is, who it is for, what it saves you. The class scores each pitch by show of hands on one question only: would you actually go? Tally the scores on the board. Ask what made the winning pitch work, and why good things stay unused when nobody talks about them.
description.es: Each team picks the one resource on the map they think is most underused and gets ninety seconds to sell it to the class — what it is, who it is for, what it saves you. The class scores each pitch by show of hands on one question only: would you actually go? Tally the scores on the board. Ask what made the winning pitch work, and why good things stay unused when nobody talks about them.

sayThis.en: "Monday to Friday, using only what's on this map, spending nothing. Plan one family's week."
sayThis.es: "Monday to Friday, using only what's on this map, spending nothing. Plan one family's week."

doneWhen.en: One complete week has been presented to the class.
doneWhen.es: One complete week has been presented to the class.

watchFor.en: Five days of the same thing. Push for variety across the categories.
watchFor.es: Five days of the same thing. Push for variety across the categories.

description.en: As a class, design a hypothetical "Week of Free Activities" using only resources on the map. What would you do Monday through Friday that costs $0? Present one family's week.
description.es: As a class, design a hypothetical "Week of Free Activities" using only resources on the map. What would you do Monday through Friday that costs $0? Present one family's week.

discussionQuestions: The library uses tax money. You and your family already paid for it — are you getting your money's worth?
Ellis said 'how can everything be free?' Is it actually free, or is the cost hidden? Who pays and how?
What's the most valuable free resource in our neighborhood that most people don't use?
Could you live an entire month using only free community resources for entertainment and learning? What would you miss?
Mr. Mason says 'the best things in life are free.' Is that true? What's the limit of that idea?
extensionIdeas: Visit the local library and get library cards for anyone who doesn't have one
Assign: "Resource Hunt" — find one free or borrowable resource at home you've never used and report back
Research: what's in the "Library of Things" at your nearest library? (Many lend tools, instruments, games, even seeds!)

beforeClass.en: Write the six categories on the board before the lesson. Have two local examples ready for each; the brainstorm dies without seeds. Put the class map up where four teams can reach it at once.
beforeClass.es: Write the six categories on the board before the lesson. Have two local examples ready for each; the brainstorm dies without seeds. Put the class map up where four teams can reach it at once.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the sticky-note step and fold it into the pitch. Short: add a round where each team must find a resource nobody else listed.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the sticky-note step and fold it into the pitch. Short: add a round where each team must find a resource nobody else listed.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: One large shared map. Every student adds a resource profile to it.
items: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Markers — 1 set of 10, shared
Index cards — 100, for resource profiles
Sticky notes — 2 pads
Masking tape — 1 roll
Pencils — 20
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply
Timer — teacher phone, for the 90-second pitches

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: One large shared map. Tape and pencils are already in the room.
items: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Markers — 1 set of 10, shared
Index cards — 100, for resource profiles
Sticky notes — 2 pads
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply
Timer — teacher phone, for the 90-second pitches

focus: Name one free thing in your school or town
Add it to the class map (draw it)
Tell who can use it
Words: free, share, help, map
List and group free or low-cost resources
Mark them on a community map
Decide one need you can meet without money
Vocabulary: resource, free, borrow, community
Categorize resources and map them with a key
Build a borrow-vs-buy comparison
Explain how shared resources help everyone
Vocabulary: low-cost, access, public, compare
Audit community resources and rank them by value
Analyze which needs can be met without spending
Propose how to share resources more widely
Vocabulary: equity, access, allocation, cost-saving

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Draw a small picture next to each category or sorting word, like a book for Learn and a ball for Play.
Let students draw the resource on their card and label it with one word.
Give a sentence frame: "___ is free. It helps ___."

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Write the questions on the card ahead — who can use it, what you get, what it costs — so students fill in answers only.
Let a student say their resource to a partner who writes it down.
Give one clear job at the map, like drawing the symbols, instead of writing notes.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Estimate what one resource saves a family in a year and show the math.
Find something on the Must Buy side that could be borrowed and explain how.
Write a short guide entry for the most underused resource on the map.

description.en: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.
description.es: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

description.en: "The friends grew more vegetables than they could use. They gave them away. In return, neighbors gave them jam, cookies, and flowers. Today we're going to see what happens when everyone shares." Distribute 3 tokens per student.
description.es: "The friends grew more vegetables than they could use. They gave them away. In return, neighbors gave them jam, cookies, and flowers. Today we're going to see what happens when everyone shares." Distribute 3 tokens per student.

sayThis.en: "The friends grew lots of vegetables. They gave them away, and their neighbors gave them jam, cookies and flowers. Here are three tokens. Let's see what happens when we share."
sayThis.es: "The friends grew lots of vegetables. They gave them away, and their neighbors gave them jam, cookies and flowers. Here are three tokens. Let's see what happens when we share."

watchFor.en: Students playing with tokens right away. Tokens stay in the envelope until the round starts.
watchFor.es: Students playing with tokens right away. Tokens stay in the envelope until the round starts.

doneWhen.en: Every student has three tokens.
doneWhen.es: Every student has three tokens.

description.en: "Give ONE token to someone you think needs it or would appreciate it. You choose who. You may give to anyone in the room." Observe: every student gives one and (likely) receives one or more.
description.es: "Give ONE token to someone you think needs it or would appreciate it. You choose who. You may give to anyone in the room." Observe: every student gives one and (likely) receives one or more.

sayThis.en: "Give one token to someone. You pick who. Then sit back down."
sayThis.es: "Give one token to someone. You pick who. Then sit back down."

watchFor.en: Nobody giving to the quiet students. Don't fix it now — bring it up in Discussion.
watchFor.es: Nobody giving to the quiet students. Don't fix it now — bring it up in Discussion.

doneWhen.en: Every student has given one token and is back in their seat.
doneWhen.es: Every student has given one token and is back in their seat.

description.en: "Count your tokens. Did you end up with more, less, or the same as you started?" Class show of hands: more / same / fewer. Tally.
description.es: "Count your tokens. Did you end up with more, less, or the same as you started?" Class show of hands: more / same / fewer. Tally.

sayThis.en: "Count your tokens. Hands up if you have more than three. The same. Fewer."
sayThis.es: "Count your tokens. Hands up if you have more than three. The same. Fewer."

watchFor.en: Miscounting. Have them lay the tokens in a row and touch each one.
watchFor.es: Miscounting. Have them lay the tokens in a row and touch each one.

doneWhen.en: The more, same and fewer tally is on the board.
doneWhen.es: The more, same and fewer tally is on the board.

description.en: "What happened? Did giving away one token leave you with less? Why or why not?"
description.es: "What happened? Did giving away one token leave you with less? Why or why not?"

sayThis.en: "You gave one away. Did you end up with less? Why, or why not?"
sayThis.es: "You gave one away. Did you end up with less? Why, or why not?"

watchFor.en: Students with fewer feeling left out. Ask how it felt to give, not only to get.
watchFor.es: Students with fewer feeling left out. Ask how it felt to give, not only to get.

doneWhen.en: At least two students have said what happened to their tokens and why.
doneWhen.es: At least two students have said what happened to their tokens and why.

discussionQuestions: Frances said there's always enough when we share. Did today show that?
Did anyone give more than one token? Did they end up with less?
What if nobody gave any tokens — would that be better?

beforeClass.en: Cut construction paper into small squares, 3 per student, and put each set in an envelope or folded paper pocket. Every square counts as one token.
beforeClass.es: Cut construction paper into small squares, 3 per student, and put each set in an envelope or folded paper pocket. Every square counts as one token.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Count, skip the tally and just ask for hands. Short: run a second giving round before Discussion and count again.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Count, skip the tally and just ask for hands. Short: run a second giving round before Discussion and count again.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

description.en: Distribute 5 tokens. Students write "5" in the START row of their journal.
description.es: Distribute 5 tokens. Students write "5" in the START row of their journal.

sayThis.en: "Here are five tokens. Count them. Write 5 in the Start row of your journal."
sayThis.es: "Here are five tokens. Count them. Write 5 in the Start row of your journal."

watchFor.en: Journals with no rows. Point to the rows on the board and have them copy.
watchFor.es: Journals with no rows. Point to the rows on the board and have them copy.

doneWhen.en: Every journal says 5 in the Start row.
doneWhen.es: Every journal says 5 in the Start row.

description.en: "Give however many tokens you want to whoever you want. You don't have to give any. You don't have to give equally." After round: count tokens, record in journal row.
description.es: "Give however many tokens you want to whoever you want. You don't have to give any. You don't have to give equally." After round: count tokens, record in journal row.

sayThis.en: "Give as many as you want to anyone you want. You can give none. When I say stop, count and write your number in Round 1."
sayThis.es: "Give as many as you want to anyone you want. You can give none. When I say stop, count and write your number in Round 1."

watchFor.en: Students taking tokens instead of waiting to be given them. Only giving counts.
watchFor.es: Students taking tokens instead of waiting to be given them. Only giving counts.

doneWhen.en: Every journal has a Round 1 number.
doneWhen.es: Every journal has a Round 1 number.

description.en: "The friends grew more than they could use — they gave the excess. This round: give away any tokens you have above 3. Keep 3 for yourself, share the rest." After round: count and record.
description.es: "The friends grew more than they could use — they gave the excess. This round: give away any tokens you have above 3. Keep 3 for yourself, share the rest." After round: count and record.

sayThis.en: "The friends had more than they could use, so they shared the extra. Keep three. Give away the rest. Then count and write."
sayThis.es: "The friends had more than they could use, so they shared the extra. Keep three. Give away the rest. Then count and write."

watchFor.en: Students with three or fewer thinking they have to give. They keep what they have.
watchFor.es: Students with three or fewer thinking they have to give. They keep what they have.

doneWhen.en: Every journal has a Round 2 number.
doneWhen.es: Every journal has a Round 2 number.

description.en: Teacher tallies: how many tokens does the class have total? Did the total go up, down, or stay the same? (It stays the same — conservation of tokens. Point this out. The distribution changed, not the total.)
description.es: Teacher tallies: how many tokens does the class have total? Did the total go up, down, or stay the same? (It stays the same — conservation of tokens. Point this out. The distribution changed, not the total.)

sayThis.en: "Let's add up every token in the room. Is it more, less, or the same as when we started?"
sayThis.es: "Let's add up every token in the room. Is it more, less, or the same as when we started?"

watchFor.en: Students expecting the total to grow. Write the starting total next to the new one.
watchFor.es: Students expecting the total to grow. Write the starting total next to the new one.

doneWhen.en: Both totals are on the board and the class can see they match.
doneWhen.es: Both totals are on the board and the class can see they match.

description.en: "What changed between Round 1 and Round 2? What does it mean to share only the 'excess'? The friends had 3 full baskets — more than enough. That's why sharing felt easy."
description.es: "What changed between Round 1 and Round 2? What does it mean to share only the 'excess'? The friends had 3 full baskets — more than enough. That's why sharing felt easy."

sayThis.en: "What was different in Round 2? The friends had three full baskets — more than enough. Why did that make sharing easy?"
sayThis.es: "What was different in Round 2? The friends had three full baskets — more than enough. Why did that make sharing easy?"

watchFor.en: Students saying sharing made more tokens. Point back to the two totals on the board.
watchFor.es: Students saying sharing made more tokens. Point back to the two totals on the board.

doneWhen.en: At least two students have said what changed between the rounds.
doneWhen.es: At least two students have said what changed between the rounds.

discussionQuestions: Why is it easier to share when you have MORE than enough?
Frances said 'sharing creates abundance.' What does that mean if the total number of tokens didn't change?
What's the difference between giving because you have extra vs. giving when you're barely getting by?
The seeds the friends planted in Frances's garden (Chapter 2) grew into enough to share. What was the 'investment' that made that possible?

beforeClass.en: Cut construction paper into squares, 5 per student, in envelopes. Draw the journal on the board for students to copy on plain paper: three rows labeled Start, Round 1 and Round 2.
beforeClass.es: Cut construction paper into squares, 5 per student, in envelopes. Draw the journal on the board for students to copy on plain paper: three rows labeled Start, Round 1 and Round 2.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Discussion, ask only the first question. Short: after Count Class Total, run a quick round where everyone gives one token, then count again.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Discussion, ask only the first question. Short: after Count Class Total, run a quick round where everyone gives one token, then count again.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

sayThis.en: "Back to chapter two. Riley planted seeds and got a whole garden. What did she put in? What came back? Today we do the same thing with tokens."
sayThis.es: "Back to chapter two. Riley planted seeds and got a whole garden. What did she put in? What came back? Today we do the same thing with tokens."

doneWhen.en: Every card names one thing invested and one thing returned.
doneWhen.es: Every card names one thing invested and one thing returned.

watchFor.en: Answers only about flowers. Push toward time and patience as the investment.
watchFor.es: Answers only about flowers. Push toward time and patience as the investment.

description.en: Students complete their Investment Card. "Think back to Chapter 2. Riley planted flower seeds. The return was a whole garden. What did she invest? What did she get back?" Then: "Today's simulation shows the same cycle with tokens." The Investment Card is a half sheet of plain paper with two lines: What I put in. What I got back.
description.es: Students complete their Investment Card. "Think back to Chapter 2. Riley planted flower seeds. The return was a whole garden. What did she invest? What did she get back?" Then: "Today's simulation shows the same cycle with tokens." The Investment Card is a half sheet of plain paper with two lines: What I put in. What I got back.

sayThis.en: "Here are your tokens." Nothing else. Don't explain the amounts.
sayThis.es: "Here are your tokens." Nothing else. Don't explain the amounts.

doneWhen.en: Every student has their envelope and at least one person has said "that's not fair".
doneWhen.es: Every student has their envelope and at least one person has said "that's not fair".

watchFor.en: The moment someone notices. Let it happen. Don't answer the question yet.
watchFor.es: The moment someone notices. Let it happen. Don't answer the question yet.

description.en: Distribute tokens unevenly: some students get 15 (the "abundant harvest" students), some get 8, some get 5, some get 3 (the "scarce" students). Do NOT announce this is unequal — let them discover.
description.es: Distribute tokens unevenly: some students get 15 (the "abundant harvest" students), some get 8, some get 5, some get 3 (the "scarce" students). Do NOT announce this is unequal — let them discover.

sayThis.en: "Give to whoever you want, as much as you want. No rules at all. Write down every give in your journal."
sayThis.es: "Give to whoever you want, as much as you want. No rules at all. Write down every give in your journal."

doneWhen.en: Every journal has at least one entry, including "gave nothing".
doneWhen.es: Every journal has at least one entry, including "gave nothing".

watchFor.en: Who gives and who gets ignored. Note two names — you'll use them in the last step.
watchFor.es: Who gives and who gets ignored. Note two names — you'll use them in the last step.

description.en: Open giving round. "Give however you want to whoever you want. No rules." Record in journal. Observe who gives, who receives, whether inequity narrows or widens.
description.es: Open giving round. "Give however you want to whoever you want. No rules." Record in journal. Observe who gives, who receives, whether inequity narrows or widens.

sayThis.en: "New rule. Five tokens is what a person needs. Anything over five is extra, and the extra gets shared first."
sayThis.es: "New rule. Five tokens is what a person needs. Anything over five is extra, and the extra gets shared first."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written their new total in their journal.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written their new total in their journal.

watchFor.en: Hoarders hiding tokens. Don't police it — record it. It's data.
watchFor.es: Hoarders hiding tokens. Don't police it — record it. It's data.

description.en: "This round: everyone identifies their 'need' (a baseline of 5 tokens). Anyone with more than 5 shares the excess first." Record. Does inequity narrow?
description.es: "This round: everyone identifies their 'need' (a baseline of 5 tokens). Anyone with more than 5 shares the excess first." Record. Does inequity narrow?

sayThis.en: "Last rule. If somebody gives to you, you have to give to somebody. Doesn't have to be back to them. Watch what happens to the room."
sayThis.es: "Last rule. If somebody gives to you, you have to give to somebody. Doesn't have to be back to them. Watch what happens to the room."

doneWhen.en: At least one chain of three is drawn on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least one chain of three is drawn on the board.

watchFor.en: Chains forming. Point one out loud as it happens.
watchFor.es: Chains forming. Point one out loud as it happens.

description.en: "This round: if someone gives to you, you must give something back — not necessarily to them, but to someone." Record. Observe the chain-reaction effect.
description.es: "This round: if someone gives to you, you must give something back — not necessarily to them, but to someone." Record. Observe the chain-reaction effect.

sayThis.en: "Three columns. After each round, the highest number in the room and the lowest. Subtract. That's the gap. Copy the three numbers down and draw the line."
sayThis.es: "Three columns. After each round, the highest number in the room and the lowest. Subtract. That's the gap. Copy the three numbers down and draw the line."

doneWhen.en: Every student has drawn the line and the winning rule is circled on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every student has drawn the line and the winning rule is circled on the board.

watchFor.en: Students reading a falling line as everyone getting poorer. Ask what happened to the class total.
watchFor.es: Students reading a falling line as everyone getting poorer. Ask what happened to the class total.

description.en: Three columns on the board: after Round 1, after Round 2, after Round 3. For each, record the highest token count in the room and the lowest, and subtract to get the gap. Students copy the three numbers and draw the line on scrap paper. The shape of that line is the whole lesson. Ask which rule closed the gap fastest, whether closing it made the room better off in total, and what happened to the people who started with the most. Tier 1 (K-1): the teacher does the subtraction on the board; students say whether the gap got bigger or smaller.
description.es: Three columns on the board: after Round 1, after Round 2, after Round 3. For each, record the highest token count in the room and the lowest, and subtract to get the gap. Students copy the three numbers and draw the line on scrap paper. The shape of that line is the whole lesson. Ask which rule closed the gap fastest, whether closing it made the room better off in total, and what happened to the people who started with the most. Tier 1 (K-1): the teacher does the subtraction on the board; students say whether the gap got bigger or smaller.

sayThis.en: "Which round felt best? Not which was fairest — which felt best. Were they the same round? And what happened to the people who started with the most?"
sayThis.es: "Which round felt best? Not which was fairest — which felt best. Were they the same round? And what happened to the people who started with the most?"

doneWhen.en: Both questions have been answered and the low-start students have spoken.
doneWhen.es: Both questions have been answered and the low-start students have spoken.

watchFor.en: The students who started with three. Ask them directly, last.
watchFor.es: The students who started with three. Ask them directly, last.

description.en: Compare all three rounds. "Which round felt best? Which reduced the gap between the most and least token-holders? Why?"
description.es: Compare all three rounds. "Which round felt best? Which reduced the gap between the most and least token-holders? Why?"

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, did the gap between the richest and poorest students get bigger or smaller? What about Round 3?
The friends grew Frances's seeds into food. The seeds cost nothing and came from nature. But the investment of TIME changed everything. What does that tell us?
Layla and her friends gave away vegetables. Neighbors gave back jam and cookies and flowers. Did they end up poorer?
Benny asked 'to who?' when they decided to share. How do you decide who to give to when you have extra?
The class as a whole had the same number of tokens the whole time. So what did 'abundance' actually mean?
extensionIdeas: Connect to real-world abundance: research community gardens, food banks, mutual aid networks — organizations built on the idea that sharing excess creates community resilience
Write Frances's speech from the episode: "You learned about investment and patience" — expand it into a 3-paragraph essay from the perspective of one of the friends
Compare: what would happen in a market economy where tokens could only be traded for equal value, not given? Run Round 4 with that rule and compare the result

beforeClass.en: Count the uneven token piles into envelopes in advance and don't label them. Decide now how you'll handle a student who refuses to give, because it's the most interesting thing that can happen.
beforeClass.es: Count the uneven token piles into envelopes in advance and don't label them. Decide now how you'll handle a student who refuses to give, because it's the most interesting thing that can happen.

runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut round three and graph two rounds instead of three. Short: add a fourth round where giving is anonymous.

focus: Start with a few tokens
Give one token in each round
Watch what happens to the group pile

Track your tokens through the giving rounds
Notice that the group total stays the same
Tell how it felt to give and receive

Record the group total each round
Explain why sharing changed who has tokens, not the total
Compare giving freely vs. holding back
Vocabulary: generosity, abundance, contribute, community
Model the group total across all rounds
Analyze how generosity creates abundance
Argue when giving benefits the whole group
Vocabulary: reciprocity, abundance, collective value, surplus

ell.label: English Language Learners

Let students use tally marks in the journal instead of words.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Let students line tokens up in a row to count them.
Draw the journal rows ahead of time so students only write numbers.
Pair with a partner who counts tokens with them after each round.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Predict the gap or the count before each round, then check the prediction.
Invent a new giving rule and explain what it would do to the gap.
Explain why the class total stays the same while each person's count changes.

title.en: My Season 1 Treasure Book & Exhibition Walk

description.en: Students create a personal "Season 1 Treasure Book" reflecting on what they've learned across the season. The book has four pages: a treasure they found, a skill they have, a savings goal, and a way they shared or gave. Books are then displayed in a class gallery walk — a miniature Treasure Exhibition. Optional: students receive their own "Junior Explorer" acknowledgment.

Focus on teamwork concept: "We work together and make more!"

description.en: Discuss: Have you or your family traveled? Where? How? Explain activity: create a pretend family travel trunk with items representing places or cultures. Review available materials.
description.es: Discuss: Have you or your family traveled? Where? How? Explain activity: create a pretend family travel trunk with items representing places or cultures. Review available materials.

description.en: Students decorate their box or container to look like a travel trunk. Add labels, drawings of destinations, or maps. Make it personal and creative.
description.es: Students decorate their box or container to look like a travel trunk. Add labels, drawings of destinations, or maps. Make it personal and creative.

description.en: Students plan what to put in their trunk: drawings of souvenirs, photos from home, items representing family heritage. List or sketch 3-5 items.
description.es: Students plan what to put in their trunk: drawings of souvenirs, photos from home, items representing family heritage. List or sketch 3-5 items.

description.en: Students create or gather items for their trunk: draw postcards, make pretend souvenirs, write travel journal entries. Fill trunk thoughtfully.
description.es: Students create or gather items for their trunk: draw postcards, make pretend souvenirs, write travel journal entries. Fill trunk thoughtfully.

description.en: Students share their travel trunks in small groups or gallery walk. Explain: Where would your family go? What's in your trunk and why? What does it tell about your family or heritage?
description.es: Students share their travel trunks in small groups or gallery walk. Explain: Where would your family go? What's in your trunk and why? What does it tell about your family or heritage?

discussionQuestions: Where does this item come from?
Why is it special to your family?
Did you have to buy it or is it something your family has always had?

Index cards or paper for item cards

description.es: Decorate paper bag as your "travel trunk." Draw or write family name, designs representing heritage

description.en: Create 3-5 item cards (one per card) - Each card includes: drawing of item, name of item, where it comes from, why it matters to your family - Items can be real objects, foods, traditions, places
description.es: Create 3-5 item cards (one per card) - Each card includes: drawing of item, name of item, where it comes from, why it matters to your family - Items can be real objects, foods, traditions, places

description.en: On classroom world map, students mark (with sticky dots or pins) where their items originate
description.es: On classroom world map, students mark (with sticky dots or pins) where their items originate

description.en: Groups of 3-4. Each student shares 1-2 items from their trunk.
description.es: Groups of 3-4. Each student shares 1-2 items from their trunk.

discussionQuestions: How many different countries/places are represented in our class?
What surprised you about someone else's trunk?
How are our trunks similar? How are they different?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Cultural Heritage Trunk with Presentation
materials: Shoebox or small box for each student (can be decorated box or plain)
Decorative materials (markers, fabric scraps, stickers, ribbon, paper)
String and pushpins for world map connections
Optional: actual items from home (if students bring them)

sayThis.en: "This box is your family's trunk. Your family name on it, and anything that says where you come from. Colors. Patterns. A flag. A food. A word in your language. All of it counts."
sayThis.es: "This box is your family's trunk. Your family name on it, and anything that says where you come from. Colors. Patterns. A flag. A food. A word in your language. All of it counts."

doneWhen.en: Every box has a family name and at least three decorations on it.
doneWhen.es: Every box has a family name and at least three decorations on it.

watchFor.en: The student who says they don't have a culture. Everyone does. Ask what their family eats on a birthday.
watchFor.es: The student who says they don't have a culture. Everyone does. Ask what their family eats on a birthday.

description.en: Decorate box as family "travel trunk" - Include family name, cultural symbols, colors representing heritage - Can include flag elements, traditional patterns, meaningful decorations
description.es: Decorate box as family "travel trunk" - Include family name, cultural symbols, colors representing heritage - Can include flag elements, traditional patterns, meaningful decorations

sayThis.en: "Three to five cards. What it is. Where it came from. How your family got it. Why it matters. Then two prices — what a shop would charge, and what it's worth to you. Priceless is allowed, but you have to finish the sentence."
sayThis.es: "Three to five cards. What it is. Where it came from. How your family got it. Why it matters. Then two prices — what a shop would charge, and what it's worth to you. Priceless is allowed, but you have to finish the sentence."

doneWhen.en: Every student has at least three cards with both price lines filled.
doneWhen.es: Every student has at least three cards with both price lines filled.

watchFor.en: Every card saying priceless with no reason under it. Make them write the because.
watchFor.es: Every card saying priceless with no reason under it. Make them write the because.

description.en: Create 3-5 detailed item cards including: - Name of item - Country/place of origin - How it came to family (bought on trip, inherited, traditional, homemade) - Why it's valuable (personal story, tradition, memory) - Estimated store price vs. personal value ("Priceless" is an option!) - Draw or describe each item
description.es: Create 3-5 detailed item cards including: - Name of item - Country/place of origin - How it came to family (bought on trip, inherited, traditional, homemade) - Why it's valuable (personal story, tradition, memory) - Estimated store price vs. personal value ("Priceless" is an option!) - Draw or describe each item

sayThis.en: "Pin your card where the thing came from. Then run string from there back to us. When we're finished, the map shows how far this one room reaches."
sayThis.es: "Pin your card where the thing came from. Then run string from there back to us. When we're finished, the map shows how far this one room reaches."

doneWhen.en: Every card is on the map with a string running back to the classroom.
doneWhen.es: Every card is on the map with a string running back to the classroom.

watchFor.en: Students who don't know the country. "Somewhere my grandmother lived" is a real answer and a real pin.
watchFor.es: Students who don't know the country. "Somewhere my grandmother lived" is a real answer and a real pin.

description.en: Each student places item card on world map at origin point - Use string to connect student's location to item origins - Visual web shows global connections
description.es: Each student places item card on world map at origin point - Use string to connect student's location to item origins - Visual web shows global connections

sayThis.en: "One or two things. What it is, where it's from, why it matters. Then the class gets one question."
sayThis.es: "One or two things. What it is, where it's from, why it matters. Then the class gets one question."

doneWhen.en: Every student has presented at least one item and taken one question.
doneWhen.es: Every student has presented at least one item and taken one question.

watchFor.en: Presentations running to three minutes. Time the first one out loud so the room hears the length.
watchFor.es: Presentations running to three minutes. Time the first one out loud so the room hears the length.

description.en: Students present 1-2 items to class - Explain: what it is, where it's from, why it matters - Class asks questions: "How did your family get this?" "What's your favorite thing about it?"
description.es: Students present 1-2 items to class - Explain: what it is, where it's from, why it matters - Class asks questions: "How did your family get this?" "What's your favorite thing about it?"

discussionQuestions: Look at our class map. How many countries are represented?
What's the farthest place any item came from?
Did anyone have items from the same place? What were they?
How did items travel from those places to here? (Trade routes, immigration, online shopping, family trips)
Is something worth more because of its story or its price?
What's the difference between buying a souvenir and inheriting a family treasure?
How does trade connect people around the world?
extensionIdeas: Invite family members to visit and share their heritage stories
Research trade routes connecting represented countries
Create class "Global Heritage Museum"
Write family interview: "Tell me about something important from your heritage"
Map how one item (like chocolate or spices) travels from origin to local store

beforeClass.en: Have ten family-story prompt cards ready for students who bring nothing from home. Nobody sits this one out because their family didn't send anything. Get the world map up and the string cut.
beforeClass.es: Have ten family-story prompt cards ready for students who bring nothing from home. Nobody sits this one out because their family didn't send anything. Get the world map up and the string cut.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: take presentations from volunteers only. Short: add a second string to the map — where would this item go next?
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: take presentations from volunteers only. Short: add a second string to the map — where would this item go next?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5 common spices in containers (cinnamon, pepper, oregano, garlic powder, vanilla)
Numbered containers (paper cups with lids or small jars)

description.en: Show variety of spices (or pictures). Discuss: What are spices? Where do they come from? How do people use them? Explain smell-and-guess game rules.
description.es: Show variety of spices (or pictures). Discuss: What are spices? Where do they come from? How do people use them? Explain smell-and-guess game rules.

description.en: Students smell different spices in containers (cinnamon, pepper, herbs). Try to identify each. Notice: sweet, spicy, strong, mild. Record observations with drawings or words.
description.es: Students smell different spices in containers (cinnamon, pepper, herbs). Try to identify each. Notice: sweet, spicy, strong, mild. Record observations with drawings or words.

description.en: Sort spices into categories students choose: by smell (strong/mild), by use (cooking/baking), by color, or by preference (like/don't like). Create sorting chart.
description.es: Sort spices into categories students choose: by smell (strong/mild), by use (cooking/baking), by color, or by preference (like/don't like). Create sorting chart.

description.en: Pretend spices are valuable trade goods. Students 'trade' spice cards with partners. Discuss: Why were spices valuable in history? Why did people trade them across long distances?
description.es: Pretend spices are valuable trade goods. Students 'trade' spice cards with partners. Discuss: Why were spices valuable in history? Why did people trade them across long distances?

description.en: Discuss: What surprised you about spices? Which was your favorite smell? How do spices add value to food? Where do spices in our kitchen come from?
description.es: Discuss: What surprised you about spices? Which was your favorite smell? How do spices add value to food? Where do spices in our kitchen come from?

discussionQuestions: Which spice smelled best to you?
If everyone wants cinnamon but there's only a little, what happens to its price?
Where do spices come from?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 6-8 spices in small containers or bags
Trading cards (each student gets 3 spice packets)
Optional: paper clips as trade tokens

description.en: Introduce spices from around the world. Discuss trade routes, how spices traveled, why they were valuable. Explain detective activity: smell, identify, sort, and trade spices.
description.es: Introduce spices from around the world. Discuss trade routes, how spices traveled, why they were valuable. Explain detective activity: smell, identify, sort, and trade spices.

description.en: Students smell spice samples and try to identify them. Use observation sheets to record: smell description, color, texture, guess what it is. Compare guesses with actual spice names.
description.es: Students smell spice samples and try to identify them. Use observation sheets to record: smell description, color, texture, guess what it is. Compare guesses with actual spice names.

description.en: Sort spices multiple ways: by origin (where they come from), by use (cooking vs baking), by intensity (mild to strong), by preference. Create detailed sorting charts or graphs.
description.es: Sort spices multiple ways: by origin (where they come from), by use (cooking vs baking), by intensity (mild to strong), by preference. Create detailed sorting charts or graphs.

description.en: Simulate spice trade: students receive spice cards and 'trade' to collect full sets. Discuss why certain spices were worth more. Learn about historical spice routes and economics of scarcity.
description.es: Simulate spice trade: students receive spice cards and 'trade' to collect full sets. Discuss why certain spices were worth more. Learn about historical spice routes and economics of scarcity.

description.en: Reflect on activity: What makes spices valuable? How does smell affect value? Why do people pay more for certain spices? Connect to modern grocery store prices. Discuss cultural importance of spices.
description.es: Reflect on activity: What makes spices valuable? How does smell affect value? Why do people pay more for certain spices? Connect to modern grocery store prices. Discuss cultural importance of spices.

discussionQuestions: Which spices were easiest to trade for? Why?
Which were hardest? Why?
How does rarity affect value?
How did you decide what to trade?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 10+ spice varieties (mix of common and rare)
Small bags or containers for samples
Paper clips as coins, about 200, collected back and reused
Market stall setup materials (signs, fabric, etc.)
Optional: Mortar and pestle for grinding demonstration

sayThis.en: "There was a time when a bag of pepper was worth more than the same weight in silver. People sailed for years to get it. Today it's three dollars at the shop. Today you work out what changed."
sayThis.es: "There was a time when a bag of pepper was worth more than the same weight in silver. People sailed for years to get it. Today it's three dollars at the shop. Today you work out what changed."

doneWhen.en: The route map is up and one reason spices were valuable is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: The route map is up and one reason spices were valuable is written on the board.

watchFor.en: Flat disbelief that a spice could be money. Stay with it. That disbelief is the hook.
watchFor.es: Flat disbelief that a spice could be money. Stay with it. That disbelief is the hook.

description.en: Discuss historical spice trade: ancient routes, why spices were valuable as gold, cultural significance across civilizations. Show map of spice routes. Explain extended spice detective investigation.
description.es: Discuss historical spice trade: ancient routes, why spices were valuable as gold, cultural significance across civilizations. Show map of spice routes. Explain extended spice detective investigation.

sayThis.en: "Smell only. Wave your hand over the jar towards your nose — don't put your face in it. Three words for each one: the color, the smell, and what it reminds you of. Nothing goes in a mouth today."
sayThis.es: "Smell only. Wave your hand over the jar towards your nose — don't put your face in it. Three words for each one: the color, the smell, and what it reminds you of. Nothing goes in a mouth today."

doneWhen.en: Every observation sheet has three words for every jar.
doneWhen.es: Every observation sheet has three words for every jar.

watchFor.en: Tasting. Say the rule before the jars come out, not after. Also the student who says everything smells the same — hand them cinnamon and pepper back to back.
watchFor.es: Tasting. Say the rule before the jars come out, not after. Also the student who says everything smells the same — hand them cinnamon and pepper back to back.

description.en: Students rotate through spice stations: smell, observe color/texture, describe the smell in words, record detailed observations. Use scientific observation sheets. Compare fresh vs dried versions where possible.
description.es: Students rotate through spice stations: smell, observe color/texture, describe the smell in words, record detailed observations. Use scientific observation sheets. Compare fresh vs dried versions where possible.

sayThis.en: "Sort them. Any way you like, but you have to defend it. Strong and mild. Sweet and sharp. Near and far. Cheap and dear. Then draw it so we can see your thinking."
sayThis.es: "Sort them. Any way you like, but you have to defend it. Strong and mild. Sweet and sharp. Near and far. Cheap and dear. Then draw it so we can see your thinking."

doneWhen.en: Every group's chart is drawn with every spice placed on it.
doneWhen.es: Every group's chart is drawn with every spice placed on it.

watchFor.en: Groups sorting one way and stopping. Ask for a second way of sorting the same jars.
watchFor.es: Groups sorting one way and stopping. Ask for a second way of sorting the same jars.

description.en: Students create complex classification systems: organize spices by multiple characteristics (origin, use, intensity, price, cultural significance). Create Venn diagrams or multi-category charts. Research where spices come from.
description.es: Students create complex classification systems: organize spices by multiple characteristics (origin, use, intensity, price, cultural significance). Create Venn diagrams or multi-category charts. Research where spices come from.

sayThis.en: "You're a merchant. Some of you are holding something everybody wants and nobody else has. Some of you have what everyone already has. Fill your order — and watch what your rare one is worth by the end."
sayThis.es: "You're a merchant. Some of you are holding something everybody wants and nobody else has. Some of you have what everyone already has. Fill your order — and watch what your rare one is worth by the end."

doneWhen.en: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.
doneWhen.es: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.

watchFor.en: Rare-spice holders trading them away at the same rate as common ones. Ask what something is worth when there's only one of it.
watchFor.es: Rare-spice holders trading them away at the same rate as common ones. Ask what something is worth when there's only one of it.

description.en: Extended trading simulation: students are merchants with different spices. Some spices are rare (high value), some common (low value). Trade to complete orders. Track profit. Discuss supply, demand, and scarcity.
description.es: Extended trading simulation: students are merchants with different spices. Some spices are rare (high value), some common (low value). Trade to complete orders. Track profit. Discuss supply, demand, and scarcity.

sayThis.en: "Pick a country. Find one spice that country cooks with nearly every day. Two facts and one dish. Then tell us."
sayThis.es: "Pick a country. Find one spice that country cooks with nearly every day. Two facts and one dish. Then tell us."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has reported a country, a spice and a dish.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has reported a country, a spice and a dish.

watchFor.en: Pairs reading a whole page aloud. Two facts and one dish. Hold them to it.
watchFor.es: Pairs reading a whole page aloud. Two facts and one dish. Hold them to it.

description.en: In pairs, students research how different cultures use specific spices: Indian curry, Mexican chili, Italian basil, Chinese five-spice. Present findings. Discuss how spices connect to cultural identity.
description.es: In pairs, students research how different cultures use specific spices: Indian curry, Mexican chili, Italian basil, Chinese five-spice. Present findings. Discuss how spices connect to cultural identity.

sayThis.en: "Rank them. Most valuable down to least. Not which you like — which you'd pay for. Then tell me why your number one is number one."
sayThis.es: "Rank them. Most valuable down to least. Not which you like — which you'd pay for. Then tell me why your number one is number one."

doneWhen.en: Every group has a written ranking with a reason on the top one.
doneWhen.es: Every group has a written ranking with a reason on the top one.

watchFor.en: Ranking by favorite smell. Push back once: would you hand over money for it?
watchFor.es: Ranking by favorite smell. Push back once: would you hand over money for it?

description.en: Synthesize learning: Why were spices worth traveling thousands of miles? How do spices connect cultures? What determines spice value today vs historically? Create spice value ranking and justify choices.
description.es: Synthesize learning: Why were spices worth traveling thousands of miles? How do spices connect cultures? What determines spice value today vs historically? Create spice value ranking and justify choices.

discussionQuestions: Which spices sold out first? Why?
What happened when a spice was rare and popular?
Was it easier to buy at fixed prices or negotiate? Why?
How did you decide what price to offer/accept?
Why did spices travel such long distances historically? (Profit!)
How does smell/appearance affect willingness to pay?
What's the relationship between scarcity and price?
extensionIdeas: Research Silk Road and spice trade routes
Calculate: If it costs $1 to buy pepper in India and you sell for $5 here, what's your profit?
Create spice blend recipes and cost them out
Make cinnamon ornaments or spice sachets (craft using actual spices)
Write persuasive ad for spice stall

beforeClass.en: Open the jars and check the smell is still there. Old spice smells of nothing and the whole lesson dies. One jar and one spoon per station. Nothing is tasted and nothing is eaten — check for allergies before the jars come out.
beforeClass.es: Open the jars and check the smell is still there. Old spice smells of nothing and the whole lesson dies. One jar and one spoon per station. Nothing is tasted and nothing is eaten — check for allergies before the jars come out.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: turn the cultural research into one whole-class list. Short: add a blind round — name it with your eyes shut.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: turn the cultural research into one whole-class list. Short: add a blind round — name it with your eyes shut.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5 desirable classroom items (stickers, pencils, bookmarks, small prizes)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($20 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Explain how auctions work: items for sale, people bid (offer price), highest bid wins. Show bidding paddle. Practice auction calls: 'Going once, going twice, sold!' Each bidder writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card.
description.es: Explain how auctions work: items for sale, people bid (offer price), highest bid wins. Show bidding paddle. Practice auction calls: 'Going once, going twice, sold!' Each bidder writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card.

description.en: Display classroom auction items (books, supplies, privileges like line leader). Students preview items and decide what they want most. Plan bidding strategy: save money for favorite item or spread out bids?
description.es: Display classroom auction items (books, supplies, privileges like line leader). Students preview items and decide what they want most. Plan bidding strategy: save money for favorite item or spread out bids?

description.en: Students create bidding paddles from scrap paper. Check the number on their budget card. Review auction rules: raise paddle to bid, teacher/auctioneer decides when sold, you cannot bid more than your card says. Practice raising paddles.
description.es: Students create bidding paddles from scrap paper. Check the number on their budget card. Review auction rules: raise paddle to bid, teacher/auctioneer decides when sold, you cannot bid more than your card says. Practice raising paddles.

description.en: Run the auction! Auctioneer presents each item. Students bid by raising paddles. Track winning bids on board. The highest bidder crosses out the number on their budget card, writes what is left, and receives the item.
description.es: Run the auction! Auctioneer presents each item. Students bid by raising paddles. Track winning bids on board. The highest bidder crosses out the number on their budget card, writes what is left, and receives the item.

description.en: Discuss: What sold for the most? Why? Did you get what you wanted? What happens when many people want the same thing? How is an auction different from a regular store?
description.es: Discuss: What sold for the most? Why? Did you get what you wanted? What happens when many people want the same thing? How is an auction different from a regular store?

discussionQuestions: What item sold for the most? Why?
Did you spend your money wisely?
What happens when lots of people want the same thing?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 10 auction items (mix of desirable and less popular)
Budget card for each student — they write $50 as the starting balance and subtract each winning bid

description.en: Each student writes $50 on a budget card as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase
description.es: Each student writes $50 on a budget card as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase

description.en: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet
description.es: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet

description.en: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"
description.es: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"

description.en: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items — mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending
description.es: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items — mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending

description.en: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess
description.es: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess

discussionQuestions: What was your strategy?
Did you run out of money before getting something you wanted?
What would you do differently next time?
How did competition affect prices?
extensionIdeas: Students calculate "satisfaction rating" for purchases - did high-priced items make them happier?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 15+ auction items (variety: highly desirable, medium, and less popular)
Budget card for each student — they write $100 as the starting balance and subtract each winning bid
Auction catalog (list of all items with descriptions)
Optional: bonus $10 added to a student's budget card for good behavior before the auction

sayThis.en: "One hundred dollars on your card. That is all the money you will ever have today. Go through the catalogue and write the most you'd pay for each thing. Write it now, before the bidding, because once it starts you'll want everything."
sayThis.es: "One hundred dollars on your card. That is all the money you will ever have today. Go through the catalogue and write the most you'd pay for each thing. Write it now, before the bidding, because once it starts you'll want everything."

doneWhen.en: Every budget card shows $100 and a maximum written beside at least five lots.
doneWhen.es: Every budget card shows $100 and a maximum written beside at least five lots.

watchFor.en: A maximum of one hundred written on every line. Ask what they'll bid with on lot two.
watchFor.es: A maximum of one hundred written on every line. Ask what they'll bid with on lot two.

description.en: Students write $100 on their budget card and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices)
description.es: Students write $100 on their budget card and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices)

sayThis.en: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear five? Ten? Going once — going twice — sold to number seven."
sayThis.es: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear five? Ten? Going once — going twice — sold to number seven."

doneWhen.en: Five lots are sold and each winning price is on the chart.
doneWhen.es: Five lots are sold and each winning price is on the chart.

watchFor.en: Winners who forget to subtract. Stop after every second lot and make the whole room update the card.
watchFor.es: Winners who forget to subtract. Stop after every second lot and make the whole room update the card.

description.en: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets
description.es: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets

sayThis.en: "Five prices up there. Which went high? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if you've got less than thirty dollars left."
sayThis.es: "Five prices up there. Which went high? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if you've got less than thirty dollars left."

doneWhen.en: The five prices are charted and the number of students under $30 is counted out loud.
doneWhen.es: The five prices are charted and the number of students under $30 is counted out loud.

watchFor.en: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Point at two lots that went for the same money and look nothing alike.
watchFor.es: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Point at two lots that went for the same money and look nothing alike.

description.en: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price
description.es: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price

sayThis.en: "You can't see inside. You bid anyway. So — what's a maybe worth?"
sayThis.es: "You can't see inside. You bid anyway. So — what's a maybe worth?"

doneWhen.en: All three mystery lots are sold, opened and held up for the room.
doneWhen.es: All three mystery lots are sold, opened and held up for the room.

watchFor.en: Nobody bidding at all. Open at one dollar to get it moving.
watchFor.es: Nobody bidding at all. Open at one dollar to get it moving.

description.en: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks
description.es: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks

sayThis.en: "You run it now. Take a bid, say it back louder, ask for more. Then going once, going twice, sold."
sayThis.es: "You run it now. Take a bid, say it back louder, ask for more. Then going once, going twice, sold."

doneWhen.en: Every remaining lot has been sold by a student auctioneer.
doneWhen.es: Every remaining lot has been sold by a student auctioneer.

watchFor.en: A quiet auctioneer losing the room. Stand beside them and repeat the bids for the first lot.
watchFor.es: A quiet auctioneer losing the room. Stand beside them and repeat the bids for the first lot.

description.en: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting
description.es: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting

sayThis.en: "Every lot and every price on the graph. Highest. Lowest. Now — who's still got money, and did they lose out, or did they play it smarter?"
sayThis.es: "Every lot and every price on the graph. Highest. Lowest. Now — who's still got money, and did they lose out, or did they play it smarter?"

doneWhen.en: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.
doneWhen.es: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.

watchFor.en: Winner-takes-all framing. Ask the student with cash left what they chose not to buy.
watchFor.es: Winner-takes-all framing. Ask the student with cash left what they chose not to buy.

description.en: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"
description.es: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"

discussionQuestions: What was your bidding strategy? Did it work?
Did you change your strategy during the auction? Why?
What happens when people compete for the same item?
Is the highest-priced item always the best? Why or why not?
How does an auction determine the 'true' value of something?
When might auctions be better than fixed prices? When might fixed prices be better?
What emotions did you feel during bidding?
How did you decide when to stop bidding on something?
extensionIdeas: Students sell their own items in a second auction
Research real auctions (art, antiques, livestock, online)
Calculate: if you could return items for refund, which would you return?
Write reflection: "The most important thing I learned about money and value"
Compare auction prices to "store prices" - which would you choose and why?

beforeClass.en: Lay the lots out where they can be seen and not handled, and number them. Write or print the catalogue. Choose your three mystery bags now and make sure what's inside is worth winning — a disappointing mystery bag kills the next round.
beforeClass.es: Lay the lots out where they can be seen and not handled, and number them. Write or print the catalogue. Choose your three mystery bags now and make sure what's inside is worth winning — a disappointing mystery bag kills the next round.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the student auctioneer round to two lots. Short: add a final lot and let everyone bid whatever they have left.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the student auctioneer round to two lots. Short: add a final lot and let everyone bid whatever they have left.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: Assumes the room has nothing. Season 1 kit already bought.
items: Craft sticks, 1 pack of 100 — numbered bidding paddles, collected back and reused every year
Paper clips as coins — reused from Chapter 2; no new purchase
Items to auction come from the room: books, supplies, class privileges; no purchase
A bell, or any classroom object that makes a sound, to close each lot; no purchase
