lowCost.description: Assumes scissors, glue, tape, pencils, paper, rulers and crayons are on hand.
items: Craft sticks, 1 pack of 100 — numbered bidding paddles, collected back and reused every year
Paper clips as coins — reused from Chapter 2; no new purchase
Items to auction come from the room: books, supplies, class privileges; no purchase

focus: Very simple budget ($10-20)
Clear yes/no bidding (raise hand for yes)
Teacher tracks money for students
Focus on experience over strategy
Vocabulary: auction, bid, money, buy
Moderate budget ($30-50)
Simple competitive bidding
Guided budget tracking with help
Basic strategy discussion
Vocabulary: budget, spend, save, price, highest bidder
Full budget ($50-100)
Independent money management
Written budget planning
Understanding of opportunity cost
Vocabulary: opportunity cost, market value, strategy, competition
Complex budget scenarios
Strategic planning with trade-offs
Data analysis of auction results
Advanced economic concepts
Advanced vocabulary: market dynamics, perceived value, bidding war, reserve price

title.en: Baker's Math: Recipe Costs & Bakery Economics
title.es: Baker's Math: Recipe Costs & Bakery Economics

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
20.activityName: Paper Pastry with Quick Cost Tracking
materials: Four parts laid out in trays — bases, frosting layers, wrappers, toppers
A large poster with the four part prices on it
One paper plate per student to build on

description.en: Show the four parts. Point to the price poster: "A base costs 25¢. A frosting layer costs 50¢. A wrapper costs 25¢. A topper costs 75¢."
description.es: Show the four parts. Point to the price poster: "A base costs 25¢. A frosting layer costs 50¢. A wrapper costs 25¢. A topper costs 75¢."

description.en: Each student takes one of each part, glues them together on their plate, and writes their name on the wrapper.
description.es: Each student takes one of each part, glues them together on their plate, and writes their name on the wrapper.

description.en: Write on the board: 25¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ + 75¢. Students help count: "What's 25 plus 50? Now add 25 more..." Total: $1.75
description.es: Write on the board: 25¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ + 75¢. Students help count: "What's 25 plus 50? Now add 25 more..." Total: $1.75

description.en: "Our pastry costs $1.75 to make. Should we sell it for $1.75?" (No, no profit!) "How about $2.00? $2.50? $3.00?"
description.es: "Our pastry costs $1.75 to make. Should we sell it for $1.75?" (No, no profit!) "How about $2.00? $2.50? $3.00?"

discussionQuestions: How much did our trail mix cost to make?
Would you buy it for $2.00?
Why do we need to charge MORE than it costs to make?
What could a bakery do with the extra money? (Pay workers, buy more ingredients, keep lights on)

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Cost tracking worksheet, one per student or group
Small bags or folded paper boxes for packaging
A price comparison card showing what a party shop charges for a paper cake topper

description.en: Display the build recipe on the board with what each part costs in bulk. Example: "Cardstock $2.00 (we need 4 sheets), Tissue paper $1.50 (we need 1 pack), Tape 50¢ (we need 2 feet)"
description.es: Display the build recipe on the board with what each part costs in bulk. Example: "Cardstock $2.00 (we need 4 sheets), Tissue paper $1.50 (we need 1 pack), Tape 50¢ (we need 2 feet)"

description.en: Groups measure, cut and assemble following the recipe. One student is the parts tracker, marking off every piece used — including the ones cut wrong.
description.es: Groups measure, cut and assemble following the recipe. One student is the parts tracker, marking off every piece used — including the ones cut wrong.

description.en: Fill out the cost worksheet: list each part and its cost - Add all costs together to find TOTAL COST - Count the number of pastries finished - Divide total cost by pastries: COST PER ITEM
description.es: Fill out the cost worksheet: list each part and its cost - Add all costs together to find TOTAL COST - Count the number of pastries finished - Divide total cost by pastries: COST PER ITEM

description.en: Groups decide a selling price. It has to be higher than the cost per item. Compare to the shop card: "A paper cake topper at the party shop costs $1.50. Ours costs 40¢ to make. What should we charge?"
description.es: Groups decide a selling price. It has to be higher than the cost per item. Compare to the shop card: "A paper cake topper at the party shop costs $1.50. Ours costs 40¢ to make. What should we charge?"

description.en: Share prices across the class. Discuss: "Why are prices different? Which would make the most profit? Who wasted the most cardstock?"
description.es: Share prices across the class. Discuss: "Why are prices different? Which would make the most profit? Who wasted the most cardstock?"

discussionQuestions: What was our total cost for all ingredients?
How many servings did we make?
What's the cost for ONE serving?
How much should we charge to make a profit?
Is our price fair compared to the store price?
What happens if we charge less than it costs to make?
extensionIdeas: Create price tags and packaging labels for finished product

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Cardstock, tissue paper, colored paper and tape
Bakery branding materials (markers, cardstock for signs)
Shop comparison cards showing party-store prices for similar paper pieces

sayThis.en: "You're opening a bakery, and nothing you make can be eaten. You build paper pastries. People buy them for parties and to put on top of presents. Pick your product. Then guess two numbers: what will one cost to build, and what will you charge?"
sayThis.es: "You're opening a bakery, and nothing you make can be eaten. You build paper pastries. People buy them for parties and to put on top of presents. Pick your product. Then guess two numbers: what will one cost to build, and what will you charge?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has a product, four named roles, and a guessed cost and price written down.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a product, four named roles, and a guessed cost and price written down.

watchFor.en: Teams picking the fanciest build without reading the parts prices. Make them read the sheet first.
watchFor.es: Teams picking the fanciest build without reading the parts prices. Make them read the sheet first.

description.en: Teams choose a build from 2-3 options (a simple cupcake, a layered cake slice, a decorated cookie shape) - Receive the parts cost sheet - Predict: "How much will this cost to make? How much should we charge?" - Assign roles: Head Baker, Parts Manager, Cost Tracker, Packaging Designer
description.es: Teams choose a build from 2-3 options (a simple cupcake, a layered cake slice, a decorated cookie shape) - Receive the parts cost sheet - Predict: "How much will this cost to make? How much should we charge?" - Assign roles: Head Baker, Parts Manager, Cost Tracker, Packaging Designer

sayThis.en: "Build it. Parts Manager — count every piece you use, including the ones you ruin. A wasted part still cost money. That's the whole point of this."
sayThis.es: "Build it. Parts Manager — count every piece you use, including the ones you ruin. A wasted part still cost money. That's the whole point of this."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a finished pastry and a tally of every part used, mistakes included.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a finished pastry and a tally of every part used, mistakes included.

watchFor.en: Mis-cuts going quietly in the bin. Say up front that you'll be checking the bin.
watchFor.es: Mis-cuts going quietly in the bin. Say up front that you'll be checking the bin.

description.en: Follow the build recipe, measuring and cutting each part - Parts Manager tracks the ACTUAL pieces used, mis-cuts included (waste costs money!) - Note any mistakes or extra parts needed - Package the finished pastries attractively
description.es: Follow the build recipe, measuring and cutting each part - Parts Manager tracks the ACTUAL pieces used, mis-cuts included (waste costs money!) - Note any mistakes or extra parts needed - Package the finished pastries attractively

sayThis.en: "Add up the parts you actually used, not just the ones that worked. Then packaging — bag ten cents, label five, ribbon three. Then divide by how many you made. That last number is the one that matters: what one costs."
sayThis.es: "Add up the parts you actually used, not just the ones that worked. Then packaging — bag ten cents, label five, ribbon three. Then divide by how many you made. That last number is the one that matters: what one costs."

doneWhen.en: Every worksheet shows a total cost and a cost per item.
doneWhen.es: Every worksheet shows a total cost and a cost per item.

watchFor.en: Teams counting only the parts in the finished item. Send them back to the tally.
watchFor.es: Teams counting only the parts in the finished item. Send them back to the tally.

description.en: Calculate parts costs (actual pieces used, not just the ones that worked) - Add packaging costs (bags: 10¢ each, labels: 5¢ each, ribbon: 3¢ each) - Add "labor cost" (optional advanced concept): "If each team member earned $5/hour and you worked 20 minutes, that's $1.67 in labor" - Calculate cost PER ITEM (total cost ÷ number of pastries made) - Document all calculations on the worksheet
description.es: Calculate parts costs (actual pieces used, not just the ones that worked) - Add packaging costs (bags: 10¢ each, labels: 5¢ each, ribbon: 3¢ each) - Add "labor cost" (optional advanced concept): "If each team member earned $5/hour and you worked 20 minutes, that's $1.67 in labor" - Calculate cost PER ITEM (total cost ÷ number of pastries made) - Document all calculations on the worksheet

sayThis.en: "Now set your price. It has to cover the cost or you go out of business. Then write the sentence: we charge this much because it costs this much and we want this much profit."
sayThis.es: "Now set your price. It has to cover the cost or you go out of business. Then write the sentence: we charge this much because it costs this much and we want this much profit."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a price tag and the because sentence written out.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a price tag and the because sentence written out.

watchFor.en: A price set below cost. Don't correct it. Ask them to work out where they are after fifty sales.
watchFor.es: A price set below cost. Don't correct it. Ask them to work out where they are after fifty sales.

description.en: Research: display the party-shop prices for similar paper pieces - Set a price that covers ALL costs plus the profit you want - Write the justification: "We charge $2.50 because it costs $1.20 to make and we want $1.30 profit per item" - Design price tags showing the price and why it is worth it - Create a bakery name and logo for the labels
description.es: Research: display the party-shop prices for similar paper pieces - Set a price that covers ALL costs plus the profit you want - Write the justification: "We charge $2.50 because it costs $1.20 to make and we want $1.30 profit per item" - Design price tags showing the price and why it is worth it - Create a bakery name and logo for the labels

sayThis.en: "Price times how many you made — that's revenue. Take your costs off it. What's left is profit. Now look around the room. Why is their price different from yours?"
sayThis.es: "Price times how many you made — that's revenue. Take your costs off it. What's left is profit. Now look around the room. Why is their price different from yours?"

doneWhen.en: Every team's profit number is on the board next to its price.
doneWhen.es: Every team's profit number is on the board next to its price.

watchFor.en: Teams treating another team's price as wrong. Ask what that team's costs were first.
watchFor.es: Teams treating another team's price as wrong. Ask what that team's costs were first.

description.en: Calculate: if you sold every pastry at your price, what is the total revenue? - Subtract total cost = TOTAL PROFIT - Discuss: "Is this a sustainable business?" - Compare prices across teams: "Why are prices different?" - "What could you do with the profit?" (Reinvest, pay yourself, expand the bakery)
description.es: Calculate: if you sold every pastry at your price, what is the total revenue? - Subtract total cost = TOTAL PROFIT - Discuss: "Is this a sustainable business?" - Compare prices across teams: "Why are prices different?" - "What could you do with the profit?" (Reinvest, pay yourself, expand the bakery)

discussionQuestions: What surprised you about the costs?
Was any ingredient more expensive than you expected?
How much profit should a business make—a little or a lot? Why?
What happens if you price too low? Too high?
Why do real bakeries charge different prices for different items?
Besides ingredients, what OTHER costs does a real bakery have? (Rent, electricity, wages, equipment)
How does knowing exact costs help you run a business?
Could your family run a bakery business with what you learned today?
extensionIdeas: Actually "sell" to another class using paper-clip coins, track real profit
Compare costs of making vs. buying (make a batch vs. buy from store)
Research local bakery pricing and cost structures
Design complete business plan including monthly costs and revenue projections
Calculate break-even point (how many items must you sell to cover costs?)

beforeClass.en: Cut the parts sheets and check every part on the table has a price on the sheet. A part with no price breaks the math for that whole team. Nothing here is edible; these are paper pastries for parties and gift tops.
beforeClass.es: Cut the parts sheets and check every part on the table has a price on the sheet. A part with no price breaks the math for that whole team. Nothing here is edible; these are paper pastries for parties and gift tops.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: drop the labor cost from the analysis step. Short: give teams a second product and make them compare cost per item.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: drop the labor cost from the analysis step. Short: give teams a second product and make them compare cost per item.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: Assumes the room has nothing. Season 1 kit already bought.
items: Cardstock in two colors, 1 pack of 50 sheets — one sheet cuts into four paper pastry bases; recycled cereal boxes and old file folders work instead at no cost
Tissue paper in three colors, 1 pack — the paper frosting layers
Paper ribbon, 1 roll — boxing up the finished pieces
The parts price list written on the board by the teacher — four parts, four prices; nothing printed

items: Cardstock in two colors, 1 pack of 50 sheets — one sheet cuts into four paper pastry bases

focus: Count ingredient scoops: "1, 2, 3 scoops"
Simple price recognition: $1, $2, etc.
Teacher does all calculations, students watch and participate verbally
Focus on making the recipe and enjoying the process
Basic vocabulary: cost, price, ingredient, recipe, money
Visual ingredient cards with pictures and prices
Add 2-4 simple prices with teacher support (50¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ = $1.25)
Understand difference between "cost to make" and "selling price"
Use tally marks or pictures to track ingredients used
Discuss concepts of "more expensive" and "less expensive"
Introduction to profit concept: "extra money left over"
Sentence frames: "This costs ___. We charge ___."
Add multiple costs independently with regrouping
Calculate cost per serving with teacher support (simple division)
Set appropriate selling prices that include profit
Compare homemade costs to store-bought prices
Understand that profit is necessary for businesses
Begin to track "what if" scenarios (What if we made 20 instead of 10?)
Complex cost calculations including packaging, labor, and waste
Independent calculation of profit margins
Percentage calculations (cost is 40% of selling price)
Compare making vs. buying economics across multiple products
Research real bakery business models and economics
Write business justifications and pricing strategies
Calculate break-even point and return on investment

title.en: The Morning Market: Fresh or Not?
title.es: The Morning Market: Fresh or Not?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
20.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: * - 10-15 picture cards showing various items (food and non-food)
Two sorting areas (circles on floor or desk sections)

description.en: Show students a banana: "Fresh today, brown tomorrow—why?". Explain some things last, others don't. Introduce sorting challenge
description.es: Show students a banana: "Fresh today, brown tomorrow—why?". Explain some things last, others don't. Introduce sorting challenge

description.en: Students take turns selecting a card. Place in correct category: Spoils Fast or Lasts Long. Class votes if unsure. Discuss each placement
description.es: Students take turns selecting a card. Place in correct category: Spoils Fast or Lasts Long. Class votes if unsure. Discuss each placement

description.en: Teacher calls out items. Students point to correct category. Speed increases for challenge
description.es: Teacher calls out items. Students point to correct category. Speed increases for challenge

description.en: "Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?". "What happens if you wait to sell milk?". Connect to morning market story Items to Include:. Spoils Fast: fish, milk, bread, lettuce, bananas, strawberries. Lasts Long: toys, books, clothes, pencils, rocks, jewelry
description.es: "Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?". "What happens if you wait to sell milk?". Connect to morning market story Items to Include:. Spoils Fast: fish, milk, bread, lettuce, bananas, strawberries. Lasts Long: toys, books, clothes, pencils, rocks, jewelry

discussionQuestions: Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?
What happens if you wait to sell milk?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Item cards (3 per student: 1 perishable, 2 non-perishable)
Price chart showing rounds and values
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($20 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Each student receives: * 1 perishable card (fish, bread, milk, fruit) * 2 non-perishable cards (toys, books, tools, clothes). Explain three trading rounds. Show price chart on board
description.es: Each student receives: * 1 perishable card (fish, bread, milk, fruit) * 2 non-perishable cards (toys, books, tools, clothes). Explain three trading rounds. Show price chart on board

description.en: Timer set for 3 minutes. Prices: Perishables $10, Non-perishables $5. Students can sell to "market buyer" (teacher/volunteer). Buyers walk around making offers. Record what each student sells
description.es: Timer set for 3 minutes. Prices: Perishables $10, Non-perishables $5. Students can sell to "market buyer" (teacher/volunteer). Buyers walk around making offers. Record what each student sells

description.en: Timer set for 2 minutes. Prices: Perishables DROP to $5, Non-perishables stay $5. Students who held perishables see value decrease. More selling happens. Visual: Update price chart dramatically
description.es: Timer set for 2 minutes. Prices: Perishables DROP to $5, Non-perishables stay $5. Students who held perishables see value decrease. More selling happens. Visual: Update price chart dramatically

description.en: Timer set for 1 minute. Prices: Perishables DROP to $1, Non-perishables stay $5. Last chance to sell. Those who held perishables feel real impact
description.es: Timer set for 1 minute. Prices: Perishables DROP to $1, Non-perishables stay $5. Last chance to sell. Those who held perishables feel real impact

description.en: Students count final money. Graph results on board. Who made the most? What strategy did they use?. Who sold perishables early? Late?
description.es: Students count final money. Graph results on board. Who made the most? What strategy did they use?. Who sold perishables early? Late?

discussionQuestions: Who sold fish in Round 1? Why?
Who waited? How did that work out?
What would you do differently next time?
Why don't toy prices drop like fish prices?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Mixed inventory cards (10 items per student: 4 perishable, 6 non-perishable)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($50 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

sayThis.en: "Fifty dollars each. Your stall has fresh things and things that keep. Write down everything you're holding before we open, because you will not remember later."
sayThis.es: "Fifty dollars each. Your stall has fresh things and things that keep. Write down everything you're holding before we open, because you will not remember later."

doneWhen.en: Every stall has its inventory written on the sheet and $50 counted out on the desk.
doneWhen.es: Every stall has its inventory written on the sheet and $50 counted out on the desk.

watchFor.en: Stalls trying to open before the sheet is filled in. Hold the bell.
watchFor.es: Stalls trying to open before the sheet is filled in. Hold the bell.

description.en: Students set up stalls with inventory. Receive starting cash $50. Review price tracking sheet. Assign initial "buyers" (rotating role). Practice using tracking sheet
description.es: Students set up stalls with inventory. Receive starting cash $50. Review price tracking sheet. Assign initial "buyers" (rotating role). Practice using tracking sheet

sayThis.en: "Market's open. Fish, fruit, milk and bread are eight dollars. Everything else is five. Sell what you can and mark every sale as it happens, not at the end."
sayThis.es: "Market's open. Fish, fruit, milk and bread are eight dollars. Everything else is five. Sell what you can and mark every sale as it happens, not at the end."

doneWhen.en: Every seller has at least one line written in the Period 1 row.
doneWhen.es: Every seller has at least one line written in the Period 1 row.

watchFor.en: Sellers holding out for a better price on the fresh goods. Say nothing yet. That's the trap and it should spring on its own.
watchFor.es: Sellers holding out for a better price on the fresh goods. Say nothing yet. That's the trap and it should spring on its own.

description.en: Timer: 5 minutes of active trading. Starting prices: * Perishables: $8 each (fish, fruit, milk, bread) * Non-perishables: $5 each (toys, books, tools, clothes, crafts, jewelry). Buyers visit stalls, negotiate, purchase. Sellers mark sales on tracking sheet. Rotate buyer badges after 3 minutes
description.es: Timer: 5 minutes of active trading. Starting prices: * Perishables: $8 each (fish, fruit, milk, bread) * Non-perishables: $5 each (toys, books, tools, clothes, crafts, jewelry). Buyers visit stalls, negotiate, purchase. Sellers mark sales on tracking sheet. Rotate buyer badges after 3 minutes

sayThis.en: "Price change. Fresh things are four dollars now. Everything else is still five. If you're holding fish, your fish just lost half its value while you stood there."
sayThis.es: "Price change. Fresh things are four dollars now. Everything else is still five. If you're holding fish, your fish just lost half its value while you stood there."

doneWhen.en: Every tracking sheet has a Period 2 row filled in, even if the line says nothing sold.
doneWhen.es: Every tracking sheet has a Period 2 row filled in, even if the line says nothing sold.

watchFor.en: Students who don't see why. Say it plainly: fresh things go off, things that keep don't.
watchFor.es: Students who don't see why. Say it plainly: fresh things go off, things that keep don't.

description.en: Timer: 4 minutes of active trading. Price changes announced dramatically: * Perishables: DROP to $4 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Discussion pause: "Notice anything about your fish value?". Continue trading. Sellers see depreciation impact. Rotate buyers again
description.es: Timer: 4 minutes of active trading. Price changes announced dramatically: * Perishables: DROP to $4 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Discussion pause: "Notice anything about your fish value?". Continue trading. Sellers see depreciation impact. Rotate buyers again

sayThis.en: "Last change. Fresh is two dollars. Three minutes. If you're still holding fresh goods, this is the last money you will ever get for them."
sayThis.es: "Last change. Fresh is two dollars. Three minutes. If you're still holding fresh goods, this is the last money you will ever get for them."

doneWhen.en: The market is closed and every Period 3 row is filled.
doneWhen.es: The market is closed and every Period 3 row is filled.

watchFor.en: Panic selling turning into shouting. Set the rule: one seller talking at a time at each stall.
watchFor.es: Panic selling turning into shouting. Set the rule: one seller talking at a time at each stall.

description.en: Timer: 3 minutes of active trading. Final price changes: * Perishables: DROP to $2 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Urgent selling begins. Some students stuck with near-worthless perishables. Close market
description.es: Timer: 3 minutes of active trading. Final price changes: * Perishables: DROP to $2 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Urgent selling begins. Some students stuck with near-worthless perishables. Close market

sayThis.en: "Add your three periods together. That's your revenue. Now what was your stall worth at the start? Take one from the other. Who lost money — and what were they holding?"
sayThis.es: "Add your three periods together. That's your revenue. Now what was your stall worth at the start? Take one from the other. Who lost money — and what were they holding?"

doneWhen.en: Every bar graph shows a starting value and a final revenue.
doneWhen.es: Every bar graph shows a starting value and a final revenue.

watchFor.en: Subtraction done the wrong way round. Do the first one on the board together.
watchFor.es: Subtraction done the wrong way round. Do the first one on the board together.

description.en: Students calculate total revenue. Create bar graphs showing: * Starting inventory value * Final revenue * Difference (profit/loss). Class data: graph average revenue by strategy. Identify patterns: early sellers vs. holders Price Tracking Sheet Format: ``` Name: ________________ Stall #: ____ INVENTORY: Perishables: [ ] Fish [ ] Fruit [ ] Milk [ ] Bread Non-perishables: [ ] Toy [ ] Book [ ] Tool [ ] Clothes [ ] Craft [ ] Jewelry PERIOD 1 (Perish=$8, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 2 (Perish=$4, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 3 (Perish=$2, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ TOTAL REVENUE: $______ Starting inventory value: $______ Profit/Loss: $______ ```
description.es: Students calculate total revenue. Create bar graphs showing: * Starting inventory value * Final revenue * Difference (profit/loss). Class data: graph average revenue by strategy. Identify patterns: early sellers vs. holders Price Tracking Sheet Format: ``` Name: ________________ Stall #: ____ INVENTORY: Perishables: [ ] Fish [ ] Fruit [ ] Milk [ ] Bread Non-perishables: [ ] Toy [ ] Book [ ] Tool [ ] Clothes [ ] Craft [ ] Jewelry PERIOD 1 (Perish=$8, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 2 (Perish=$4, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 3 (Perish=$2, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ TOTAL REVENUE: $______ Starting inventory value: $______ Profit/Loss: $______ ```

discussionQuestions: What strategy worked best? Why?
Who sold all perishables in Period 1? How did that turn out?
Who held onto fish until Period 3? What happened?
Would you change your strategy if we played again?
Why do real markets work this way?
What items in real life work like our perishables?

beforeClass.en: Sort the inventory cards into stall piles and count the cash out before anyone arrives. Write the three price periods on the board and cover them, so you can reveal each one. Everything sold is a drawn or printed card; no real food.
beforeClass.es: Sort the inventory cards into stall piles and count the cash out before anyone arrives. Write the three price periods on the board and cover them, so you can reveal each one. Everything sold is a drawn or printed card; no real food.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut period three to two minutes of trading. Short: add a fourth period where fresh goods are worth nothing and see who is still holding them.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut period three to two minutes of trading. Short: add a fourth period where fresh goods are worth nothing and see who is still holding them.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Paper with grid (or blank paper and ruler)

description.en: Show picture of community garden. Explain: "Many families share one big garden". Everyone helps, everyone gets vegetables
description.es: Show picture of community garden. Explain: "Many families share one big garden". Everyone helps, everyone gets vegetables

description.en: Each student gets grid paper (4-6 plots). Draw or place picture cards to "plant" garden. Color different plots for different families. Label with family names or numbers
description.es: Each student gets grid paper (4-6 plots). Draw or place picture cards to "plant" garden. Color different plots for different families. Label with family names or numbers

description.en: Post designs around room. Students walk and observe others' gardens. Notice different ways to organize plots
description.es: Post designs around room. Students walk and observe others' gardens. Notice different ways to organize plots

description.en: "Why is sharing a garden helpful?". "What if you don't have a yard? Could a community garden help?". Connect to La Vecina's garden story
description.es: "Why is sharing a garden helpful?". "What if you don't have a yard? Could a community garden help?". Connect to La Vecina's garden story

discussionQuestions: Why is sharing a garden helpful?
What if you don't have a yard? Could a community garden help?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Large poster paper or chart paper
Grid overlay or ruler for sections
Seed catalog pictures (cut from magazines or printed)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($20 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Divide class into groups of 4-5 students. Scenario: "Your neighborhood wants a community garden, but gardens cost money". Costs: * Garden plot: $40 * Seeds: $20 * Tools: $20 * Soil: $20. Each student has $20 to contribute
description.es: Divide class into groups of 4-5 students. Scenario: "Your neighborhood wants a community garden, but gardens cost money". Costs: * Garden plot: $40 * Seeds: $20 * Tools: $20 * Soil: $20. Each student has $20 to contribute

description.en: Groups discuss: "Should we each make our own tiny garden, or pool our money for one big garden?". Calculate: * Individual: $20 buys very little * Pooled: $80-100 buys full garden with all supplies. Make group decision (guided toward pooling for lesson)
description.es: Groups discuss: "Should we each make our own tiny garden, or pool our money for one big garden?". Calculate: * Individual: $20 buys very little * Pooled: $80-100 buys full garden with all supplies. Make group decision (guided toward pooling for lesson)

description.en: Groups draw garden on poster paper. Divide into plots (one per student). Add paths, shared tool area, water source. Select seeds/plants from catalog. Glue pictures in each plot
description.es: Groups draw garden on poster paper. Divide into plots (one per student). Add paths, shared tool area, water source. Select seeds/plants from catalog. Glue pictures in each plot

description.en: Decide: "If tomatoes grow in one plot, does only that person get them?". Discuss fair sharing since everyone contributed. Record sharing agreement
description.es: Decide: "If tomatoes grow in one plot, does only that person get them?". Discuss fair sharing since everyone contributed. Record sharing agreement

description.en: Each group shows garden design. Shares one thing about their sharing plan
description.es: Each group shows garden design. Shares one thing about their sharing plan

discussionQuestions: Why did pooling money help more than individual spending?
How should you share the vegetables when they grow?
What if someone contributed seeds instead of money—should they still get vegetables?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Large grid paper or poster board (one per group)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($30 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)
Resource cards (seeds, tools, soil, water access, time/labor)
Seed catalog or printed plant images
Measuring tools (rulers, tape measures for scale)

sayThis.en: "Empty lot down the street. Two hundred dollars turns it into a garden — fence, soil, seeds, tools, water. Between you, you have a hundred and eighty in cash. You're twenty short. Somebody in this room is not holding money."
sayThis.es: "Empty lot down the street. Two hundred dollars turns it into a garden — fence, soil, seeds, tools, water. Between you, you have a hundred and eighty in cash. You're twenty short. Somebody in this room is not holding money."

doneWhen.en: The $200 breakdown and the $20 gap are both written on the board.
doneWhen.es: The $200 breakdown and the $20 gap are both written on the board.

watchFor.en: The jump straight to cutting something. Let it sit. The seeds and the tools are the answer.
watchFor.es: The jump straight to cutting something. Let it sit. The seeds and the tools are the answer.

description.en: Present community garden challenge: * Neighborhood has empty lot (12' x 16' = 192 sq ft) * Could become community garden if neighbors invest. Show cost breakdown: * Fence: $50 * Soil (all plots): $40 * Seeds: $30 * Shared tools: $30 * Water hookup: $50 * Total needed: $200. Class has combined $180 in cash (6 students × $30). Gap: $20—someone needs to contribute non-monetary resources
description.es: Present community garden challenge: * Neighborhood has empty lot (12' x 16' = 192 sq ft) * Could become community garden if neighbors invest. Show cost breakdown: * Fence: $50 * Soil (all plots): $40 * Seeds: $30 * Shared tools: $30 * Water hookup: $50 * Total needed: $200. Class has combined $180 in cash (6 students × $30). Gap: $20—someone needs to contribute non-monetary resources

sayThis.en: "Write down what you're putting in. Cash in one column, not-cash in the other. Seeds are worth ten dollars. Tools are worth twenty. Then put it all in the middle and count it."
sayThis.es: "Write down what you're putting in. Cash in one column, not-cash in the other. Seeds are worth ten dollars. Tools are worth twenty. Then put it all in the middle and count it."

doneWhen.en: The pooled total is counted out loud and reaches $200.
doneWhen.es: The pooled total is counted out loud and reaches $200.

watchFor.en: The non-cash students being treated as having given less. Say the number out loud: their seeds closed the gap.
watchFor.es: The non-cash students being treated as having given less. Say the number out loud: their seeds closed the gap.

description.en: Students receive varied resources: * 4 students: $30 cash each * 1 student: $20 cash + seed packets (worth $10) * 1 student: $10 cash + tools to share (worth $20). Complete contribution worksheet: * Name * Cash contributed: $_____ * Non-cash contributed: _____ * Total value: $_____. Pool all resources in center table. Calculate if goal met ($200 total)
description.es: Students receive varied resources: * 4 students: $30 cash each * 1 student: $20 cash + seed packets (worth $10) * 1 student: $10 cash + tools to share (worth $20). Complete contribution worksheet: * Name * Cash contributed: $_____ * Non-cash contributed: _____ * Total value: $_____. Pool all resources in center table. Calculate if goal met ($200 total)

sayThis.en: "Each square is two feet. Everyone gets a plot. You also need a path, somewhere for the tools and a tap. And you have to choose: same size plots for everyone, or bigger plots for whoever put in more. Your group decides, and you have to be able to defend it."
sayThis.es: "Each square is two feet. Everyone gets a plot. You also need a path, somewhere for the tools and a tap. And you have to choose: same size plots for everyone, or bigger plots for whoever put in more. Your group decides, and you have to be able to defend it."

doneWhen.en: Every grid shows labeled plots for all members, a path, a tool space and a water point.
doneWhen.es: Every grid shows labeled plots for all members, a path, a tool space and a water point.

watchFor.en: Groups drawing plots and forgetting the paths. Ask how anyone reaches the plot in the middle.
watchFor.es: Groups drawing plots and forgetting the paths. Ask how anyone reaches the plot in the middle.

description.en: Groups (6-8 students) design garden layout: * Use grid paper (each square = 2 sq ft) * Divide into individual plots (4-6 sq ft per person) * Include shared spaces: tool shed area, compost bin, pathways, water access point. Assign plots fairly: * Option A: Equal sizes for all * Option B: Larger plots for larger investors * Group decides which is "fair". Select plants for each plot from catalog. Label everything clearly
description.es: Groups (6-8 students) design garden layout: * Use grid paper (each square = 2 sq ft) * Divide into individual plots (4-6 sq ft per person) * Include shared spaces: tool shed area, compost bin, pathways, water access point. Assign plots fairly: * Option A: Equal sizes for all * Option B: Larger plots for larger investors * Group decides which is "fair". Select plants for each plot from catalog. Label everything clearly

sayThis.en: "Your plot grows this much. Work out what that's worth. Take off what you put in. Divide by what you put in. That's your return — put thirty in, get sixty back, you doubled it."
sayThis.es: "Your plot grows this much. Work out what that's worth. Take off what you put in. Divide by what you put in. That's your return — put thirty in, get sixty back, you doubled it."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written an investment, a harvest value and a return.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written an investment, a harvest value and a return.

watchFor.en: Division the wrong way round. Work the first example on the board with the whole room.
watchFor.es: Division the wrong way round. Work the first example on the board with the whole room.

description.en: Use provided data for expected harvest: * Tomatoes: 20 lbs per plot * Lettuce: 10 heads per plot * Carrots: 15 bunches per plot. Students calculate: * Their investment: $______ * Their expected harvest value (at market price): $______ * ROI: (Harvest value − Investment) ÷ Investment. Example: Invested $30, harvest worth $60 → ROI = 100% (doubled money)
description.es: Use provided data for expected harvest: * Tomatoes: 20 lbs per plot * Lettuce: 10 heads per plot * Carrots: 15 bunches per plot. Students calculate: * Their investment: $______ * Their expected harvest value (at market price): $______ * ROI: (Harvest value − Investment) ÷ Investment. Example: Invested $30, harvest worth $60 → ROI = 100% (doubled money)

sayThis.en: "One sentence, and everybody signs it. How are you splitting the vegetables? Equally, by what people put in, by who needs it most, or your own mix of those."
sayThis.es: "One sentence, and everybody signs it. How are you splitting the vegetables? Equally, by what people put in, by who needs it most, or your own mix of those."

doneWhen.en: Every group's agreement is written and signed by every member.
doneWhen.es: Every group's agreement is written and signed by every member.

watchFor.en: Groups choosing equal because it's quickest. Ask the biggest investor whether they agree, out loud.
watchFor.es: Groups choosing equal because it's quickest. Ask the biggest investor whether they agree, out loud.

description.en: Create written agreement: * "We agree that vegetables will be shared by: _____" * Options: equally, by contribution, by need, combination. All group members sign. Post agreements with garden designs
description.es: Create written agreement: * "We agree that vegetables will be shared by: _____" * Options: equally, by contribution, by need, combination. All group members sign. Post agreements with garden designs

sayThis.en: "Walk the room. Find one group that split the harvest differently from you."
sayThis.es: "Walk the room. Find one group that split the harvest differently from you."

doneWhen.en: Every group has named another group's sharing rule.
doneWhen.es: Every group has named another group's sharing rule.

watchFor.en: A lap with no reading. Give them the one thing to find before they stand up.
watchFor.es: A lap with no reading. Give them the one thing to find before they stand up.

description.en: View other groups' designs. Notice different solutions to fair distribution Investment Tracking Sheet Format: ``` COMMUNITY GARDEN INVESTMENT TRACKER Group Name: _____________________ CONTRIBUTIONS: Name Cash Seeds Tools Time TOTAL VALUE ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ TOTAL GROUP INVESTMENT: $______ GOAL: $200 ✅ Met / ❌ Short by $____ PLOT ASSIGNMENTS: Name Plot Size (sq ft) Reason for Size _____________ ________ ______________ _____________ ________ ______________ SHARING AGREEMENT: We agree to share the harvest by: □ Equal shares for everyone □ Proportional to investment □ Based on need □ Other: _______________ Signed: _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ ```
description.es: View other groups' designs. Notice different solutions to fair distribution Investment Tracking Sheet Format: ``` COMMUNITY GARDEN INVESTMENT TRACKER Group Name: _____________________ CONTRIBUTIONS: Name Cash Seeds Tools Time TOTAL VALUE ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ TOTAL GROUP INVESTMENT: $______ GOAL: $200 ✅ Met / ❌ Short by $____ PLOT ASSIGNMENTS: Name Plot Size (sq ft) Reason for Size _____________ ________ ______________ _____________ ________ ______________ SHARING AGREEMENT: We agree to share the harvest by: □ Equal shares for everyone □ Proportional to investment □ Based on need □ Other: _______________ Signed: _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ ```

discussionQuestions: Is it fair to give bigger plots to bigger investors, or should everyone get equal space?
What if someone contributed tools instead of money—should they get less vegetables?
How does a community garden help people who can't afford their own garden?
What's the return on investment if you invest $30 and get $60 worth of vegetables?
Could this idea work for other community projects? What else?

beforeClass.en: Hand out the resource cards before the lesson so the cash and the non-cash are already split. The twenty-dollar gap only teaches anything if somebody is holding seeds instead of money. Grid paper on every table.
beforeClass.es: Hand out the resource cards before the lesson so the cash and the non-cash are already split. The twenty-dollar gap only teaches anything if somebody is holding seeds instead of money. Grid paper on every table.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: run the sharing agreement and the gallery walk together in four minutes. Short: add a second design done with half the money.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: run the sharing agreement and the gallery walk together in four minutes. Short: add a second design done with half the money.

description.en: Discuss handmade gifts: why make instead of buy? What makes handmade special? Review available materials for making holiday items.
description.es: Discuss handmade gifts: why make instead of buy? What makes handmade special? Review available materials for making holiday items.

description.es: Students choose what to make: card, ornament, bookmark, or simple craft. Plan design and gather materials.

description.es: Students create their handmade holiday items using craft materials. Work carefully with attention to quality and thoughtfulness.

materials: Craft materials (paper, felt scraps, beads, pipe cleaners, glue)
Timer or clock visible to all
Sample store-bought item to compare (e.g., beaded bracelet from dollar store)

description.en: Show handmade bracelet and store-bought bracelet side-by-side. Discuss differences: "Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?". Introduce concept: "Today you'll make something AND track how long it takes". Explain time tracking sheet
description.es: Show handmade bracelet and store-bought bracelet side-by-side. Discuss differences: "Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?". Introduce concept: "Today you'll make something AND track how long it takes". Explain time tracking sheet

description.en: Students choose a simple craft project: * Beaded bracelet or necklace * Felt bookmark * Decorated card or frame. As they work, they track time on worksheet: * Start time: _____ * End time: _____ * Total minutes: _____. Teacher calls out 5-minute intervals
description.es: Students choose a simple craft project: * Beaded bracelet or necklace * Felt bookmark * Decorated card or frame. As they work, they track time on worksheet: * Start time: _____ * End time: _____ * Total minutes: _____. Teacher calls out 5-minute intervals

description.en: Materials cost discussion: * "Our beads cost $3 for 100. You used 20 beads = about 60¢" * "If your time is worth $6/hour and you worked 15 minutes, that's $1.50 of labor". Students add: Materials + Labor = Total Cost. Example: 60¢ + $1.50 = $2.10
description.es: Materials cost discussion: * "Our beads cost $3 for 100. You used 20 beads = about 60¢" * "If your time is worth $6/hour and you worked 15 minutes, that's $1.50 of labor". Students add: Materials + Labor = Total Cost. Example: 60¢ + $1.50 = $2.10

description.en: Show store-bought bracelet: "This costs $1 at the store". Handmade bracelet costs $2.10 to make. Discuss: "Why might handmade cost more?" * More time * Unique design * Personal touch * Quality materials. "But does your handmade bracelet have special value to you?"

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Calculators for older students Craft Station Options:

sayThis.en: "You're a stall at a holiday market. You make one thing, and you write down everything it takes — every bead, every inch of ribbon, and every minute. Time is a cost too. Start your timer when you start."
sayThis.es: "You're a stall at a holiday market. You make one thing, and you write down everything it takes — every bead, every inch of ribbon, and every minute. Time is a cost too. Start your timer when you start."

doneWhen.en: Every student is at a station with a tracking sheet and a running timer.
doneWhen.es: Every student is at a station with a tracking sheet and a running timer.

watchFor.en: Students building before starting the timer. Count the whole room in together.
watchFor.es: Students building before starting the timer. Count the whole room in together.

description.en: Introduce scenario: "You're craft vendors at a holiday market!". Explain stations and tracking system. Show sample finished products. Demonstrate time tracking: start timer when you begin, stop when done
description.es: Introduce scenario: "You're craft vendors at a holiday market!". Explain stations and tracking system. Show sample finished products. Demonstrate time tracking: start timer when you begin, stop when done

sayThis.en: "Make one good one, not three fast ones. Write down what you take as you take it. If you go back for more ribbon, that goes on the sheet too."
sayThis.es: "Make one good one, not three fast ones. Write down what you take as you take it. If you go back for more ribbon, that goes on the sheet too."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a finished item and a materials list with a number beside every line.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a finished item and a materials list with a number beside every line.

watchFor.en: Materials taken and never recorded. Walk the stations and ask one student per table to read their sheet back to you.
watchFor.es: Materials taken and never recorded. Walk the stations and ask one student per table to read their sheet back to you.

description.en: Students choose one station. Create one item, carefully tracking: * Materials used * Time spent * Quality level (self-assessment). Aim for quality over speed. Teacher circulates, provides support
description.es: Students choose one station. Create one item, carefully tracking: * Materials used * Time spent * Quality level (self-assessment). Aim for quality over speed. Teacher circulates, provides support

sayThis.en: "Beads three cents. Felt twenty-five. Ribbon ten cents a foot. Paper five. Glue five. Add up your materials. Then your time, at ten cents a minute — ten minutes is a dollar. Materials plus time is what it cost you."
sayThis.es: "Beads three cents. Felt twenty-five. Ribbon ten cents a foot. Paper five. Glue five. Add up your materials. Then your time, at ten cents a minute — ten minutes is a dollar. Materials plus time is what it cost you."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows a materials total, a labor total and the two added together.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows a materials total, a labor total and the two added together.

watchFor.en: Time being left out. It's usually the bigger number and it's the surprise.
watchFor.es: Time being left out. It's usually the bigger number and it's the surprise.

description.en: Students calculate total cost of their creation: * Materials cost: Use provided price list. Beads: 3¢ each. Felt squares: 25¢ each. Ribbon: 10¢ per foot. Paper/cardstock: 5¢ per sheet. Glue: 5¢ * Labor cost: Time spent × $6/hour (or $0.10/minute). Example: 10 minutes × $0.10 = $1.00 labor cost * Total cost: Materials + Labor. Record on worksheet
description.es: Students calculate total cost of their creation: * Materials cost: Use provided price list. Beads: 3¢ each. Felt squares: 25¢ each. Ribbon: 10¢ per foot. Paper/cardstock: 5¢ per sheet. Glue: 5¢ * Labor cost: Time spent × $6/hour (or $0.10/minute). Example: 10 minutes × $0.10 = $1.00 labor cost * Total cost: Materials + Labor. Record on worksheet

sayThis.en: "Cost is what you spent. Price is what you charge. The gap between them is profit. Your price has to be above your cost — that isn't greed, that's staying open next week."
sayThis.es: "Cost is what you spent. Price is what you charge. The gap between them is profit. Your price has to be above your cost — that isn't greed, that's staying open next week."

doneWhen.en: Every item has a price tag showing a price above its own cost.
doneWhen.es: Every item has a price tag showing a price above its own cost.

watchFor.en: Prices set at exactly cost. Ask what they've earned after a hundred sales.
watchFor.es: Prices set at exactly cost. Ask what they've earned after a hundred sales.

description.en: Introduce pricing concepts: * Cost: What it cost you to make * Price: What you charge customers (must be higher than cost!) * Profit: Price − Cost. Students decide on selling price: * Must cover costs * Add profit margin * Consider quality and uniqueness. Create price tag for their item
description.es: Introduce pricing concepts: * Cost: What it cost you to make * Price: What you charge customers (must be higher than cost!) * Profit: Price − Cost. Students decide on selling price: * Must cover costs * Add profit margin * Consider quality and uniqueness. Create price tag for their item

sayThis.en: "A shop bracelet is a dollar and a machine made it in thirty seconds. Yours cost three fifty and took twelve minutes. Which would you rather be given? And why is yours more?"
sayThis.es: "A shop bracelet is a dollar and a machine made it in thirty seconds. Yours cost three fifty and took twelve minutes. Which would you rather be given? And why is yours more?"

doneWhen.en: At least three reasons a handmade thing costs more are written on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least three reasons a handmade thing costs more are written on the board.

watchFor.en: "Mine is worse because it costs more." Turn it round: who made the shop one, and how long did they get?
watchFor.es: "Mine is worse because it costs more." Turn it round: who made the shop one, and how long did they get?

description.en: Compare handmade items to store-bought equivalents: * Handmade beaded bracelet: $3.50 (took 12 minutes) * Store-bought bracelet: $1.00 (factory made in 30 seconds). Discuss questions: * "Why does the handmade one cost more?" * "Which would you rather receive as a gift? Why?" * "What's the difference in quality?" * "Does the handmade one have special value beyond the price?"
description.es: Compare handmade items to store-bought equivalents: * Handmade beaded bracelet: $3.50 (took 12 minutes) * Store-bought bracelet: $1.00 (factory made in 30 seconds). Discuss questions: * "Why does the handmade one cost more?" * "Which would you rather receive as a gift? Why?" * "What's the difference in quality?" * "Does the handmade one have special value beyond the price?"

sayThis.en: "Everything out on the table. Walk past all of it. Every single one is the only one of its kind, because you made it."
sayThis.es: "Everything out on the table. Walk past all of it. Every single one is the only one of its kind, because you made it."

doneWhen.en: Every item is on the table with its price tag and every student has walked the length of it.
doneWhen.es: Every item is on the table with its price tag and every student has walked the length of it.

watchFor.en: Ranking and comparing. Ask them to find one thing they'd never have thought of themselves.
watchFor.es: Ranking and comparing. Ask them to find one thing they'd never have thought of themselves.

description.en: Set up mini "market display" of all creations. Students walk through, observe variety and uniqueness. Reflection: "Every item is one-of-a-kind because you made it!" beforeClass.en: Put the price list at every station, big enough to read from a seated child's eye height. One timer per station. The costing only works if the prices are visible while they build, not afterwards.
beforeClass.es: Put the price list at every station, big enough to read from a seated child's eye height. One timer per station. The costing only works if the prices are visible while they build, not afterwards.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the gallery to a walk past the table. Short: add a second item at a different station and compare the two costs.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the gallery to a walk past the table. Short: add a second item at a different station and compare the two costs.

title.en: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
title.es: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
20.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

description.en: Show two items: a dollar bill and a family photo. Ask: "Which can you buy? Which is priceless?". Explain: "Priceless means so special you could never buy it". Share: "Today we'll draw something priceless to you"
description.es: Show two items: a dollar bill and a family photo. Ask: "Which can you buy? Which is priceless?". Explain: "Priceless means so special you could never buy it". Share: "Today we'll draw something priceless to you"

description.en: Students draw something priceless to them: * A person they love (family member, friend, teacher, pet) * A special memory (birthday party, family trip, special day) * Something they treasure (not for its cost, but for meaning). Encourage detail and color. Circulate and ask: "Why is this priceless to you?"
description.es: Students draw something priceless to them: * A person they love (family member, friend, teacher, pet) * A special memory (birthday party, family trip, special day) * Something they treasure (not for its cost, but for meaning). Encourage detail and color. Circulate and ask: "Why is this priceless to you?"

description.en: Simple sentence frame: * K: Dictate to teacher: "My _____ is priceless because _____" * 1st: Copy and complete: "_____ is priceless to me."
description.es: Simple sentence frame: * K: Dictate to teacher: "My _____ is priceless because _____" * 1st: Copy and complete: "_____ is priceless to me."

description.en: Volunteers share drawings with class. "This is priceless to me because.". Celebrate diversity of what people treasure
description.es: Volunteers share drawings with class. "This is priceless to me because.". Celebrate diversity of what people treasure

discussionQuestions: Can you buy love at a store?
Is a hug worth money? Why is it important anyway?
What's something you love that doesn't cost anything?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
materials: Magazines or printed images for collage
Optional: printed family photo if families consent

description.en: Discuss value beyond price: sentimental value, memories, who gave it to you. Share examples of items that are special but didn't cost much.
description.es: Discuss value beyond price: sentimental value, memories, who gave it to you. Share examples of items that are special but didn't cost much.

description.en: Students think about special memory or important person. Choose what to create: memory drawing, thank-you card, or story illustration.
description.es: Students think about special memory or important person. Choose what to create: memory drawing, thank-you card, or story illustration.

description.en: Students create memory art project thoughtfully. Include who/what it's about, why it's special. Add details that show meaning.
description.es: Students create memory art project thoughtfully. Include who/what it's about, why it's special. Add details that show meaning.

description.en: Students write 2-3 sentences about their memory art: who, what, when, why it matters. Practice reading their story.
description.es: Students write 2-3 sentences about their memory art: who, what, when, why it matters. Practice reading their story.

description.en: Students share memory art and stories with class. Discuss: What makes these items valuable even if they didn't cost money? How do memories add value?
description.es: Students share memory art and stories with class. Discuss: What makes these items valuable even if they didn't cost money? How do memories add value?

discussionQuestions: Why can't you buy the thing you drew?
If someone offered you a million dollars for your [family/pet/memory], would you sell? Why not?
How is priceless different from expensive?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project
materials: Quality art paper, card stock, or small canvases
Variety of art supplies (paints, markers, colored pencils, pastels)
Collage materials (magazines, fabric scraps, decorative paper)
Frames or decorative borders (can be hand-made)
Display materials (easels, stands, or wall space)
Cultural resources: images of Day of the Dead altars, book about tradition

sayThis.en: "Some things can't be bought. Not because they're expensive — because money is the wrong thing to offer. A grandmother. A Sunday morning. A song your family sings. Today you make something for one of those."
sayThis.es: "Some things can't be bought. Not because they're expensive — because money is the wrong thing to offer. A grandmother. A Sunday morning. A song your family sings. Today you make something for one of those."

doneWhen.en: At least five different priceless things are written on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least five different priceless things are written on the board.

watchFor.en: Jokes covering discomfort. Take the first serious answer and stay with it a moment; the room follows.
watchFor.es: Jokes covering discomfort. Take the first serious answer and stay with it a moment; the room follows.

description.en: Read short book or show images about Day of the Dead tradition. Discuss key concept: "People honor loved ones with priceless offerings—photos, favorite foods, treasured items". Introduce FL concept: Intrinsic Value * "Value that exists inside something, not based on money" * "Things that matter for what they ARE, not what they cost". Examples of priceless things: * People you love (can't buy family) * Memories (can't purchase experiences after they happen) * Cultural traditions (can't buy heritage) * Feelings (love, joy, connection). Students brainstorm: "What's priceless to you?"
description.es: Read short book or show images about Day of the Dead tradition. Discuss key concept: "People honor loved ones with priceless offerings—photos, favorite foods, treasured items". Introduce FL concept: Intrinsic Value * "Value that exists inside something, not based on money" * "Things that matter for what they ARE, not what they cost". Examples of priceless things: * People you love (can't buy family) * Memories (can't purchase experiences after they happen) * Cultural traditions (can't buy heritage) * Feelings (love, joy, connection). Students brainstorm: "What's priceless to you?"

sayThis.en: "Twenty minutes on one piece. Not a doodle — the real thing. Draw it, cut things out, write words into it. If a stranger looked at this without you standing there, would they know what it's about?"
sayThis.es: "Twenty minutes on one piece. Not a doodle — the real thing. Draw it, cut things out, write words into it. If a stranger looked at this without you standing there, would they know what it's about?"

doneWhen.en: Every student has a piece with at least two different materials on it.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a piece with at least two different materials on it.

watchFor.en: The student finished in four minutes. Ask what else belongs in it, then leave them to it.
watchFor.es: The student finished in four minutes. Ask what else belongs in it, then leave them to it.

description.en: Students create artwork honoring something priceless: * Theme A: Person who is priceless to me (family, friend, teacher, mentor) * Theme B: Memory that's priceless (special day, tradition, experience) * Theme C: Value that matters more than money (kindness, love, honesty, family). Use mixed media for depth: * Drawing/painting base * Collage elements * Written words incorporated * Symbolic representations. Quality encouraged: this is honoring something precious. Teacher circulates, asks guiding questions: "Why is this priceless? What does it represent?"
description.es: Students create artwork honoring something priceless: * Theme A: Person who is priceless to me (family, friend, teacher, mentor) * Theme B: Memory that's priceless (special day, tradition, experience) * Theme C: Value that matters more than money (kindness, love, honesty, family). Use mixed media for depth: * Drawing/painting base * Collage elements * Written words incorporated * Symbolic representations. Quality encouraged: this is honoring something precious. Teacher circulates, asks guiding questions: "Why is this priceless? What does it represent?"

sayThis.en: "Everything in a museum has a card. Title. Your name. What it's made of. Who or what it honours. And the line that matters — what would you say if someone offered you a million dollars for it?"
sayThis.es: "Everything in a museum has a card. Title. Your name. What it's made of. Who or what it honours. And the line that matters — what would you say if someone offered you a million dollars for it?"

doneWhen.en: Every card has a title, an artist name and the honours line filled in.
doneWhen.es: Every card has a title, an artist name and the honours line filled in.

watchFor.en: Cards left blank because the words are hard. Give them a sentence to finish out loud.
watchFor.es: Cards left blank because the words are hard. Give them a sentence to finish out loud.

description.en: Students complete detailed museum card: ``` TITLE: _________________________ Artist: ________________________ Medium: ________________________ ARTIST'S STATEMENT: This artwork honors: ____________________ This is priceless to me because: ____________________________________ ____________________________________ REFLECTION ON VALUE: Market value (what you could buy it for): $_____ or ☑ Cannot be bought Intrinsic value (what it's worth to me): ____________________ Emotional value: _______________________ If someone offered me $1,000,000 for this, I would: □ Never sell—it's priceless □ Consider it, but probably say no □ Explain why you can't put a price on it: _______________ ```
description.es: Students complete detailed museum card: ``` TITLE: _________________________ Artist: ________________________ Medium: ________________________ ARTIST'S STATEMENT: This artwork honors: ____________________ This is priceless to me because: ____________________________________ ____________________________________ REFLECTION ON VALUE: Market value (what you could buy it for): $_____ or ☑ Cannot be bought Intrinsic value (what it's worth to me): ____________________ Emotional value: _______________________ If someone offered me $1,000,000 for this, I would: □ Never sell—it's priceless □ Consider it, but probably say no □ Explain why you can't put a price on it: _______________ ```

sayThis.en: "Card beside the piece, not underneath it. Quiet from here on. This is a gallery now, not a classroom."
sayThis.es: "Card beside the piece, not underneath it. Quiet from here on. This is a gallery now, not a classroom."

doneWhen.en: Every piece is displayed with a readable card beside it.
doneWhen.es: Every piece is displayed with a readable card beside it.

watchFor.en: Pieces stacked or half hidden. Every one gets its own space.
watchFor.es: Pieces stacked or half hidden. Every one gets its own space.

description.en: Arrange classroom as art gallery. Display artwork with museum cards. Create respectful viewing environment (quiet, thoughtful). Optional: Add battery-operated candles, flowers for Day of the Dead altar aesthetic
description.es: Arrange classroom as art gallery. Display artwork with museum cards. Create respectful viewing environment (quiet, thoughtful). Optional: Add battery-operated candles, flowers for Day of the Dead altar aesthetic

sayThis.en: "Walk it in silence. Read every card. Then one note on one piece that isn't yours — say what you noticed, not whether you liked it."
sayThis.es: "Walk it in silence. Read every card. Then one note on one piece that isn't yours — say what you noticed, not whether you liked it."

doneWhen.en: Every piece has at least one note on it.
doneWhen.es: Every piece has at least one note on it.

watchFor.en: Notes going to friends only. Set the rule out loud: nobody's piece is left with nothing on it.
watchFor.es: Notes going to friends only. Set the rule out loud: nobody's piece is left with nothing on it.

description.en: Students walk through gallery silently, reading museum cards. Observe what classmates treasure. Notice diversity of priceless things. Appreciation activity: Place sticky notes with positive messages
description.es: Students walk through gallery silently, reading museum cards. Observe what classmates treasure. Notice diversity of priceless things. Appreciation activity: Place sticky notes with positive messages

discussionQuestions: What's priceless to you?
Why is this priceless? What does it represent?
Can you put a price on nature? Clean air? Friendship?

beforeClass.en: Decide now how you'll handle a student whose priceless thing is somebody who died. Have a quiet word ready and a second theme they can take instead. Lay the materials out before the room comes in; this lesson should start calm.
beforeClass.es: Decide now how you'll handle a student whose priceless thing is somebody who died. Have a quiet word ready and a second theme they can take instead. Lay the materials out before the room comes in; this lesson should start calm.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the gallery setup to pushing two tables together. Short: add one line to the museum card — who else should see this, and why?
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the gallery setup to pushing two tables together. Short: add one line to the museum card — who else should see this, and why?

materials: Student-made items (one per student from previous activities: paper ornaments from CH10, drawings from CH11, etc.)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($5 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Arrange students in circle on floor. Each student places their item in front of them and writes $5 on a scrap-paper budget card. Explain: "We're having a market! You can buy one thing from a friend."
description.es: Arrange students in circle on floor. Each student places their item in front of them and writes $5 on a scrap-paper budget card. Explain: "We're having a market! You can buy one thing from a friend."

description.en: Students walk around circle looking at items. Decide what they want to buy. Approach vendor: "I'd like to buy your ___. How much?". Vendor sets price (teacher supports: "What's fair?"). Simple transaction: exchange money for item. Everyone buys exactly one thing
description.es: Students walk around circle looking at items. Decide what they want to buy. Approach vendor: "I'd like to buy your ___. How much?". Vendor sets price (teacher supports: "What's fair?"). Simple transaction: exchange money for item. Everyone buys exactly one thing

description.en: Return to circle seats. Each student shows what they bought. "I bought ___ from ___ for $___ because ___". Celebrate: everyone traded successfully!
description.es: Return to circle seats. Each student shows what they bought. "I bought ___ from ___ for $___ because ___". Celebrate: everyone traded successfully!

description.en: "What did you learn about markets this year?". "What was your favorite FL lesson?"
description.es: "What did you learn about markets this year?". "What was your favorite FL lesson?"

description.en: Divide class into booth vendors and shoppers (will rotate) - Booth Types: * Handmade Crafts (items from CH10) * Art Gallery (items from CH11) * Paper Goods (paper treats drawn and cut from card—discuss cost of goods) * Repair Shop (Diego-style—fix broken toys or sharpen pencils for fee).
