ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Hold up a plain box and a decorated box and point as you name each part: name, logo, colors.
Put box, brand, logo and color on the board with a picture beside each word.
Let the student use a picture logo and a one-word brand name.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Give a box that is already folded so the time goes to decorating.
Offer a logo shape to trace, or stickers to decorate with.
Let the student say the brand name and write it for them.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Design two packages for the same product for two different customers, and say which would sell better.
Add up the full packaging cost and work out how much more you must charge to make it worth it.
Design a package that uses the least material but still looks good.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Playdough or homemade clay (one ball per student)
Paper or plastic mat for work surface
Simple goal: "Make a bowl or cup"

description.en: Introduce clay: what it is, how it's used, why makers use it. Demonstrate basic techniques: rolling, pinching, smoothing. Review clay safety: wet hands, gentle handling, cleanup procedures.
description.es: Introduce clay: what it is, how it's used, why makers use it. Demonstrate basic techniques: rolling, pinching, smoothing. Review clay safety: wet hands, gentle handling, cleanup procedures.

sayThis.en: "This is clay. People have made pots from it for a very long time. Watch: I roll it, I pinch it, I smooth it. A wet finger helps. Clay stays on your plate."
sayThis.es: "This is clay. People have made pots from it for a very long time. Watch: I roll it, I pinch it, I smooth it. A wet finger helps. Clay stays on your plate."

watchFor.en: Kids squeezing the clay while you talk. Say "Hands in your lap until I say go."
watchFor.es: Kids squeezing the clay while you talk. Say "Hands in your lap until I say go."

doneWhen.en: You have shown rolling, pinching and smoothing once each.
doneWhen.es: You have shown rolling, pinching and smoothing once each.

description.en: Students explore clay through play: squeeze, roll into balls, make coils (snakes), flatten into pancakes. Get familiar with how clay feels and moves. Experiment with basic shapes.
description.es: Students explore clay through play: squeeze, roll into balls, make coils (snakes), flatten into pancakes. Get familiar with how clay feels and moves. Experiment with basic shapes.

sayThis.en: "Play with it. Squeeze it. Roll a ball. Roll a snake. Press it flat like a pancake. See what it does."
sayThis.es: "Play with it. Squeeze it. Roll a ball. Roll a snake. Press it flat like a pancake. See what it does."

watchFor.en: Clay drying and cracking. Dip a finger in the water and smooth it.
watchFor.es: Clay drying and cracking. Dip a finger in the water and smooth it.

doneWhen.en: Every child has made a ball, a snake and a pancake.
doneWhen.es: Every child has made a ball, a snake and a pancake.

description.en: Students create simple clay object: bowl, animal, cup, or decorative item. Practice techniques: pinching to shape, smoothing cracks, joining pieces. Work carefully and thoughtfully.
description.es: Students create simple clay object: bowl, animal, cup, or decorative item. Practice techniques: pinching to shape, smoothing cracks, joining pieces. Work carefully and thoughtfully.

sayThis.en: "Now make one thing: a bowl, a cup or an animal. Pinch to shape it. Rub out cracks with a wet finger. Press pieces on hard so they stick."
sayThis.es: "Now make one thing: a bowl, a cup or an animal. Pinch to shape it. Rub out cracks with a wet finger. Press pieces on hard so they stick."

watchFor.en: Legs and ears falling off. Show how to scratch both pieces with the craft stick and press them together.
watchFor.es: Legs and ears falling off. Show how to scratch both pieces with the craft stick and press them together.

doneWhen.en: Every child has one object on the plate.
doneWhen.es: Every child has one object on the plate.

description.en: Students add details to their clay creation: texture with tools, carved patterns, smoothed surfaces. Refine shape and appearance. Prepare for drying.
description.es: Students add details to their clay creation: texture with tools, carved patterns, smoothed surfaces. Refine shape and appearance. Prepare for drying.

sayThis.en: "Use your stick to add lines or dots. Smooth the rest. Then leave it on the plate to dry."
sayThis.es: "Use your stick to add lines or dots. Smooth the rest. Then leave it on the plate to dry."

watchFor.en: Kids poking holes right through. Say "Press soft. Just the top."
watchFor.es: Kids poking holes right through. Say "Press soft. Just the top."

doneWhen.en: Every piece has a detail and sits on its plate in the drying spot.
doneWhen.es: Every piece has a detail and sits on its plate in the drying spot.

description.en: Students display their clay creations for gallery walk. Discuss: What was challenging about clay? What techniques worked? How is clay different from other art materials? What would you make next time?
description.es: Students display their clay creations for gallery walk. Discuss: What was challenging about clay? What techniques worked? How is clay different from other art materials? What would you make next time?

sayThis.en: "Walk and look. Don't touch. What was hard? What would you make next time?"
sayThis.es: "Walk and look. Don't touch. What was hard? What would you make next time?"

watchFor.en: Kids picking up other pieces. Hands behind backs for the walk.
watchFor.es: Kids picking up other pieces. Hands behind backs for the walk.

doneWhen.en: Every piece is on show and a few kids have said what was hard.
doneWhen.es: Every piece is on show and a few kids have said what was hard.

discussionQuestions: Was it easy or hard to shape clay?
Did your bowl turn out perfect?
What would happen if you practiced every day?

beforeClass.en: Split the clay into one ball per child and set each on a paper plate with a craft stick. Put a cup of water on every table and pick a spot where pieces can dry.
beforeClass.es: Split the clay into one ball per child and set each on a paper plate with a craft stick. Put a cup of water on every table and pick a spot where pieces can dry.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Detail & Finishing, skip the carving and just smooth the shape. Short: in Gallery & Reflection, have each child tell a partner what they would make next time.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Detail & Finishing, skip the carving and just smooth the shape. Short: in Gallery & Reflection, have each child tell a partner what they would make next time.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Guided Clay Project with Value Discussion
materials: Air-dry clay or playdough (sufficient for each student to make 2-3 small items)
Simple tools (popsicle sticks, plastic knives, straws for texture)
Optional: water in small cups for smoothing

description.en: Examine different clay types. Brief discussion: people have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It's free from the earth, moldable, and useful. Only one clay? Compare the air-dry clay with a clay pot or mug from home, or a photo of one.
description.es: Examine different clay types. Brief discussion: people have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It's free from the earth, moldable, and useful. Only one clay? Compare the air-dry clay with a clay pot or mug from home, or a photo of one.

sayThis.en: "Feel this clay. People have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It comes from the ground, it's cheap, and you can shape it."
sayThis.es: "Feel this clay. People have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It comes from the ground, it's cheap, and you can shape it."

watchFor.en: Kids starting to build now. Say "Just feel it. We build soon."
watchFor.es: Kids starting to build now. Say "Just feel it. We build soon."

doneWhen.en: Every student has touched the clay and heard why people use it.
doneWhen.es: Every student has touched the clay and heard why people use it.

description.en: Demonstrate 3-4 techniques: pinch pot, coil building, slab construction, and stamp texturing. Students practice each briefly before choosing their project. No stamps? Press the end of a craft stick or a pencil tip in a pattern.
description.es: Demonstrate 3-4 techniques: pinch pot, coil building, slab construction, and stamp texturing. Students practice each briefly before choosing their project. No stamps? Press the end of a craft stick or a pencil tip in a pattern.

sayThis.en: "Watch me make a pinch pot, a coil, a flat slab, and a pressed pattern. After each one, you try it for a minute. Then pick the one you like best."
sayThis.es: "Watch me make a pinch pot, a coil, a flat slab, and a pressed pattern. After each one, you try it for a minute. Then pick the one you like best."

watchFor.en: Kids falling behind and skipping a technique. Keep each try short; unfinished is fine.
watchFor.es: Kids falling behind and skipping a technique. Keep each try short; unfinished is fine.

doneWhen.en: Every student has tried each technique and picked one.
doneWhen.es: Every student has tried each technique and picked one.

description.en: Students create their chosen project using learned techniques. Encourage adding details and personal touches. Teacher circulates to support and challenge.
description.es: Students create their chosen project using learned techniques. Encourage adding details and personal touches. Teacher circulates to support and challenge.

sayThis.en: "Make your project with the technique you picked. Add one detail that is just yours. Keep it thick so it doesn't crack."
sayThis.es: "Make your project with the technique you picked. Add one detail that is just yours. Keep it thick so it doesn't crack."

watchFor.en: Walls pinched so thin they tear. Tell them to keep the wall as thick as a finger.
watchFor.es: Walls pinched so thin they tear. Tell them to keep the wall as thick as a finger.

doneWhen.en: Every student has a finished piece on the plate.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a finished piece on the plate.

description.en: Discuss: How much would this cost to buy in a store? How much did our materials cost? Calculate the value of skill — your hands and knowledge turned cheap clay into something valuable. Tier 1 (K-1): say if your piece is worth more than the lump of clay, and why.
description.es: Discuss: How much would this cost to buy in a store? How much did our materials cost? Calculate the value of skill — your hands and knowledge turned cheap clay into something valuable. Tier 1 (K-1): say if your piece is worth more than the lump of clay, and why.

sayThis.en: "This clay cost about fifty cents. What would a bowl like this cost in a store? The difference is what your hands added."
sayThis.es: "This clay cost about fifty cents. What would a bowl like this cost in a store? The difference is what your hands added."

watchFor.en: Kids saying the clay made it worth more. Point out that everyone had the same clay.
watchFor.es: Kids saying the clay made it worth more. Point out that everyone had the same clay.

doneWhen.en: A store price and the clay cost are on the board, with one reason for the gap.
doneWhen.es: A store price and the clay cost are on the board, with one reason for the gap.

description.en: Display all creations. Students assign a fair price to their work considering materials, time, and skill. Compare: Why are handmade items often more expensive than factory-made? Tier 1 (K-1): pick a price up to $10 for your piece.
description.es: Display all creations. Students assign a fair price to their work considering materials, time, and skill. Compare: Why are handmade items often more expensive than factory-made? Tier 1 (K-1): pick a price up to $10 for your piece.

sayThis.en: "Put your piece on show. Write a fair price beside it. Think about the clay, your time and your skill."
sayThis.es: "Put your piece on show. Write a fair price beside it. Think about the clay, your time and your skill."

watchFor.en: Prices like a hundred dollars. Ask "Would you pay that for a friend's?"
watchFor.es: Prices like a hundred dollars. Ask "Would you pay that for a friend's?"

doneWhen.en: Every piece has a price beside it.
doneWhen.es: Every piece has a price beside it.

description.en: Share one thing learned about how skill adds value to raw materials. Clean up workspace and set projects to dry.
description.es: Share one thing learned about how skill adds value to raw materials. Clean up workspace and set projects to dry.

sayThis.en: "Tell your neighbor one way skill made the clay worth more. Then plates to the drying spot and wipe your table."
sayThis.es: "Tell your neighbor one way skill made the clay worth more. Then plates to the drying spot and wipe your table."

watchFor.en: Cleanup turning into clay throwing. Collect loose lumps first, then wipe.
watchFor.es: Cleanup turning into clay throwing. Collect loose lumps first, then wipe.

doneWhen.en: Every piece is in the drying spot and every table is clean.
doneWhen.es: Every piece is in the drying spot and every table is clean.

discussionQuestions: Did your project turn out better than your practice tries?
How does practice change the value of what you make?
If clay costs $1 but a skilled potter spends an hour making a beautiful bowl, what should they charge?
Why do handmade pottery items cost more than plastic bowls?

beforeClass.en: Split the clay into equal lumps and set each on a paper plate with a craft stick, plus a cup of water per table. Have a clay pot, mug or photo ready to compare, and choose a drying spot.
beforeClass.es: Split the clay into equal lumps and set each on a paper plate with a craft stick, plus a cup of water per table. Have a clay pot, mug or photo ready to compare, and choose a drying spot.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Technique Demonstrations, show pinch pot and coil only. Short: in Gallery Walk & Pricing, have each student explain their price to a partner.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Technique Demonstrations, show pinch pot and coil only. Short: in Gallery Walk & Pricing, have each student explain their price to a partner.

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Full Pottery Workshop with Skill & Cost Analysis
materials: Air-dry clay or pottery clay (enough for multiple attempts per student)
Pottery tools (if available) or simple substitutes

sayThis.en: "Three ways to make a pot. Pinch it, coil it, or slab it. Four minutes each. You're not making anything good yet — you're finding out which one your hands like."
sayThis.es: "Three ways to make a pot. Pinch it, coil it, or slab it. Four minutes each. You're not making anything good yet — you're finding out which one your hands like."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a rough attempt at all three techniques sitting in front of them.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a rough attempt at all three techniques sitting in front of them.

watchFor.en: Students deciding after thirty seconds that they can't do it. Everyone tries all three. That's the rule.
watchFor.es: Students deciding after thirty seconds that they can't do it. Everyone tries all three. That's the rule.

description.en: Demonstrate 3 techniques: pinch pot, coil bowl, slab tile; Students try each briefly (3-4 min per technique); Take mental note of which feels most natural
description.es: Demonstrate 3 techniques: pinch pot, coil bowl, slab tile; Students try each briefly (3-4 min per technique); Take mental note of which feels most natural

sayThis.en: "Pick one. Make three. Number them one, two, three, and write down how long each took. You're not trying to make three the same. You're trying to make each one better than the last."
sayThis.es: "Pick one. Make three. Number them one, two, three, and write down how long each took. You're not trying to make three the same. You're trying to make each one better than the last."

doneWhen.en: Every student has three numbered pieces with a time written for each.
doneWhen.es: Every student has three numbered pieces with a time written for each.

watchFor.en: Students squashing attempt one and starting again. Keep all three, even the ugly one. Especially the ugly one.
watchFor.es: Students squashing attempt one and starting again. Keep all three, even the ugly one. Especially the ugly one.

description.en: Choose ONE technique and make 3 items using it; Item 1: First attempt (track time); Item 2: Second attempt with improvements (track time); Item 3: Best effort with all you've learned (track time); Goal: see visible improvement across attempts. Tier 1 (K-1): make three and line them up in order; the teacher keeps time.
description.es: Choose ONE technique and make 3 items using it; Item 1: First attempt (track time); Item 2: Second attempt with improvements (track time); Item 3: Best effort with all you've learned (track time); Goal: see visible improvement across attempts. Tier 1 (K-1): make three and line them up in order; the teacher keeps time.

sayThis.en: "Score all three out of ten. Shape, smoothness, thickness. Be hard on number one — it's supposed to be the worst. Then measure them and see how close you got."
sayThis.es: "Score all three out of ten. Shape, smoothness, thickness. Be hard on number one — it's supposed to be the worst. Then measure them and see how close you got."

doneWhen.en: Every piece has a written score and a measurement beside it.
doneWhen.es: Every piece has a written score and a measurement beside it.

watchFor.en: Every piece scored an eight. Ask what a ten would look like, then score against that.
watchFor.es: Every piece scored an eight. Ask what a ten would look like, then score against that.

description.en: Rate each item 1-10 for: shape, smoothness, thickness consistency, overall quality; Measure dimensions—how close to consistent?; Calculate average quality score for each attempt. Tier 1 (K-1): point to your best piece and say why it is best.
description.es: Rate each item 1-10 for: shape, smoothness, thickness consistency, overall quality; Measure dimensions—how close to consistent?; Calculate average quality score for each attempt. Tier 1 (K-1): point to your best piece and say why it is best.

sayThis.en: "The clay cost fifty cents a piece. Same clay in all three. So why is number three worth more than number one? Nothing changed except you. A real potter charges twenty dollars for a bowl — what are they actually selling?"
sayThis.es: "The clay cost fifty cents a piece. Same clay in all three. So why is number three worth more than number one? Nothing changed except you. A real potter charges twenty dollars for a bowl — what are they actually selling?"

doneWhen.en: A reason the value went up with no change in materials is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: A reason the value went up with no change in materials is written on the board.

watchFor.en: The answer "better clay". Point at their own three pieces, all from the same lump.
watchFor.es: The answer "better clay". Point at their own three pieces, all from the same lump.

description.en: Clay cost: $0.50 per item; Time investment: [varies by student]; Calculate: "If I charge $1 per hour for my time, item 1 costs $__ [clay + time]. But my item 3 is much better quality—could I charge $5 for it?"; Discuss: skilled potters charge $20-100 for bowls. Why? (Years of practice = high skill = high value). Tier 1 (K-1): say which piece you could sell for more, and why.
description.es: Clay cost: $0.50 per item; Time investment: [varies by student]; Calculate: "If I charge $1 per hour for my time, item 1 costs $__ [clay + time]. But my item 3 is much better quality—could I charge $5 for it?"; Discuss: skilled potters charge $20-100 for bowls. Why? (Years of practice = high skill = high value). Tier 1 (K-1): say which piece you could sell for more, and why.

discussionQuestions: "How did your third item compare to your first?"
"What improved with practice? What's still hard?"
"If you made 100 bowls, how good would the 100th one be?"
"Why do people pay more for handmade pottery than factory-made?"
"How does a potter justify charging $50 for a mug when clay costs $1?"
"What's more valuable: the clay, or the skill in shaping it?"
"Would you rather buy a perfect bowl for $5 or a slightly wobbly handmade bowl for $5? Why?"
extensionIdeas: Let pieces dry, decorate in next session, calculate added value
Research professional potters—what do they charge? How long did it take to develop their skill?
Calculate: "If I practice 1 hour per day, how long until I'm skilled enough to sell bowls?"
Create a simple production line—each student does ONE step repeatedly (specialization experiment)

beforeClass.en: Portion the clay into equal lumps before the lesson. Dividing it live costs ten minutes and starts an argument. Cover the desks, and decide now where wet pieces sit for a week.
beforeClass.es: Portion the clay into equal lumps before the lesson. Dividing it live costs ten minutes and starts an argument. Cover the desks, and decide now where wet pieces sit for a week.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: drop the third attempt and compare two. Short: add a fourth attempt with a partner watching and coaching.

title.en: Design Upgrade: Adding Value Through Decoration
title.es: Design Upgrade: Adding Value Through Decoration

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Plain items (wooden spoons, paper cups, simple boxes, or clay items from CH5)

description.en: Show two identical cups/spoons. One plain, one decorated. "If these were in a store, plain = $2, decorated = $8. Why?" Discuss.
description.es: Show two identical cups/spoons. One plain, one decorated. "If these were in a store, plain = $2, decorated = $8. Why?" Discuss.

sayThis.en: "These two cups are the same. In a store, the plain one is $2. The decorated one is $8. Why would someone pay more?"
sayThis.es: "These two cups are the same. In a store, the plain one is $2. The decorated one is $8. Why would someone pay more?"

watchFor.en: Kids saying "it's pretty" and stopping. Ask "What did someone have to do to make it pretty?"
watchFor.es: Kids saying "it's pretty" and stopping. Ask "What did someone have to do to make it pretty?"

doneWhen.en: Someone has said time, work or skill.
doneWhen.es: Someone has said time, work or skill.

description.en: Each student decorates their plain item. Encourage: make it special, unique, beautiful.
description.es: Each student decorates their plain item. Encourage: make it special, unique, beautiful.

sayThis.en: "Make your plain item special. Use colors and patterns. Make it the only one like it."
sayThis.es: "Make your plain item special. Use colors and patterns. Make it the only one like it."

watchFor.en: One quick scribble and done. Ask "Would someone pay $8 for this yet?"
watchFor.es: One quick scribble and done. Ask "Would someone pay $8 for this yet?"

doneWhen.en: Every item is decorated.
doneWhen.es: Every item is decorated.

description.en: Display all items. "Which would you pay more for? Why?" Count votes for most valuable-looking.
description.es: Display all items. "Which would you pay more for? Why?" Count votes for most valuable-looking.

sayThis.en: "Look at them all. Hands up for the one you would pay the most for. Why?"
sayThis.es: "Look at them all. Hands up for the one you would pay the most for. Why?"

watchFor.en: Kids voting only for their own. The rule: vote for someone else's.
watchFor.es: Kids voting only for their own. The rule: vote for someone else's.

doneWhen.en: Votes are counted and one child has said why.
doneWhen.es: Votes are counted and one child has said why.

discussionQuestions: Does decoration make something worth more?
Would you pay more for the decorated one?
How much more time did decorating take?

beforeClass.en: Decorate one of two matching cups or spoons ahead of time and keep the plain one beside it. Put a plain item and markers, crayons or stickers at every seat.
beforeClass.es: Decorate one of two matching cups or spoons ahead of time and keep the plain one beside it. Put a plain item and markers, crayons or stickers at every seat.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Quick Decoration, stop at four minutes and go to the vote. Short: in Value Vote, have kids tell a partner what price they'd put on their own item.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Quick Decoration, stop at four minutes and go to the vote. Short: in Value Vote, have kids tell a partner what price they'd put on their own item.

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Before & After Decoration with Price Tags
materials: Plain items to decorate (wood, paper, clay from previous session)
Full art supplies (paint, markers, stickers, stamps, ribbons)

description.en: Students receive plain item. "What's this worth in a store? $2? $5?" Write "before" price.
description.es: Students receive plain item. "What's this worth in a store? $2? $5?" Write "before" price.

sayThis.en: "Look at your plain item. If it sat in a store, what would it cost? Write that on your before card."
sayThis.es: "Look at your plain item. If it sat in a store, what would it cost? Write that on your before card."

watchFor.en: Wild guesses like $100. Give a range: between $1 and $5.
watchFor.es: Wild guesses like $100. Give a range: between $1 and $5.

doneWhen.en: Every before card has a price on it.
doneWhen.es: Every before card has a price on it.

description.en: Sketch quick design plan. What colors? What patterns? What will make it special?
description.es: Sketch quick design plan. What colors? What patterns? What will make it special?

sayThis.en: "Quick plan on paper. Draw the colors and the pattern you'll use. What will make yours special?"
sayThis.es: "Quick plan on paper. Draw the colors and the pattern you'll use. What will make yours special?"

watchFor.en: Kids skipping the plan to grab paint. Paint stays closed until the sketch is done.
watchFor.es: Kids skipping the plan to grab paint. Paint stays closed until the sketch is done.

doneWhen.en: Every student has a sketch with colors marked.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a sketch with colors marked.

description.en: Decorate item with quality and care. Track time spent. Tier 1 (K-1): decorate slowly; the teacher keeps time.
description.es: Decorate item with quality and care. Track time spent. Tier 1 (K-1): decorate slowly; the teacher keeps time.

sayThis.en: "Decorate with care. Slow and neat. Write down when you start and when you stop."
sayThis.es: "Decorate with care. Slow and neat. Write down when you start and when you stop."

watchFor.en: Kids done in three minutes. Ask "Would a store sell it like this?" and send them back to add detail.
watchFor.es: Kids done in three minutes. Ask "Would a store sell it like this?" and send them back to add detail.

doneWhen.en: Every item is decorated and has a start and stop time written.
doneWhen.es: Every item is decorated and has a start and stop time written.

description.en: "Now what's it worth? Would someone pay $10? $15? Why?" Write "after" price. Calculate value added. Tier 1 (K-1): say if the after price is more than the before price.
description.es: "Now what's it worth? Would someone pay $10? $15? Why?" Write "after" price. Calculate value added. Tier 1 (K-1): say if the after price is more than the before price.

sayThis.en: "Now what's it worth? Write your after price. Take away the before price. That's the value you added."
sayThis.es: "Now what's it worth? Write your after price. Take away the before price. That's the value you added."

watchFor.en: After prices with no reason. Ask "Why would someone pay that?"
watchFor.es: After prices with no reason. Ask "Why would someone pay that?"

doneWhen.en: Every student has a before price, an after price and the difference written down.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a before price, an after price and the difference written down.

discussionQuestions: How much did decoration increase the value?
Was the decoration time worth it?
If decoration took 15 minutes, and you charge $10 per hour for your time, decoration costs $2.50. If you can now charge $8 more, is that a good deal?
What makes some decoration more valuable than others?
extensionIdeas: Create price tags explaining why item is worth the new price ("Hand-painted by [name], one-of-a-kind design, hours of careful work").

beforeClass.en: Give each student one plain item, like a Chapter 5 clay piece or a paper cup, with a before and an after price card. Set out paint, brushes, stickers, markers and scrap paper for plans, and note the clock time when decorating starts.
beforeClass.es: Give each student one plain item, like a Chapter 5 clay piece or a paper cup, with a before and an after price card. Set out paint, brushes, stickers, markers and scrap paper for plans, and note the clock time when decorating starts.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Decoration Execution, stop at eight minutes and write the time. Short: in New Value Assessment, have partners price each other's items too.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Decoration Execution, stop at eight minutes and write the time. Short: in New Value Assessment, have partners price each other's items too.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Plain items (ideally pottery from CH5, or wood items, boxes, etc.)
Professional art supplies (acrylic paint, fine brushes, markers, stamps, gold leaf/metallic accents if available)

sayThis.en: "Same clay all the way along. One dollar as a lump. Five as a plain bowl. Twenty-five once somebody painted it. Nobody added any material. So what got added?"
sayThis.es: "Same clay all the way along. One dollar as a lump. Five as a plain bowl. Twenty-five once somebody painted it. Nobody added any material. So what got added?"

doneWhen.en: The three prices and at least two reasons for the jump are on the board.
doneWhen.es: The three prices and at least two reasons for the jump are on the board.

watchFor.en: The answer stopping at "paint". Push for the word behind it — time, skill, design.
watchFor.es: The answer stopping at "paint". Push for the word behind it — time, skill, design.

description.en: Show progression: Raw materials → Basic product → Decorated product - Real example: Clay $1 → Plain bowl $5 → Decorated bowl $25 - Each step adds value through labor, skill, design
description.es: Show progression: Raw materials → Basic product → Decorated product - Real example: Clay $1 → Plain bowl $5 → Decorated bowl $25 - Each step adds value through labor, skill, design

sayThis.en: "Look at the professional ones first. Then plan yours on paper — where the pattern goes, which colors, how long you think it'll take. Hand-painted is worth more than a sticker. That isn't an opinion, it's a price."
sayThis.es: "Look at the professional ones first. Then plan yours on paper — where the pattern goes, which colors, how long you think it'll take. Hand-painted is worth more than a sticker. That isn't an opinion, it's a price."

doneWhen.en: Every plan shows a drawn design, named techniques and an estimated time.
doneWhen.es: Every plan shows a drawn design, named techniques and an estimated time.

watchFor.en: Plans with no time estimate on them. You need that number two steps from now.
watchFor.es: Plans with no time estimate on them. You need that number two steps from now.

description.en: Research: look at professional decorated pottery/items (examples or photos) - Design detailed decoration plan - Choose techniques that add value (hand-painted > stickers in professional market) - Estimate time needed. Tier 1 (K-1): draw your plan; skip the time guess.
description.es: Research: look at professional decorated pottery/items (examples or photos) - Design detailed decoration plan - Choose techniques that add value (hand-painted > stickers in professional market) - Estimate time needed. Tier 1 (K-1): draw your plan; skip the time guess.

sayThis.en: "Fifteen minutes. Slow and good beats fast and messy, because the whole point is that skill is the thing worth paying for. Keep track of your real time, not your guess."
sayThis.es: "Fifteen minutes. Slow and good beats fast and messy, because the whole point is that skill is the thing worth paying for. Keep track of your real time, not your guess."

doneWhen.en: Every piece is decorated and an actual time is written beside the estimate.
doneWhen.es: Every piece is decorated and an actual time is written beside the estimate.

watchFor.en: Rushing to finish early. Ask them whether they'd hand over money for it as it stands.
watchFor.es: Rushing to finish early. Ask them whether they'd hand over money for it as it stands.

description.en: Execute design with quality focus - Track actual time spent - Take "before" and "after" photos - Quality check: Does this look professional enough to sell? Tier 1 (K-1): decorate slowly; the teacher keeps time.
description.es: Execute design with quality focus - Track actual time spent - Take "before" and "after" photos - Quality check: Does this look professional enough to sell? Tier 1 (K-1): decorate slowly; the teacher keeps time.

sayThis.en: "Add your materials, then your time at ten dollars an hour. That's your cost. Now go and ask five people what they'd pay. Then set your price — and check whether anyone would actually hand it over."
sayThis.es: "Add your materials, then your time at ten dollars an hour. That's your cost. Now go and ask five people what they'd pay. Then set your price — and check whether anyone would actually hand it over."

doneWhen.en: Every piece has a cost, a survey result and a final price written down.
doneWhen.es: Every piece has a cost, a survey result and a final price written down.

watchFor.en: Prices set from pride rather than from the survey. Show them their own survey numbers.
watchFor.es: Prices set from pride rather than from the survey. Show them their own survey numbers.

description.en: Calculate costs: materials + time (at $10/hour labor) + skill premium - Survey classmates: "Would you buy this? For how much?" - Compare estimated value to actual market prices - Determine optimal price point - Calculate profit margin: (price − cost) / price = margin %. Tier 1 (K-1): ask two friends if they would buy it, then pick a price up to $10.
description.es: Calculate costs: materials + time (at $10/hour labor) + skill premium - Survey classmates: "Would you buy this? For how much?" - Compare estimated value to actual market prices - Determine optimal price point - Calculate profit margin: (price − cost) / price = margin %. Tier 1 (K-1): ask two friends if they would buy it, then pick a price up to $10.

discussionQuestions: Your plain item was worth $5. Decoration cost you $3 in time and materials. You can now sell for $15. What's your profit?
Why do people pay more for hand-decorated items?
Is decoration always worth it? When might it not be?
How does uniqueness affect value? (One-of-a-kind vs. mass-produced)
What decoration techniques add the most value? Why?
If you decorated 100 items, would you get faster? Would that change your pricing?
Compare to factory decoration—why does hand-painted cost more?
extensionIdeas: A/B test: create two versions (simple decoration vs. elaborate), survey which people prefer
Cost different decoration levels: minimal (+$2), moderate (+$5), elaborate (+$10)
Research professional decorators—what do they charge? Calculate hourly rates
Create "artist statement" explaining decoration choices
Photography for marketing—does good photo increase perceived value?

beforeClass.en: Put the three-stage example out where everyone can see it: the raw material, the plain item, the decorated one, labeled one dollar, five dollars, twenty-five. That single row of objects is the lesson.
beforeClass.es: Put the three-stage example out where everyone can see it: the raw material, the plain item, the decorated one, labeled one dollar, five dollars, twenty-five. That single row of objects is the lesson.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the classmate survey to five people. Short: add a second decoration in a different style and price both.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the classmate survey to five people. Short: add a second decoration in a different style and price both.

strategies: Hold up the plain and decorated items side by side and say: before, after, worth more.

strategies: Make a simple and a fancy version, and survey which one people would pay more for.

20.bestFor: Tight schedules, daily scheduling
materials: Ice cubes and a bowl of water for the melting demo
Two colors of washable paint for the color-mixing demo
Squares of scrap paper for the origami demo

description.en: Three demonstrations showing materials changing form: ice melting (solid to liquid), mixing colors (two become one new), folding paper into origami (flat to 3D). Ask: Is the new thing worth more?
description.es: Three demonstrations showing materials changing form: ice melting (solid to liquid), mixing colors (two become one new), folding paper into origami (flat to 3D). Ask: Is the new thing worth more?

sayThis.en: "Watch three things change. Ice turns to water. Two colors make a new color. Flat paper becomes a shape. Is the new thing worth more?"
sayThis.es: "Watch three things change. Ice turns to water. Two colors make a new color. Flat paper becomes a shape. Is the new thing worth more?"

watchFor.en: Yes as the answer every time. Point at the melted ice and ask if a puddle is worth more than ice.
watchFor.es: Yes as the answer every time. Point at the melted ice and ask if a puddle is worth more than ice.

doneWhen.en: All three demos are done and the class has voted worth more or worth less on each.
doneWhen.es: All three demos are done and the class has voted worth more or worth less on each.

description.en: Show a simple value chain: wheat → flour → bread → sandwich. Each step adds value. Raw materials are cheap, finished products cost more because of the work to transform them.
description.es: Show a simple value chain: wheat → flour → bread → sandwich. Each step adds value. Raw materials are cheap, finished products cost more because of the work to transform them.

sayThis.en: "Wheat makes flour. Flour makes bread. Bread makes a sandwich. Each time, someone did work. The work makes it cost more."
sayThis.es: "Wheat makes flour. Flour makes bread. Bread makes a sandwich. Each time, someone did work. The work makes it cost more."

watchFor.en: Kids who have never seen wheat. Draw a quick stalk on the board so they have a picture.
watchFor.es: Kids who have never seen wheat. Draw a quick stalk on the board so they have a picture.

doneWhen.en: The four-stage chain is on the board with an arrow between each stage.
doneWhen.es: The four-stage chain is on the board with an arrow between each stage.

description.en: Rotate through 3-4 stations where students transform materials: weaving strips into placemats, mixing sorted beads and buttons into craft kits, assembling parts into simple structures. Track time spent at each.
description.es: Rotate through 3-4 stations where students transform materials: weaving strips into placemats, mixing sorted beads and buttons into craft kits, assembling parts into simple structures. Track time spent at each.

sayThis.en: "Now you are the maker. Weave the paper, fill a craft kit, or build with cardboard. Make one thing. When I ring, stop and write your time."
sayThis.es: "Now you are the maker. Weave the paper, fill a craft kit, or build with cardboard. Make one thing. When I ring, stop and write your time."

watchFor.en: Beads and buttons going in mouths or noses with little ones. Keep the bead tray where you can see it and count it back in.
watchFor.es: Beads and buttons going in mouths or noses with little ones. Keep the bead tray where you can see it and count it back in.

doneWhen.en: Every student is holding one finished thing with a time written on it.
doneWhen.es: Every student is holding one finished thing with a time written on it.

description.es: For each station, calculate: raw material cost vs. finished product value. How much did transformation add? sayThis.en: "Here is the stuff before. Here is the thing after. Which one costs more? Look at the card. How much did your work add?"
sayThis.es: "Here is the stuff before. Here is the thing after. Which one costs more? Look at the card. How much did your work add?"

watchFor.en: Kids guessing the numbers. The numbers are on the station cards. Point to them.
watchFor.es: Kids guessing the numbers. The numbers are on the station cards. Point to them.

doneWhen.en: Each station has a raw cost and a finished value on the board, and the gap is circled.
doneWhen.es: Each station has a raw cost and a finished value on the board, and the gap is circled.

description.en: Groups research one everyday item (t-shirt, juice box, pencil) and map its transformation from raw materials. Present the chain to class. Which step adds the most value? Tier 1 (K-1): build one chain together as a class and draw each stage on the board.
description.es: Groups research one everyday item (t-shirt, juice box, pencil) and map its transformation from raw materials. Present the chain to class. Which step adds the most value? Tier 1 (K-1): build one chain together as a class and draw each stage on the board.

sayThis.en: "Pick a pencil, a t-shirt or a juice box. What was it before? And before that? Go back until you find a plant, a rock or an animal."
sayThis.es: "Pick a pencil, a t-shirt or a juice box. What was it before? And before that? Go back until you find a plant, a rock or an animal."

watchFor.en: Chains that stop at the store. Ask where the store got it.
watchFor.es: Chains that stop at the store. Ask where the store got it.

doneWhen.es: At least two groups have told the class a chain of three or more stages.

description.es: Write or discuss: Why does a wooden table cost more than a pile of lumber? How does transformation create value? What transformations can YOU do that add value?

sayThis.es: "A pile of wood is cheap. A table costs a lot. Why? Tell your partner one thing you could make that is worth more than what it is made from."

watchFor.es: Answers like "because it's a table." Ask who did the work to make it.

doneWhen.en: Every student has told a partner one thing they could make.
doneWhen.es: Every student has told a partner one thing they could make.

ell.label: English Language Learners

title.es: Invention Challenge: Solve a Real Problem

materials: Chart paper for class problems list

description.en: Walk around classroom or school. Students look for problems: things that are broken, annoying, or could work better. Each student finds 2-3 problems. List them on paper. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each problem or tell it to a partner instead of writing it.
description.es: Walk around classroom or school. Students look for problems: things that are broken, annoying, or could work better. Each student finds 2-3 problems. List them on paper. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each problem or tell it to a partner instead of writing it.

sayThis.es: "We are problem hunters. Look for things that are broken, annoying, or could work better. Find two or three. Draw or write each one."

description.es: Students share their problems. Teacher lists common themes on board. Vote on which problem is most important to solve.

sayThis.es: "Tell us one problem you found. If you found the same one, put your thumb up. Then we vote on the most important one to fix."

watchFor.es: Wishes dressed as problems, like "I want a robot." Ask what the robot would fix.

doneWhen.es: The common problems are on the board and the class vote has picked one.

sayThis.es: "Pick one problem. Draw a thing that fixes it. Label the parts. Then finish this: my invention solves ___."

discussionQuestions: What problem does your invention solve?

title.en: Blueprint Your Product: From Idea to Plan
title.es: Blueprint Your Product: From Idea to Plan

materials: Simple object to blueprint (block, box, or book)

description.en: Explain blueprints: detailed plans showing how to make something. Look at simple blueprint examples. Discuss: What information does a blueprint need? Why do makers create blueprints before building?
description.es: Explain blueprints: detailed plans showing how to make something. Look at simple blueprint examples. Discuss: What information does a blueprint need? Why do makers create blueprints before building?

sayThis.en: "This is a blueprint. It is a plan for making something. Look — it has lines, numbers and labels. Why would a maker draw a plan before building?"
sayThis.es: "This is a blueprint. It is a plan for making something. Look — it has lines, numbers and labels. Why would a maker draw a plan before building?"

watchFor.en: Kids looking only at the picture. Point at one number and one label and ask what each tells a builder.
watchFor.es: Kids looking only at the picture. Point at one number and one label and ask what each tells a builder.

doneWhen.en: The class has named at least two things a blueprint shows.
doneWhen.es: The class has named at least two things a blueprint shows.

description.en: Students choose a simple product to blueprint (from earlier activities or new idea). Plan all details: size, materials needed, steps to build it, special features. List materials and tools required. Tier 1 (K-1): pick one thing and draw or tell what it is made of.
description.es: Students choose a simple product to blueprint (from earlier activities or new idea). Plan all details: size, materials needed, steps to build it, special features. List materials and tools required. Tier 1 (K-1): pick one thing and draw or tell what it is made of.

sayThis.es: "Pick one thing to make. How big is it? What is it made of? What do you need to build it? Write or draw your list."

watchFor.es: Students picking something huge, like a house. Steer them to something that fits on a desk.

doneWhen.en: Every student has a chosen product and a materials list, written or drawn.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a chosen product and a materials list, written or drawn.

description.en: Students draw detailed blueprint on grid paper: top view, side view, measurements. Label all parts, materials, and important details. Use ruler for straight lines. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.
description.es: Students draw detailed blueprint on grid paper: top view, side view, measurements. Label all parts, materials, and important details. Use ruler for straight lines. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.

sayThis.en: "Now the blueprint. Draw it from the top and from the side. Ruler on every line. Put a number on each side and a label on each part."
sayThis.es: "Now the blueprint. Draw it from the top and from the side. Ruler on every line. Put a number on each side and a label on each part."

watchFor.en: Wobbly freehand lines. Draw one ruler line on the board so they see how to hold it.
watchFor.es: Wobbly freehand lines. Draw one ruler line on the board so they see how to hold it.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a drawing with at least one measurement and labeled parts.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a drawing with at least one measurement and labeled parts.

description.en: Students share blueprints with partners or small groups. Explain their product: what it is, how to make it, why they designed it this way. Receive feedback: Is blueprint clear? What's missing? Would someone else be able to build this from your blueprint?
description.es: Students share blueprints with partners or small groups. Explain their product: what it is, how to make it, why they designed it this way. Receive feedback: Is blueprint clear? What's missing? Would someone else be able to build this from your blueprint?

sayThis.en: "Swap with a partner. Tell them what it is and how to make it. Partner, could you build this? What is missing?"
sayThis.es: "Swap with a partner. Tell them what it is and how to make it. Partner, could you build this? What is missing?"

watchFor.en: Partners saying only "it's good." Ask them to name one thing that is missing.
watchFor.es: Partners saying only "it's good." Ask them to name one thing that is missing.

doneWhen.es: Every blueprint has had one missing thing named by a partner.

discussionQuestions: What did you measure?
Why do blueprints need measurements?

beforeClass.es: Put one real blueprint up on screen or print it before class. A ruler and a sheet of graph paper on every desk. Have one desk object, like a book or pencil case, ready to model with.

runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in Blueprint Drawing, draw one view only, with measurements. Short: after Blueprint Presentation & Feedback, have students add the missing detail their partner named.

materials: Blueprint paper or graph paper (3 sheets per student)
Rulers with inch and centimeter markings
Simple 3D objects for reference (blocks, boxes, containers)

description.en: Study professional blueprints: construction, product design, invention plans. Discuss blueprint elements: multiple views, measurements, materials list, labels, scale. Explain blueprint project.
description.es: Study professional blueprints: construction, product design, invention plans. Discuss blueprint elements: multiple views, measurements, materials list, labels, scale. Explain blueprint project.

sayThis.en: "These are real blueprints. Find the views, the measurements, the materials list and the labels. Builders use these so nobody has to guess. Today you make one."
sayThis.es: "These are real blueprints. Find the views, the measurements, the materials list and the labels. Builders use these so nobody has to guess. Today you make one."

watchFor.en: Students looking at the picture and skipping the numbers. Point at the measurements on purpose.
watchFor.es: Students looking at the picture and skipping the numbers. Point at the measurements on purpose.

doneWhen.en: The blueprint elements are named and listed on the board.
doneWhen.es: The blueprint elements are named and listed on the board.

description.en: Students develop detailed product concept. Consider: Who would use this? What problem does it solve? What materials? How big? How much would materials cost? Sketch rough ideas and refine to final concept. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the idea and say who would use it — no costs.
description.es: Students develop detailed product concept. Consider: Who would use this? What problem does it solve? What materials? How big? How much would materials cost? Sketch rough ideas and refine to final concept. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the idea and say who would use it — no costs.

sayThis.en: "Think of a product. Who uses it? What problem does it fix? How big is it? What is it made of? Sketch rough ideas on scrap paper, then pick one."
sayThis.es: "Think of a product. Who uses it? What problem does it fix? How big is it? What is it made of? Sketch rough ideas on scrap paper, then pick one."

watchFor.es: Students jumping straight to the final drawing. Rough ideas go on scrap paper first.

doneWhen.en: Every student has rough sketches and one chosen idea with its size and materials written down.
doneWhen.es: Every student has rough sketches and one chosen idea with its size and materials written down.

description.en: Students create multi-view blueprint on grid paper: front view, side view, top view. Add precise measurements (even if estimated), material labels, and construction notes. Use ruler and careful drawing. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.
description.es: Students create multi-view blueprint on grid paper: front view, side view, top view. Add precise measurements (even if estimated), material labels, and construction notes. Use ruler and careful drawing. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.

sayThis.en: "Three views on grid paper: front, side and top. Ruler on every line. Put a size on each side — your best guess is fine."
sayThis.es: "Three views on grid paper: front, side and top. Ruler on every line. Put a size on each side — your best guess is fine."

watchFor.en: Views drawn at different sizes. If it is four squares tall from the front, it is four squares tall from the side.
watchFor.es: Views drawn at different sizes. If it is four squares tall from the front, it is four squares tall from the side.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has three labeled views with at least one measurement on each.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has three labeled views with at least one measurement on each.

description.en: Students create detailed materials list: what's needed, quantities, estimated costs. Research prices if possible. Calculate total material cost. Consider: Is this affordable? Could cheaper materials work? Prices come from the price list on the board. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each material and count how many you need — no costs.
description.es: Students create detailed materials list: what's needed, quantities, estimated costs. Research prices if possible. Calculate total material cost. Consider: Is this affordable? Could cheaper materials work? Prices come from the price list on the board. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each material and count how many you need — no costs.

sayThis.en: "List everything you need and how many. Use the price list on the board to put a cost on each line. Add them up. Too much? What cheaper material could work?"
sayThis.es: "List everything you need and how many. Use the price list on the board to put a cost on each line. Add them up. Too much? What cheaper material could work?"

watchFor.en: Lists with no quantities. Ask "how many?" for every line.
watchFor.es: Lists with no quantities. Ask "how many?" for every line.

doneWhen.en: Every list has quantities, a cost on each line and a total.
doneWhen.es: Every list has quantities, a cost on each line and a total.

description.en: Students exchange blueprints with partners. Review for clarity: Could you build this from the blueprint? What's missing? Suggest improvements. Revise blueprints based on feedback.
description.es: Students exchange blueprints with partners. Review for clarity: Could you build this from the blueprint? What's missing? Suggest improvements. Revise blueprints based on feedback.

sayThis.en: "Swap. Could you build this from the paper alone? Tell your partner one thing that is missing. Then fix yours."
sayThis.es: "Swap. Could you build this from the paper alone? Tell your partner one thing that is missing. Then fix yours."

watchFor.en: Designers explaining their drawing. The paper has to do the talking.
watchFor.es: Designers explaining their drawing. The paper has to do the talking.

doneWhen.en: Every blueprint has one piece of feedback written on it.
doneWhen.es: Every blueprint has one piece of feedback written on it.

discussionQuestions: Why do we need more than one view of an object?
How does measuring carefully save money when building?
What would happen if your measurements were wrong?
Could a friend build your product using only your blueprint?
How is a blueprint different from a regular drawing?

beforeClass.en: Put two or three real blueprints up on screen or print them. A ruler and graph paper on every desk, plus scrap paper for rough sketches. Write a short price list on the board — cardboard, wood, glue, tape — with a made-up price for each, for the cost estimate.
beforeClass.es: Put two or three real blueprints up on screen or print them. A ruler and graph paper on every desk, plus scrap paper for rough sketches. Write a short price list on the board — cardboard, wood, glue, tape — with a made-up price for each, for the cost estimate.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in Detailed Blueprint Creation, draw the front and side views only. Short: in Blueprint Peer Review, add a second swap with a new partner.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Large blueprint paper or grid paper (11x17 preferred)
Technical drawing tools: rulers, protractors (for angles), compasses (for circles)
Materials cost reference sheet (wood = $X per foot, plastic = $Y per sheet, etc.)

sayThis.en: "This is how something gets built by a person who never met the one who designed it. Look for the box in the corner, the scale, the measurements, and the little list of changes. Every one of those is there because something once went wrong."
sayThis.es: "This is how something gets built by a person who never met the one who designed it. Look for the box in the corner, the scale, the measurements, and the little list of changes. Every one of those is there because something once went wrong."

doneWhen.es: Four blueprint elements are named and listed on the board.

description.es: Examine real blueprint examples (teacher provides or projects) Identify key elements: title block, scale notation, dimensions, multiple views, materials notes, revision history Discuss how professionals use these to communicate building plans across teams and time

sayThis.es: "Pick one thing. Your invention, a new idea, or something you'd improve. Rough sketch on scrap paper — not the real drawing yet. Then list every part it has."

doneWhen.es: Every student has a rough sketch and a written parts list.

watchFor.es: Students starting the good drawing straight away. Scrap first.

description.es: Choose product to blueprint (invention from CH8, new design, or improvement to existing item) Sketch rough concept on scrap paper List all parts and features that must be shown

sayThis.en: "Three drawings of one thing. From the front. From the side. From above. Four minutes each, ruler on every line. And they have to agree — if it's four inches tall from the front, it's four inches tall from the side too."
sayThis.es: "Three drawings of one thing. From the front. From the side. From above. Four minutes each, ruler on every line. And they have to agree — if it's four inches tall from the front, it's four inches tall from the side too."

doneWhen.es: Every sheet has three labeled views with measurements on each.

Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.
description.es: **Front view** (4 min): Draw primary view with all measurements, use ruler for straight lines, include scale (1:1, 1:2, etc.) **Side view** (4 min): Draw from side angle showing depth and profile, maintain consistent scale **Top view** (4 min): Draw overhead view showing layout and spacing, add any internal features All views must align properly and show same proportions. Tier 1 (K-1): draw the front view only, and label two or three parts with words or pictures.

sayThis.es: "Now pull it apart on paper. Every piece floating on its own, numbered, with arrows showing what goes into what. It's the picture in the flat-pack instructions."

doneWhen.es: Every diagram shows numbered parts with assembly arrows.

watchFor.es: Pieces drawn apart but not numbered. The numbers are the whole point.

description.es: Draw parts separated to show how they fit together Number each part Add assembly arrows showing order of construction. Tier 1 (K-1): draw two parts side by side with an arrow showing how they go together.

sayThis.es: "A list a shop could actually fill. Part name, what it's made of, how many, what size, what each one costs. Add it up. That total is what one of these costs before anybody gets paid."

doneWhen.es: Every list has a cost per part and a total at the bottom.

watchFor.es: Missing quantities. A list with no numbers can't be bought from.

description.es: Create detailed materials list: part name, material type, quantity, dimensions, cost per unit, total cost Calculate total materials cost for one unit Include tools needed for assembly. Tier 1 (K-1): draw each material and count how many you need — no costs.

sayThis.es: "Numbered steps, in order, like a recipe. Cut this. Sand that. Glue those. Then put a time on each one and add them up."

doneWhen.es: Every sheet has numbered steps with a time on each and a total.

watchFor.es: Steps out of order, gluing before cutting. Read one out and let the class catch it.

description.es: Write numbered assembly instructions (1. Cut wood to size, 2. Sand edges, 3. Attach with glue...) Estimate time for each step Calculate total production time. Tier 1 (K-1): draw three steps in order — first, next, last — with no times.

sayThis.es: "Swap. Don't explain anything. Your partner has to work out what it is and how to build it from the paper alone. If they can't, that isn't their fault."

doneWhen.es: Every blueprint has written feedback from a partner on it.

title.en: Would You Buy This? Survey & Market Research
title.es: Would You Buy This? Survey & Market Research
