focus: Simple setup: 1-2 items per student, clear price tags with numbers
Shopping with teacher guidance: "Give them this money. They give you the toy."
Focus on the experience of buying and selling, not complex math
Draw pictures of "best sale" instead of writing reflections
Basic vocabulary: sell, buy, customer, money, faire
Celebrate participation over profit
Multiple items with simple price tags
Practice counting money and making change with small amounts ($1, $5, $10)
Simple sales tracking: tally marks for each item sold
Product cards with sentence frames: "I made a ___. It is made from ___."
Vocabulary expansion: revenue, booth, display, customer service, faire
Count total money collected, discuss what "a lot" or "a little" means
Full booth setup with varied pricing
Calculate change for purchases up to $20-50
Detailed sales logs: item name, price, customer (first name)
Product story cards explaining creation process
Vocabulary: profit, cost, materials, market, entrepreneur
Calculate simple profit: money collected minus estimated costs
Professional booth with strategic pricing based on material costs and time investment
Complex transactions with bills and coins, accurate change-making
Comprehensive business reporting: revenue, itemized costs, profit calculation, profit margin
Written reflections on business success and lessons learned
Advanced vocabulary: revenue vs. profit, overhead costs, market positioning, value proposition, return on investment
Compare booth performance: who sold most? Who had highest profit margin? Why?
Strategic analysis: which products should they make more of for future faires?

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Act out one sale before the faire opens: point to the tag, count the tokens, say thank you.
Give the frame: "I want ___. It costs ___. Here is the money."
Write prices in big numbers so shoppers can match tokens to the number.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Keep the booth to one to three items with whole-token prices so no change is needed.
Post a picture sales script: greet, show, say the price, take the tokens, say thank you.
Let students share a booth with a partner.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Make a bar graph from the sales log showing which items sold most.
Work out the profit on each item, not just the whole booth.
Use the sales log to recommend which products to make more of next time.

title.en: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?
title.es: Solo Challenge: Can You Do It All Alone?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 3 task stations per student: drawing paper, folding paper (origami or paper airplanes), organizing supplies (blocks or crayons)

description.en: Introduce 3 tasks students must complete alone: 1) Write name in bubble letters, 2) Stack 10 books tallest to shortest, 3) Create paper airplane. No help allowed.
description.es: Introduce 3 tasks students must complete alone: 1) Write name in bubble letters, 2) Stack 10 books tallest to shortest, 3) Create paper airplane. No help allowed.

description.en: Students work individually on bubble letters. Monitor but don't help. Students problem-solve independently.
description.es: Students work individually on bubble letters. Monitor but don't help. Students problem-solve independently.

description.en: Students complete book stacking and airplane tasks. Continue working independently. Raise hand when all 3 tasks done.
description.es: Students complete book stacking and airplane tasks. Continue working independently. Raise hand when all 3 tasks done.

description.en: Count how many finished. Discuss: What was hardest? What did you wish you had? Would it be easier with a partner? Chart responses.
description.es: Count how many finished. Discuss: What was hardest? What did you wish you had? Would it be easier with a partner? Chart responses.

discussionQuestions: Did anyone finish everything? How did you feel?
If you could only pick ONE task, which would it be? What happens to the others?
How is this like the story when Riley kept remaking mugs while Ellis was walking across town?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Solo vs. Team Challenge with Productivity Tracking
materials: 4 task stations: poster drawing, paper airplane folding, supply organizing, price list writing

description.en: Explain extended solo challenge: 5 tasks to complete independently. Review all tasks and success criteria. Set time limit: 18 minutes.
description.es: Explain extended solo challenge: 5 tasks to complete independently. Review all tasks and success criteria. Set time limit: 18 minutes.

description.en: Students work on first 3 tasks without help: writing, organizing, creating. Monitor progress but don't assist. Encourage problem-solving.
description.es: Students work on first 3 tasks without help: writing, organizing, creating. Monitor progress but don't assist. Encourage problem-solving.

description.en: Students complete remaining 2 tasks independently. Continue self-directed work. Some may finish early, others may not complete all tasks.
description.es: Students complete remaining 2 tasks independently. Continue self-directed work. Some may finish early, others may not complete all tasks.

description.en: Count completions. Chart: which tasks were hardest? Create class data graph. Discuss what made solo work challenging.
description.es: Count completions. Chart: which tasks were hardest? Create class data graph. Discuss what made solo work challenging.

description.en: Reflect: When is working alone good? When do we need help? What are benefits and challenges of solo work vs. teamwork?
description.es: Reflect: When is working alone good? When do we need help? What are benefits and challenges of solo work vs. teamwork?

discussionQuestions: Which was less stressful - doing everything or specializing in one thing?
How much more did we produce as a team?
Why do you think Ellis said 'I walk more than I work'?
When might working alone be better than working with others?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Solo-to-Partnership Simulation with Financial Analysis
materials: 5 task stations (drawing, folding, organizing, writing, decorating)
Detailed tracking sheets with time logs
Paper clips as tokens (1 per completed task), collected back and reused
Large chart paper for class data visualization

sayThis.en: "Seven jobs. Twenty-five minutes. No help from anyone, including me. This is what it feels like to run a business on your own, and most of you are not going to finish. That's fine. Finding out is the point."
sayThis.es: "Seven jobs. Twenty-five minutes. No help from anyone, including me. This is what it feels like to run a business on your own, and most of you are not going to finish. That's fine. Finding out is the point."

doneWhen.en: Every student has all seven task cards in front of them and the clock is showing.
doneWhen.es: Every student has all seven task cards in front of them and the clock is showing.

watchFor.en: Students hearing "you won't finish" as permission to give up. Say the other half out loud: how far you get is the data.
watchFor.es: Students hearing "you won't finish" as permission to give up. Say the other half out loud: how far you get is the data.

description.en: Introduce ambitious solo challenge: 7 tasks requiring different skills. Explain: this simulates running a business alone. Set 25-minute time limit.
description.es: Introduce ambitious solo challenge: 7 tasks requiring different skills. Explain: this simulates running a business alone. Set 25-minute time limit.

sayThis.en: "Don't start yet. Read all seven first. Then number them in the order you'll do them. Quick ones first, or hard ones first — your call, but decide now and write it down."
sayThis.es: "Don't start yet. Read all seven first. Then number them in the order you'll do them. Quick ones first, or hard ones first — your call, but decide now and write it down."

doneWhen.en: Every student has all seven tasks numbered in an order on paper.
doneWhen.es: Every student has all seven tasks numbered in an order on paper.

watchFor.en: Students starting task one while you're still talking. Hold the room until the orders are written.
watchFor.es: Students starting task one while you're still talking. Hold the room until the orders are written.

description.en: Students review all 7 tasks and plan approach: which to do first, which will take longest, which might be hardest. Create task order strategy.
description.es: Students review all 7 tasks and plan approach: which to do first, which will take longest, which might be hardest. Create task order strategy.

sayThis.en: "Go. Alone means alone. Don't ask your neighbor, don't ask me. Tick each one off as you finish it."
sayThis.es: "Go. Alone means alone. Don't ask your neighbor, don't ask me. Tick each one off as you finish it."

doneWhen.en: Every student is working and has ticked at least one task off the list.
doneWhen.es: Every student is working and has ticked at least one task off the list.

watchFor.en: Quiet partnerships forming at shared tables. Name it once, kindly, and move them apart if it continues.
watchFor.es: Quiet partnerships forming at shared tables. Name it once, kindly, and move them apart if it continues.

description.en: Students begin working through task list independently. Complete easier/quicker tasks first or hardest tasks first, depending on strategy chosen.
description.es: Students begin working through task list independently. Complete easier/quicker tasks first or hardest tasks first, depending on strategy chosen.

sayThis.en: "Ten minutes left. Look at what's still not done. You can change your order now if it isn't working — that's allowed and it's smart."
sayThis.es: "Ten minutes left. Look at what's still not done. You can change your order now if it isn't working — that's allowed and it's smart."

doneWhen.en: Every student's card list shows which tasks are done and which are not.
doneWhen.es: Every student's card list shows which tasks are done and which are not.

watchFor.en: Students stuck on one hard task with five easy ones untouched. Ask what else is on the list. Don't tell them to switch.
watchFor.es: Students stuck on one hard task with five easy ones untouched. Ask what else is on the list. Don't tell them to switch.

description.en: Continue independent work on remaining tasks. Push through challenges without help. Some students will complete all tasks, others won't.
description.es: Continue independent work on remaining tasks. Push through challenges without help. Some students will complete all tasks, others won't.

sayThis.en: "How many did you finish out of seven? Hands up for seven. Six. Five. Now which task beat the most people? That one's the bottleneck."
sayThis.es: "How many did you finish out of seven? Hands up for seven. Six. Five. Now which task beat the most people? That one's the bottleneck."

doneWhen.en: The class chart shows a completion count for every one of the seven tasks.
doneWhen.es: The class chart shows a completion count for every one of the seven tasks.

watchFor.en: Low finishers hiding their number. Say it plainly: nobody's number is the point, the pattern is.
watchFor.es: Low finishers hiding their number. Say it plainly: nobody's number is the point, the pattern is.

description.en: Analyze data: completion rates per task, total tasks completed, time management effectiveness. Create detailed charts and graphs.
description.es: Analyze data: completion rates per task, total tasks completed, time management effectiveness. Create detailed charts and graphs.

sayThis.en: "Two questions. What did doing everything alone cost you? And when would you still want to do it alone anyway? Both answers are real."
sayThis.es: "Two questions. What did doing everything alone cost you? And when would you still want to do it alone anyway? Both answers are real."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written an answer to both questions.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written an answer to both questions.

watchFor.en: "Teams are better" as the whole answer. Ask when a team would have slowed them down.
watchFor.es: "Teams are better" as the whole answer. Ask when a team would have slowed them down.

description.en: Discuss: What did this experience teach about working alone? When is independence important in business? What did you learn about yourself? How does this relate to entrepreneurship?
description.es: Discuss: What did this experience teach about working alone? When is independence important in business? What did you learn about yourself? How does this relate to entrepreneurship?

discussionQuestions: Who made more money working solo or in partnership? Why?
How did your stress level change between rounds?
What are the ADVANTAGES of working alone? What are the DISADVANTAGES?
In the story, the friends made less than $2/hour working alone. How could working together help?
Why do real businesses have many employees instead of one person doing everything?
What jobs REQUIRE teams? What jobs can be done alone?
extensionIdeas: Calculate class total: sum all solo earnings vs. all partnership earnings - visualize the difference
Research real businesses: how do they divide labor? (Restaurant: chef, server, cashier, dishwasher)
Write reflection: "When I tried to do everything alone, I felt... When I worked with a team, I felt..."
Connect to Season 3: "At the Makers' Faire, did the friends work alone or together? How did that help?"

beforeClass.en: Build the seven task cards and lay out everything each one needs, in one place per task. If a student has to hunt for scissors, you are timing the hunt and not the work. Have a visible clock the whole room can see.
beforeClass.es: Build the seven task cards and lay out everything each one needs, in one place per task. If a student has to hunt for scissors, you are timing the hunt and not the work. Have a visible clock the whole room can see.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: merge the two work phases into one 15-minute block. Short: add an eighth task halfway through, unannounced, and watch what it does to the plans.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: merge the two work phases into one 15-minute block. Short: add an eighth task halfway through, unannounced, and watch what it does to the plans.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: Season tokens plus the basics restock — paper, pencils, crayons and tape
items: Paper clips, 1 box of 500 — $2.50. These are the task tokens, one per completed task, and they carry the whole season. Counted back in at the end of each lesson
Copy paper, 1 ream — $5.00. Covers the task stations, the tally sheets and the season's worksheets
Pencils, class pack of 20 — $3.00
Crayons, 6 boxes shared across tables — $4.50
Masking tape, 2 rolls — $3.00. Used here to mark out the station areas and again in Chapter 12 to hang posters
Scrap and recycled paper for the drawing, folding and name-art stations — free, from the recycled paper bin
Ten books from the classroom shelf for the stacking task — free
Classroom clock or the teacher's phone as the visible timer — free
Whiteboard for the class completion graph
Pencil-and-paper math for the completion rate. No calculators needed

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: One box of paper clips. Everything else is already in the room
items: Paper clips, 1 box of 500 — $2.50. The task tokens for the whole season, counted back in each lesson
Scrap and recycled paper for the drawing, folding and name-art stations — free
Ten books from the classroom shelf for the stacking task — free
Classroom clock or the teacher's phone as the visible timer — free
Paper, pencils, crayons and masking tape from the classroom supply
Whiteboard for the class completion graph

focus: Only 2-3 simple tasks (draw a shape, fold paper once, put toys in a box)
Focus on feeling: "Is this hard? Do you want help?"
Partner pairs for team round instead of larger groups
Basic vocabulary: alone, together, help, team
Concrete understanding: "One person can't do everything at once"
4 tasks with simple tracking (check boxes for completed)
Introduction to counting productivity
Small teams (3-4 students)
Vocabulary expansion: business, task, alone, partnership, complete
Beginning to understand time as a resource
4-5 tasks with time tracking (how long did each take?)
Calculate simple earnings ($1 per task)
Teams of 4-5 with assigned roles
Vocabulary: efficiency, productivity, opportunity cost, earnings
Understanding that working alone has limits
5+ tasks with detailed time logs
Full financial calculation (earnings per minute, comparison of solo vs. team hourly rates)
Strategic team formation and role selection
Advanced vocabulary: specialization, division of labor, productivity rate, time management, partnership structure
Deep analysis of why partnerships make economic sense

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Simple one-page business plan template (photocopied or drawn on board)
Optional: example business names on cards for inspiration

description.en: Explain business plan: document describing what business will do and how. Review simple business plan template: What will you sell? Who will buy? How much will it cost? Discuss examples.
description.es: Explain business plan: document describing what business will do and how. Review simple business plan template: What will you sell? Who will buy? How much will it cost? Discuss examples.

description.en: Students brainstorm simple business ideas: selling bookmarks, offering classroom helper service, making greeting cards. Choose one idea. Answer key questions: What exactly is your product or service? Why would people want it?
description.es: Students brainstorm simple business ideas: selling bookmarks, offering classroom helper service, making greeting cards. Choose one idea. Answer key questions: What exactly is your product or service? Why would people want it?

description.en: Students identify their customers: Who would buy this? Why? Decide on price: How much would you charge? Why that amount? Is it fair? Would customers pay it? Write down customer description and price.
description.es: Students identify their customers: Who would buy this? Why? Decide on price: How much would you charge? Why that amount? Is it fair? Would customers pay it? Write down customer description and price.

description.en: Students complete simple business plan template: Business name, what you sell, who will buy it, price, materials needed. Draw picture of product or service. Write 2-3 sentences explaining the business.
description.es: Students complete simple business plan template: Business name, what you sell, who will buy it, price, materials needed. Draw picture of product or service. Write 2-3 sentences explaining the business.

description.en: Students share business plans in pairs or small groups. Explain: What's your business? Why would it work? Get quick feedback: Would you be a customer? Any suggestions?
description.es: Students share business plans in pairs or small groups. Explain: What's your business? Why would it work? Get quick feedback: Would you be a customer? Any suggestions?

discussionQuestions: Why did Mr. Mason want the friends to make a plan?
What's the difference between cost and price?
Why does everyone need a job in the business?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: One-Page Business Plan with Pricing Calculations
materials: Business plan template with sections: Name, Products, Costs, Prices, Profit, Roles, Customers
Simple calculator or hundreds chart for math support
Sample cost lists (optional: pretend prices for clay, wood, paper, etc.)

description.en: Review business plan components: product/service, customers, pricing, materials, costs. Show detailed template. Discuss what makes a strong business plan.
description.es: Review business plan components: product/service, customers, pricing, materials, costs. Show detailed template. Discuss what makes a strong business plan.

description.en: Students brainstorm multiple business ideas. For each, consider: Who would buy? Why? How much would it cost to make? What's the competition? Choose best idea.
description.es: Students brainstorm multiple business ideas. For each, consider: Who would buy? Why? How much would it cost to make? What's the competition? Choose best idea.

description.en: Students complete comprehensive business plan: product description, target customers, pricing strategy with justification, materials list with costs, expected profit, competition analysis.
description.es: Students complete comprehensive business plan: product description, target customers, pricing strategy with justification, materials list with costs, expected profit, competition analysis.

description.en: Students calculate: cost to make product, selling price, profit per item, how many sales needed to break even. Create simple financial forecast.
description.es: Students calculate: cost to make product, selling price, profit per item, how many sales needed to break even. Create simple financial forecast.

description.en: Exchange business plans with partner. Give feedback: Is it clear? Realistic? Missing anything? Revise plans based on feedback.
description.es: Exchange business plans with partner. Give feedback: Is it clear? Realistic? Missing anything? Revise plans based on feedback.

discussionQuestions: How did you decide what to charge for your product?
What happens if your price is LOWER than your cost?
Why did Layla make a RESERVE jar? What's that for?
How did you decide who does which job?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Business Plan with Multi-Product Pricing and Investor Pitch
materials: Comprehensive business plan template with all sections from story
Sample materials cost sheet (wood: $4, clay: $3, paint: $2, etc.)
Chart paper or poster board for final presentation
Optional: extra paper clips as "investment" tokens

sayThis.en: "A business plan is the paper you hand someone when you want their money. It says what you'll sell, who buys it, what it costs and what you'll make. Investors read the numbers first. Everything else is decoration."
sayThis.es: "A business plan is the paper you hand someone when you want their money. It says what you'll sell, who buys it, what it costs and what you'll make. Investors read the numbers first. Everything else is decoration."

doneWhen.en: The sections of a business plan are listed on the board.
doneWhen.es: The sections of a business plan are listed on the board.

watchFor.en: The idea that a plan is a wish list. Point at the money section on the real one you brought.
watchFor.es: The idea that a plan is a wish list. Point at the money section on the real one you brought.

description.en: Explore professional business plans: structure, detail level, financial projections. Discuss what investors look for. Introduce comprehensive planning project.
description.es: Explore professional business plans: structure, detail level, financial projections. Discuss what investors look for. Introduce comprehensive planning project.

sayThis.en: "Go and find out if anybody actually wants this. Ask real people. Write down what they say, not what you hoped they'd say. And find out what already exists — if nothing does, that's either a gap or a warning."
sayThis.es: "Go and find out if anybody actually wants this. Ask real people. Write down what they say, not what you hoped they'd say. And find out what already exists — if nothing does, that's either a gap or a warning."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written responses from at least five people.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written responses from at least five people.

watchFor.en: Research that is just asking a friend if it's a good idea. Require a number: how many said yes.
watchFor.es: Research that is just asking a friend if it's a good idea. Require a number: how many said yes.

description.en: Students conduct market research: Who are potential customers? What do they need? What exists already? Survey classmates. Analyze data to find market opportunity.
description.es: Students conduct market research: Who are potential customers? What do they need? What exists already? Survey classmates. Analyze data to find market opportunity.

sayThis.en: "Now the hard question. Somebody already sells something like this. Why would anyone pick yours? Cheaper, better, faster, or for a customer nobody's bothered with. Pick one and write it in a sentence."
sayThis.es: "Now the hard question. Somebody already sells something like this. Why would anyone pick yours? Cheaper, better, faster, or for a customer nobody's bothered with. Pick one and write it in a sentence."

doneWhen.en: Every plan has a one-sentence reason someone would choose it over what exists.
doneWhen.es: Every plan has a one-sentence reason someone would choose it over what exists.

watchFor.en: "Mine is just better" with nothing under it. Ask better at what, measured how.
watchFor.es: "Mine is just better" with nothing under it. Ask better at what, measured how.

description.en: Develop detailed product/service concept: What makes it unique? Why better than competition? What's the value proposition? Create product sketch or prototype plan.
description.es: Develop detailed product/service concept: What makes it unique? Why better than competition? What's the value proposition? Create product sketch or prototype plan.

sayThis.en: "Every cost, itemized. Then your price. Then the one that matters — how many do you have to sell before you stop losing money? That number is your break-even, and every real business owner knows theirs."
sayThis.es: "Every cost, itemized. Then your price. Then the one that matters — how many do you have to sell before you stop losing money? That number is your break-even, and every real business owner knows theirs."

doneWhen.en: Every plan shows itemized costs, a price, a margin and a break-even number.
doneWhen.es: Every plan shows itemized costs, a price, a margin and a break-even number.

watchFor.en: Costs that forget time, packaging or waste. Ask what happens to the ones that come out wrong.
watchFor.es: Costs that forget time, packaging or waste. Ask what happens to the ones that come out wrong.

description.en: Comprehensive financial plan: itemized cost breakdown, pricing strategy, profit margin calculations, break-even analysis, sales forecasts. Create detailed budget.
description.es: Comprehensive financial plan: itemized cost breakdown, pricing strategy, profit margin calculations, break-even analysis, sales forecasts. Create detailed budget.

sayThis.en: "Pull it together into one document, in order. Summary at the top, even though you write it last. Neat counts — if it looks careless, people assume the numbers are careless too."
sayThis.es: "Pull it together into one document, in order. Summary at the top, even though you write it last. Neat counts — if it looks careless, people assume the numbers are careless too."

doneWhen.en: Every plan has all five sections present with nothing blank.
doneWhen.es: Every plan has all five sections present with nothing blank.

watchFor.en: Sections left half-finished from earlier steps. A quick page check catches it.
watchFor.es: Sections left half-finished from earlier steps. A quick page check catches it.

description.en: Complete full written business plan with all sections: executive summary, product description, market analysis, financial projections, timeline. Professional formatting.
description.es: Complete full written business plan with all sections: executive summary, product description, market analysis, financial projections, timeline. Professional formatting.

sayThis.en: "Short and clear. What it is, who buys it, what you'll make. Lead with the number."
sayThis.es: "Short and clear. What it is, who buys it, what you'll make. Lead with the number."

doneWhen.en: Every plan has written feedback from at least one other person on it.
doneWhen.es: Every plan has written feedback from at least one other person on it.

watchFor.en: Presenters reading the whole plan aloud. Stop the first one at thirty seconds and set the pace.
watchFor.es: Presenters reading the whole plan aloud. Stop the first one at thirty seconds and set the pace.

description.en: Present business plans to class or small groups. Practice pitch: clear, persuasive, data-driven. Receive feedback for improvements.
description.es: Present business plans to class or small groups. Practice pitch: clear, persuasive, data-driven. Receive feedback for improvements.

discussionQuestions: What was the hardest part of making your business plan?
How did calculating costs change your pricing decisions?
In the story, Mr. Mason taught PRICE - COST = PROFIT. Why is this formula so important?
Why do you think Layla wanted order forms and pricing sheets written down?
What could go wrong if you DON'T make a plan first?" (Connect to Benny's mistake in CH1)
How does having clear roles prevent confusion and arguments?
extensionIdeas: Compare your business plan to a real kid business (lemonade stand, craft sale, dog walking)
Research: What business plans do adult businesses need? (Permits, insurance, marketing plans)
Create order form template like Layla made
Calculate: How many products would you need to sell to make $100 profit?

beforeClass.en: Print a real one-page business plan to hold up. Abstract structure is hard to picture; one page they can see makes it obvious. Decide who students may survey in step 2 and warn that class or adult beforehand.
beforeClass.es: Print a real one-page business plan to hold up. Abstract structure is hard to picture; one page they can see makes it obvious. Decide who students may survey in step 2 and warn that class or adult beforehand.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the presentations and have partners read each other's plans instead. Short: add a second financial pass where teams halve their price and see what breaks.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the presentations and have partners read each other's plans instead. Short: add a second financial pass where teams halve their price and see what breaks.

Teacher does most calculations on board, students copy

Template with clear sections and sentence frames
2-3 products

Introduction to profit formula with visual model

Beginning to understand that planning prevents problems

title.en: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store
title.es: Grand Opening: Run a Classroom Store

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 5-10 simple items (classroom supplies, book fair books, or pretend items)
Scrap-paper budget card per shopper, plus paper clips as $1 coins, collected back and reused

description.en: Review classroom store concept: sell simple items (pencils, bookmarks, erasers) using paper clips as coins, one clip = $1. Discuss store roles: cashier, stocker, customer. Set up store area with items and price tags.
description.es: Review classroom store concept: sell simple items (pencils, bookmarks, erasers) using paper clips as coins, one clip = $1. Discuss store roles: cashier, stocker, customer. Set up store area with items and price tags.

description.en: Run the classroom store! Students rotate through roles: being cashier (taking clips, counting out change), stocking shelves, and being customers (shopping, paying). Each customer starts with 10 clips. Track sales.
description.es: Run the classroom store! Students rotate through roles: being cashier (taking clips, counting out change), stocking shelves, and being customers (shopping, paying). Each customer starts with 10 clips. Track sales.

description.en: Students count sales: How many items sold? What was most popular? How many clips did the register take in? Create simple sales chart showing which items sold best. Discuss what made items popular.
description.es: Students count sales: How many items sold? What was most popular? How many clips did the register take in? Create simple sales chart showing which items sold best. Discuss what made items popular.

description.en: Discuss store operations: What went smoothly? What was confusing? What would make the store better? If you ran this store again, what would you change? How is running a store different from being a customer?
description.es: Discuss store operations: What went smoothly? What was confusing? What would make the store better? If you ran this store again, what would you change? How is running a store different from being a customer?

discussionQuestions: How did it feel to be the shopkeeper?
Did you count the money correctly?
What would happen if we didn't write anything down?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: 15-20 items with price tags (mix of low $2-5 and high $10-15 prices)
Paper clips as $1 tokens, 20 per customer — reused every year
Transaction log sheets (columns: Item Sold, Price, Customer Name)

description.en: Arrange items in "store" area. Assign 2-3 students as first shopkeepers. Every other student counts out 20 tokens, each worth $1.
description.es: Arrange items in "store" area. Assign 2-3 students as first shopkeepers. Every other student counts out 20 tokens, each worth $1.

description.en: Customers shop. Shopkeepers make sales, count tokens, record each transaction on the log. Practice giving change in tokens.
description.es: Customers shop. Shopkeepers make sales, count tokens, record each transaction on the log. Practice giving change in tokens.

description.en: New shopkeepers take over. Previous shopkeepers become customers.
description.es: New shopkeepers take over. Previous shopkeepers become customers.

description.en: Continue sales with new shopkeepers. Track everything.
description.es: Continue sales with new shopkeepers. Track everything.

description.en: Total all transactions from logs. Count the tokens in the register. Do they match?
description.es: Total all transactions from logs. Count the tokens in the register. Do they match?

description.en: Share: "What sold the most? What didn't sell? Why?"
description.es: Share: "What sold the most? What didn't sell? Why?"

discussionQuestions: Which items were easiest to sell? Why do you think that is?
Did the total money match your transaction log?
What was hardest about being the shopkeeper?
How did you decide what to buy?
What happened when you ran out of money?
extensionIdeas: Graph which items sold the most using tally marks or bar graph.

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Store Operation with Profit Analysis
materials: 25-30 items organized by "department" (books, supplies, crafts, toys)
Paper clips as $1 tokens, 30 per customer — reused every year
Detailed transaction logs (columns: Time, Item, Price, Cost, Profit, Customer)
"Cost sheets" showing what each item "cost the store" to stock

sayThis.en: "Four departments, each with a sign. Two shopkeepers per shift, one accountant with the log, everyone else shops. Look at your tags — there's a price on the front and a cost on the back. The gap between them is the only reason a shop stays open."
sayThis.es: "Four departments, each with a sign. Two shopkeepers per shift, one accountant with the log, everyone else shops. Look at your tags — there's a price on the front and a cost on the back. The gap between them is the only reason a shop stays open."

doneWhen.en: Four departments are signed and every role has a named student.
doneWhen.es: Four departments are signed and every role has a named student.

watchFor.en: Students reading the back tag as the price. Hold up one item and show both sides to the room.
watchFor.es: Students reading the back tag as the price. Hold up one item and show both sides to the room.

description.en: Set up 4 departments with clear signage Assign roles: 2 shopkeepers per shift, 1 "accountant" tracking logs, rest are customers Each item has TWO tags: selling price (front) and cost to store (back)
description.es: Set up 4 departments with clear signage Assign roles: 2 shopkeepers per shift, 1 "accountant" tracking logs, rest are customers Each item has TWO tags: selling price (front) and cost to store (back)

sayThis.en: "Store's open. Shopkeepers, sell and give correct change. Accountant, every sale gets a line — what sold, what it sold for, and what it cost us. Price minus cost is profit, and you write that too."
sayThis.es: "Store's open. Shopkeepers, sell and give correct change. Accountant, every sale gets a line — what sold, what it sold for, and what it cost us. Price minus cost is profit, and you write that too."

doneWhen.en: The transaction log has a price, a cost and a profit on every line.
doneWhen.es: The transaction log has a price, a cost and a profit on every line.

watchFor.en: The accountant recording the price and skipping the cost. Check the log after the first two sales.
watchFor.es: The accountant recording the price and skipping the cost. Check the log after the first two sales.

description.en: Customers shop across all departments - Shopkeepers make sales and give change - Accountant records every transaction including COST of item - Calculate profit per sale (Price − Cost = Profit)
description.es: Customers shop across all departments - Shopkeepers make sales and give change - Accountant records every transaction including COST of item - Calculate profit per sale (Price − Cost = Profit)

sayThis.en: "Shift's over. Count the register out loud with the person taking over. Hand them the log. Both of you agree on the number before you walk away."
sayThis.es: "Shift's over. Count the register out loud with the person taking over. Hand them the log. Both of you agree on the number before you walk away."

doneWhen.en: The register total is written down and agreed by both shifts.
doneWhen.es: The register total is written down and agreed by both shifts.

watchFor.en: A handover with no count. That's how a till goes missing in a real shop.
watchFor.es: A handover with no count. That's how a till goes missing in a real shop.

description.en: New team takes over store. Count register, hand off logs.
description.es: New team takes over store. Count register, hand off logs.

sayThis.en: "New team, same rules. You've watched for eight minutes — you know what sells."
sayThis.es: "New team, same rules. You've watched for eight minutes — you know what sells."

doneWhen.en: The log is still being filled and every department has a staffed counter.
doneWhen.es: The log is still being filled and every department has a staffed counter.

watchFor.en: New shopkeepers who don't know where anything is. Give ten seconds for a department walk.
watchFor.es: New shopkeepers who don't know where anything is. Give ten seconds for a department walk.

description.en: Continue operations with new staff
description.es: Continue operations with new staff

sayThis.en: "Count everything you took in. That's revenue. Now add up the cost column. Take it off. What's left is profit. Layla did exactly this: ninety-three in, twenty-two of cost, seventy-one profit."
sayThis.es: "Count everything you took in. That's revenue. Now add up the cost column. Take it off. What's left is profit. Layla did exactly this: ninety-three in, twenty-two of cost, seventy-one profit."

doneWhen.en: Revenue, total cost and profit are all three written on the board.
doneWhen.es: Revenue, total cost and profit are all three written on the board.

watchFor.en: Revenue being called profit. It's the single most common mistake in the whole season. Say both words while pointing at both numbers.
watchFor.es: Revenue being called profit. It's the single most common mistake in the whole season. Say both words while pointing at both numbers.

description.en: Count total revenue (all tokens collected) - Calculate total costs (add up costs from transaction logs) - Calculate profit: Revenue − Costs = Profit - Compare to story: "Just like Layla calculated $93 revenue − $22 costs = $71 profit"
description.es: Count total revenue (all tokens collected) - Calculate total costs (add up costs from transaction logs) - Calculate profit: Revenue − Costs = Profit - Compare to story: "Just like Layla calculated $93 revenue − $22 costs = $71 profit"

sayThis.en: "Which department made the most? Which items never moved at all? Those unsold ones cost money and earned nothing. What would you not order next week?"
sayThis.es: "Which department made the most? Which items never moved at all? Those unsold ones cost money and earned nothing. What would you not order next week?"

doneWhen.en: The best department and at least three unsold items are named on the board.
doneWhen.es: The best department and at least three unsold items are named on the board.

watchFor.en: Attention going only to the winners. The unsold pile is where the lesson is.
watchFor.es: Attention going only to the winners. The unsold pile is where the lesson is.

description.en: Which department made the most revenue? Which items sold out? Which didn't sell at all? Did we have enough customers? Too many? What would we change for next week?
description.es: Which department made the most revenue? Which items sold out? Which didn't sell at all? Did we have enough customers? Too many? What would we change for next week?

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between revenue and profit?
In the story, 2 big jobs (shelf and mugs) were $63 of their $93 total. Why did Layla worry about that?
What if a customer is unhappy? How does that affect future business?
Why is it important to track EVERY transaction, not just the big ones?
If you were running a real store, what would you sell?
How did tips work in the story? Should tips go to profit or split among workers?
extensionIdeas: Create a "Store Report" poster showing revenue, costs, profit
Graph sales by department or time of day
Compare Week 1 (this activity) to Week 2 (run the store again next week)
Research real store operations: inventory, employees, customer service
Calculate: if this were real money, what could the profit buy?

beforeClass.en: Tag every item twice before the lesson: selling price on the front, cost to the store on the back. Doing this live takes twenty minutes. Set out four department areas and a register spot.
beforeClass.es: Tag every item twice before the lesson: selling price on the front, cost to the store on the back. Doing this live takes twenty minutes. Set out four department areas and a register spot.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: run one 12-minute shift instead of two. Short: add a third shift where each department may change one price.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: run one 12-minute shift instead of two. Short: add a third shift where each department may change one price.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: Sign card and a marker set. The store stock is what the room already owns
items: Cardstock, 20 sheets — $4.00. The four department signs and the price-tag cards, written on and reused every year. Also the role badges in Chapter 4 and the capacity cards in Chapter 7
Markers, 1 shared set of 10 — $3.00. Used again in Chapter 6, Chapter 11 and Chapter 12
Classroom supplies already on hand as the store stock — pencils, erasers, bookmarks, library books returned afterwards
Paper clips from Chapter 1 as $1 coins, 20 to 30 per customer, collected back in
An empty box or tray from the supply closet as the store register — free
Blank paper — students rule their own transaction log: Item, Price, Customer
Cost sheet showing what each item cost the store to stock, written on the board
Board space for the department signs and the class sales chart

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: Card for the signs and tags. The room supplies the stock and the colour
items: Cardstock, 20 sheets, for the department signs and the price-tag cards — $4.00. Written on and reused every year
Classroom supplies already on hand as the store stock — pencils, erasers, bookmarks, library books returned afterwards

focus: Simple transactions with teacher support: "This costs $5. Can you count 5 dollars?"
Focus on identifying money amounts and polite exchanges

Practice making change with teacher guidance
Simple transaction logs: item name and price only
Counting total sales at end: add up all prices
Vocabulary expansion: price, change, total, register, receipt
Understanding: money in = revenue
Independent change-making with simple amounts
Transaction logs include customer names and running total
Introduction to costs vs. price: "This sold for $10 but cost us $3 to stock"
Vocabulary: revenue, cost, profit, transaction, inventory
Calculate simple profit: $10 - $3 = $7 profit
Complex transactions with change from $20 or $50 bills
Full transaction logs with time, item, customer, cost, price, profit

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

description.en: Teacher reads aloud: "A customer says your drawing has the wrong colors. What do you say?"
description.es: Teacher reads aloud: "A customer says your drawing has the wrong colors. What do you say?"

description.en: Turn to partner. Decide together: What's the BEST thing to say? What's the WORST thing to say?
description.es: Turn to partner. Decide together: What's the BEST thing to say? What's the WORST thing to say?

description.en: Pairs share their "best response." Teacher writes top 3 responses on board.
description.es: Pairs share their "best response." Teacher writes top 3 responses on board.

description.en: Quick repeat with new scenario. Faster decision-making.
description.es: Quick repeat with new scenario. Faster decision-making.

discussionQuestions: How would YOU feel if you ordered something and it was wrong?
What words make an unhappy customer feel better?
Is it better to argue or to fix the problem?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Customer" and "Business Owner" role badges or name tags

description.en: Teacher demonstrates WRONG way (arguing, blaming) vs. RIGHT way (listening, apologizing, solving). Exaggerate for humor and clarity.
description.es: Teacher demonstrates WRONG way (arguing, blaming) vs. RIGHT way (listening, apologizing, solving). Exaggerate for humor and clarity.

description.en: Pairs choose who's Customer first, who's Business Owner first.
description.es: Pairs choose who's Customer first, who's Business Owner first.

description.en: Customer reads their complaint from card. Business Owner responds. Aim for: Listen, Apologize, Solve.
description.es: Customer reads their complaint from card. Business Owner responds. Aim for: Listen, Apologize, Solve.

description.en: Partners swap roles. New scenario card. Repeat.
description.es: Partners swap roles. New scenario card. Repeat.

description.en: "What responses worked best? Which ones made the customer feel heard?"
description.es: "What responses worked best? Which ones made the customer feel heard?"

description.en: Students check off on worksheet: "I listened ☐ I apologized ☐ I offered a solution ☐"
description.es: Students check off on worksheet: "I listened ☐ I apologized ☐ I offered a solution ☐"

discussionQuestions: Was it hard to stay calm when the customer complained?
How did it feel to BE the unhappy customer?
What's the difference between 'I'm sorry' and 'It's not my fault'?
Would you shop there again if they fixed your problem nicely?
What if the customer is WRONG but still upset?
extensionIdeas: Create a class "Customer Service Rules" poster with student-generated ideas.

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Customer Service Training with Cost Analysis

sayThis.en: "Riley's mistake cost sixteen dollars in materials and left two dollars of profit. Now the worse part: an unhappy customer tells about ten people. One mistake, ten people who never come."
sayThis.es: "Riley's mistake cost sixteen dollars in materials and left two dollars of profit. Now the worse part: an unhappy customer tells about ten people. One mistake, ten people who never come."

doneWhen.en: The one-becomes-ten picture is on the board with a dollar figure beside it.
doneWhen.es: The one-becomes-ten picture is on the board with a dollar figure beside it.

watchFor.en: Bad service treated as just rude rather than expensive. Keep the number in front of them.
watchFor.es: Bad service treated as just rude rather than expensive. Keep the number in front of them.

description.en: Discuss: "Riley's mistake cost them $16 in materials and only $2 profit left. Let's calculate costs of bad service." Mini-lesson: One unhappy customer tells 10 people. Show visual of 1 person becoming 10 lost customers.
description.es: Discuss: "Riley's mistake cost them $16 in materials and only $2 profit left. Let's calculate costs of bad service." Mini-lesson: One unhappy customer tells 10 people. Show visual of 1 person becoming 10 lost customers.

sayThis.en: "Three L's. Listen — don't interrupt, even when they're wrong. Learn — ask questions until you understand. Love — fix it and mean it. Watch me do it badly first, then properly."
sayThis.es: "Three L's. Listen — don't interrupt, even when they're wrong. Learn — ask questions until you understand. Love — fix it and mean it. Watch me do it badly first, then properly."

doneWhen.en: The three L's are on the board and both versions have been acted out.
doneWhen.es: The three L's are on the board and both versions have been acted out.

watchFor.en: Laughter at the bad version drowning out the good one. Do the good version second and in silence.
watchFor.es: Laughter at the bad version drowning out the good one. Do the good version second and in silence.

description.en: Teacher models the 3 L's: LISTEN (don't interrupt), LEARN (ask questions to understand), LOVE (fix it with care) Show both defensive response and excellent response side-by-side
description.es: Teacher models the 3 L's: LISTEN (don't interrupt), LEARN (ask questions to understand), LOVE (fix it with care) Show both defensive response and excellent response side-by-side

sayThis.en: "Three of you. One complains, one runs the business, one watches with the sheet. Two minutes, then rotate. Observers — you score, you don't join in."
sayThis.es: "Three of you. One complains, one runs the business, one watches with the sheet. Two minutes, then rotate. Observers — you score, you don't join in."

doneWhen.en: Every group has three completed rubric sheets, one per role rotation.
doneWhen.es: Every group has three completed rubric sheets, one per role rotation.

watchFor.en: Observers joining the scene. Give them the sheet and a pen and it usually holds.
watchFor.es: Observers joining the scene. Give them the sheet and a pen and it usually holds.

description.en: Groups of 3: Customer, Business Owner, Observer Observer uses rubric to score response (Did they listen? Apologize? Solve?) 2 minutes per scenario, then switch roles
description.es: Groups of 3: Customer, Business Owner, Observer Observer uses rubric to score response (Did they listen? Apologize? Solve?) 2 minutes per scenario, then switch roles

sayThis.en: "Harder now. This customer is angry, or wants money back, or wants it free. Same three L's. Staying calm when they're not is the actual skill."
sayThis.es: "Harder now. This customer is angry, or wants money back, or wants it free. Same three L's. Staying calm when they're not is the actual skill."

doneWhen.en: Every group has scored all three of the harder scenarios.
doneWhen.es: Every group has scored all three of the harder scenarios.

watchFor.en: Anger played as comedy. Ask them to do it like they mean it, once.
watchFor.es: Anger played as comedy. Ask them to do it like they mean it, once.

description.en: Increase difficulty (angry customer, customer asking for refund, customer wants free replacement) Same rotation, new roles for each
description.es: Increase difficulty (angry customer, customer asking for refund, customer wants free replacement) Same rotation, new roles for each

sayThis.en: "Plate cost eight dollars. Riley made it twice, so sixteen. Profit dropped from ten to two. Now the big one — if one unhappy customer tells ten people and each would have spent twenty dollars, what did that mistake really cost?"
sayThis.es: "Plate cost eight dollars. Riley made it twice, so sixteen. Profit dropped from ten to two. Now the big one — if one unhappy customer tells ten people and each would have spent twenty dollars, what did that mistake really cost?"

doneWhen.en: Every worksheet has all the scenarios calculated, including the lost-future-business one.
doneWhen.es: Every worksheet has all the scenarios calculated, including the lost-future-business one.

watchFor.en: Students stopping at the materials number. The two hundred is the point of the exercise.
watchFor.es: Students stopping at the materials number. The two hundred is the point of the exercise.

description.en: Worksheet: "The plate cost $8 to make. Riley remade it ($8 more). Profit went from $10 to $2. How much did the mistake cost?" Calculate: "If an unhappy customer tells 10 people and each would have spent $20, how much future business did you lose?" ($200) Students complete 3-4 cost scenarios
description.es: Worksheet: "The plate cost $8 to make. Riley remade it ($8 more). Profit went from $10 to $2. How much did the mistake cost?" Calculate: "If an unhappy customer tells 10 people and each would have spent $20, how much future business did you lose?" ($200) Students complete 3-4 cost scenarios

sayThis.en: "Write two or three rules that stop the complaint happening at all. Riley's was show a drawing first. A rule beats an apology every time, because it happens before anything goes wrong."
sayThis.es: "Write two or three rules that stop the complaint happening at all. Riley's was show a drawing first. A rule beats an apology every time, because it happens before anything goes wrong."

doneWhen.en: Every group has at least two written rules, each naming a specific action.
doneWhen.es: Every group has at least two written rules, each naming a specific action.

watchFor.en: Rules that are just "be nice". A rule has to name an action and when it happens.
watchFor.es: Rules that are just "be nice". A rule has to name an action and when it happens.

description.en: Small groups write 2-3 "business rules" to prevent complaints (like Riley's "show a drawing first" rule) Examples: "Ask 3 questions before starting work," "Let customer approve samples," "Check finished work before delivering"
description.es: Small groups write 2-3 "business rules" to prevent complaints (like Riley's "show a drawing first" rule) Examples: "Ask 3 questions before starting work," "Let customer approve samples," "Check finished work before delivering"

sayThis.en: "Certificates from the observer scores, not from me. Then three votes — best problem-solver, calmest under pressure, best listener."
sayThis.es: "Certificates from the observer scores, not from me. Then three votes — best problem-solver, calmest under pressure, best listener."

doneWhen.en: Certificates are handed out and all three class votes are counted.
doneWhen.es: Certificates are handed out and all three class votes are counted.

watchFor.en: Votes going to the loudest performer. Point back at the rubric sheets.
watchFor.es: Votes going to the loudest performer. Point back at the rubric sheets.

description.es: Give "Excellent Service" certificates to students who scored highest on Observer rubrics Class votes: "Best problem-solver," "Calmest under pressure," "Best listener"

description.es: Divide class in half. Each side is a store selling the same items (pencils, erasers, bookmarks). Both stores set same prices. Emphasize: prices are identical.

description.es: Give stores 3 minutes to make their store different WITHOUT changing prices. Options: better signs, friendly greeting, organized display, sample item, etc.

description.en: Teacher and volunteers act as customers, each carrying 8 paper clips as coins. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.
description.es: Teacher and volunteers act as customers, each carrying 8 paper clips as coins. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.

description.en: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.
description.es: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, why did both stores end up making almost no money?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Paper clips as coins — 10 per customer — collected back and reused
Product materials (craft supplies, printed "goods," or menus)
Chart paper for data tracking and graphing

sayThis.en: "Every team is selling the same thing. Identical stock, identical start. The only way to win a customer is to take them off somebody else. That's what competition actually is."
sayThis.es: "Every team is selling the same thing. Identical stock, identical start. The only way to win a customer is to take them off somebody else. That's what competition actually is."

doneWhen.en: Every team has identical counted stock and an empty cup on the desk.
doneWhen.es: Every team has identical counted stock and an empty cup on the desk.

watchFor.en: Teams checking whether someone got more. Show them the counts out loud and settle it.
watchFor.es: Teams checking whether someone got more. Show them the counts out loud and settle it.

description.en: Divide class into 6-8 competing businesses selling similar products. Each team gets identical starting inventory and an empty cup for the paper clips they take in. Explain: you must attract customers away from competitors.
description.es: Divide class into 6-8 competing businesses selling similar products. Each team gets identical starting inventory and an empty cup for the paper clips they take in. Explain: you must attract customers away from competitors.

sayThis.en: "Round one, price only. You can't change the product, you can't advertise. All you can do is go lower than the team next to you. Off you go."
sayThis.es: "Round one, price only. You can't change the product, you can't advertise. All you can do is go lower than the team next to you. Off you go."

doneWhen.en: Every team's round-one sales and final price are on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every team's round-one sales and final price are on the board.

watchFor.en: The floor being reached in two minutes, then boredom. That's exactly the lesson — let it happen and name it.
watchFor.es: The floor being reached in two minutes, then boredom. That's exactly the lesson — let it happen and name it.

description.en: Teams can only compete on price. Customers (rotating students) shop for best deals. Track sales. Debrief: What happened to prices? (Race to the bottom.) Did anyone make profit?
description.es: Teams can only compete on price. Customers (rotating students) shop for best deals. Track sales. Debrief: What happened to prices? (Race to the bottom.) Did anyone make profit?

sayThis.en: "Now you can change the product. Add something. Bundle two together. Make a loyalty card. You don't have to be the cheapest if you're the only one who has it."
sayThis.es: "Now you can change the product. Add something. Bundle two together. Make a loyalty card. You don't have to be the cheapest if you're the only one who has it."

doneWhen.en: Every team has made at least one visible change to its product or offer.
doneWhen.es: Every team has made at least one visible change to its product or offer.

watchFor.en: Teams still just cutting prices out of habit. Ask what makes theirs different, and wait.
watchFor.es: Teams still just cutting prices out of habit. Ask what makes theirs different, and wait.

description.en: Now teams can change their product — add features, improve packaging, offer bundles, create loyalty cards. Same shopping period. Track sales and compare to Round 1.
description.es: Now teams can change their product — add features, improve packaging, offer bundles, create loyalty cards. Same shopping period. Track sales and compare to Round 1.

sayThis.en: "Everything's allowed. Price, product, service, and thirty seconds of advertising each. Tell the room why you."
sayThis.es: "Everything's allowed. Price, product, service, and thirty seconds of advertising each. Tell the room why you."

doneWhen.en: Every team has given a pitch and round-three sales are recorded.
doneWhen.es: Every team has given a pitch and round-three sales are recorded.

watchFor.en: Adverts that are only a price. Ask what else the customer gets.
watchFor.es: Adverts that are only a price. Ask what else the customer gets.

description.en: Teams can use price, differentiation, AND customer service. Introduce advertising (30-second pitches). Final shopping round. Track all transactions.
description.es: Teams can use price, differentiation, AND customer service. Introduce advertising (30-second pitches). Final shopping round. Track all transactions.

sayThis.en: "Profit for each round, not sales. Chart all three. Round one you probably sold loads and made nothing. Look at which round made you money and what you were doing differently."
sayThis.es: "Profit for each round, not sales. Chart all three. Round one you probably sold loads and made nothing. Look at which round made you money and what you were doing differently."

doneWhen.en: Every team has three profit figures charted, one per round.
doneWhen.es: Every team has three profit figures charted, one per round.

watchFor.en: Sales counts being treated as success. Keep pulling it back to profit.
watchFor.es: Sales counts being treated as success. Keep pulling it back to profit.

description.en: Calculate profit/loss for each round. Chart class results. Discuss: Which strategy worked best? Why do some businesses succeed while others fail? What made customers switch?
description.es: Calculate profit/loss for each round. Chart class results. Discuss: Which strategy worked best? Why do some businesses succeed while others fail? What made customers switch?

sayThis.en: "Name two real businesses that compete. Not what they sell — how they're different from each other. Then one lesson you'd use if this were your shop."
sayThis.es: "Name two real businesses that compete. Not what they sell — how they're different from each other. Then one lesson you'd use if this were your shop."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written two competing businesses and one lesson.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written two competing businesses and one lesson.

watchFor.en: Pairs that don't actually compete. Ask whether a customer would ever choose between them.
watchFor.es: Pairs that don't actually compete. Ask whether a customer would ever choose between them.

description.en: Name two real businesses that compete with each other. How do they differentiate? Write one lesson learned about competition that you could use if you started a business.
description.es: Name two real businesses that compete with each other. How do they differentiate? Write one lesson learned about competition that you could use if you started a business.

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, what happened to businesses that just kept lowering prices?
Give an example of a differentiation strategy a team used.
Did customers care about differentiation, or did they only want the cheapest option?
How is profit margin different from total revenue?
Connect to the story: Why did Ellis decide to RAISE prices instead of lowering them?
What was Maplewood Makers' competitive advantage? (Quality, guarantees, customer relationships)
Real world: Can you think of businesses that charge MORE but people still buy from them? (Apple, Starbucks, etc.) Why?
What's the risk of always being the cheapest option in your market?
extensionIdeas: Research real-world examples of differentiation (Southwest Airlines: friendly service; Volvo: safety; In-N-Out Burger: fresh ingredients)
Create advertising campaigns highlighting each team's competitive advantage
Write business case studies: "When [Team Name] competed on price, profit was $X. When they differentiated with [strategy], profit became $Y."
Graph long-term scenarios: "If you make $1 profit per item vs. $4 profit per item, how many must you sell to earn $100?"
Debate: "Should businesses ever compete primarily on price? When might that strategy make sense?"

beforeClass.en: Make the starting inventories genuinely identical, item for item. If one team starts with more, the whole point about differentiation is lost. One cup per team for the paper clips they take in.
beforeClass.es: Make the starting inventories genuinely identical, item for item. If one team starts with more, the whole point about differentiation is lost. One cup per team for the paper clips they take in.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut round three and analyze after two. Short: add a fourth round where two teams may merge and see what that does.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut round three and analyze after two. Short: add a fourth round where two teams may merge and see what that does.

title.en: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses
title.es: True Cost Detective: Finding Hidden Expenses

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Picture cards, drawn or printed — lemonade cup, friendship bracelet, paper airplane

description.en: Present scenario: 'You're selling lemonade for $1 per cup. You made $10. Did you make $10 profit?' Students predict yes or no. Explain: profit is what's LEFT after costs.
description.es: Present scenario: 'You're selling lemonade for $1 per cup. You made $10. Did you make $10 profit?' Students predict yes or no. Explain: profit is what's LEFT after costs.

description.en: Students brainstorm all hidden costs for lemonade stand: lemons, sugar, cups, ice, table, sign, time. List on board. Estimate cost for each item.
description.es: Students brainstorm all hidden costs for lemonade stand: lemons, sugar, cups, ice, table, sign, time. List on board. Estimate cost for each item.

description.en: Add up all costs. Subtract from $10 revenue. Calculate true profit. Chart: Revenue ($10) − Costs ($___) = Profit ($___). Discuss surprise results.
description.es: Add up all costs. Subtract from $10 revenue. Calculate true profit. Chart: Revenue ($10) − Costs ($___) = Profit ($___). Discuss surprise results.

description.en: Ask: Why do people forget about hidden costs? What's the most surprising cost? How could you reduce costs?
description.es: Ask: Why do people forget about hidden costs? What's the most surprising cost? How could you reduce costs?

discussionQuestions: What hidden costs did we find?
Why do things cost more than just the materials?
Which hidden cost surprised you most?

materials: 3-4 product picture cards: lemonade cup, paper airplane, friendship bracelet, greeting card

description.en: Present scenario: 'You're selling lemonade for $1 per cup. You made $10. Did you make $10 profit?' Students predict yes or no. Explain: profit is what's LEFT after costs.

description.en: Add up all costs. Subtract from $10 revenue. Calculate true profit. Chart: Revenue ($10) − Costs ($___) = Profit ($___). Discuss surprise results.

description.en: Ask: Why do people forget about hidden costs? What's the most surprising cost? How could you reduce costs?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete True Cost Investigation with Bulk Buying Analysis
materials: Bulk buying comparison cards (small pack vs. large pack with prices)
Paper clips as coins for the demonstration
PROFIT jar and COSTS jar (labeled containers)
Chart paper for class overhead tracking

sayThis.en: "A stand on paper, and we're going to find every single thing it costs. Not just the obvious ones. Four words to know: revenue is what comes in, expenses go out, overhead is what you pay whether you sell anything or not, and profit is what's actually left."
sayThis.es: "A stand on paper, and we're going to find every single thing it costs. Not just the obvious ones. Four words to know: revenue is what comes in, expenses go out, overhead is what you pay whether you sell anything or not, and profit is what's actually left."

doneWhen.en: All four terms are on the board with a one-line meaning each.
doneWhen.es: All four terms are on the board with a one-line meaning each.

watchFor.en: Overhead being skipped as a hard word. Give an example: you pay for the table even if nobody buys.
watchFor.es: Overhead being skipped as a hard word. Give an example: you pay for the table even if nobody buys.

description.en: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit.
description.es: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit.

sayThis.en: "Three buckets. Direct costs are the things that become the product. Overhead is what you pay anyway. Labor is your own time, and your time is not free. Fill all three."
sayThis.es: "Three buckets. Direct costs are the things that become the product. Overhead is what you pay anyway. Labor is your own time, and your time is not free. Fill all three."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has at least two items listed in all three categories.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has at least two items listed in all three categories.

watchFor.en: Empty labor columns. Ask what they'd charge someone else to stand there for two hours.
watchFor.es: Empty labor columns. Ask what they'd charge someone else to stand there for two hours.

description.en: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.
description.es: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.

sayThis.en: "Real numbers off the price sheet now, not guesses. Add up each bucket separately, then all three together. That total is what it cost before a single sale."
sayThis.es: "Real numbers off the price sheet now, not guesses. Add up each bucket separately, then all three together. That total is what it cost before a single sale."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has three category totals and a grand total written down.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has three category totals and a grand total written down.

watchFor.en: Pairs adding everything into one pile. The three separate totals are what makes the next steps work.
watchFor.es: Pairs adding everything into one pile. The three separate totals are what makes the next steps work.

description.en: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using provided price sheet. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record in cost tracking worksheet.
description.es: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using provided price sheet. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record in cost tracking worksheet.

sayThis.en: "Ten bought one at a time, against a bag of ten. Work out the saving. Then the catch — you need all the money up front, and whatever you don't use is wasted."
sayThis.es: "Ten bought one at a time, against a bag of ten. Work out the saving. Then the catch — you need all the money up front, and whatever you don't use is wasted."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows both prices and the saving calculated.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows both prices and the saving calculated.

watchFor.en: Bulk treated as always better. Ask what happens if they only sell three.
watchFor.es: Bulk treated as always better. Ask what happens if they only sell three.

description.en: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. bag of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra)
description.es: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. bag of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra)

sayThis.en: "Design the sheet you'd actually use. Columns for supplies, time and overhead. Simple enough that you'd fill it in when you're tired, because that's when people stop."
sayThis.es: "Design the sheet you'd actually use. Columns for supplies, time and overhead. Simple enough that you'd fill it in when you're tired, because that's when people stop."

doneWhen.en: Every tracking sheet has been designed and test-filled with at least three rows.
doneWhen.es: Every tracking sheet has been designed and test-filled with at least three rows.

watchFor.en: Beautiful sheets with no room to write. Ask them to fill in three rows of their own design.
watchFor.es: Beautiful sheets with no room to write. Ask them to fill in three rows of their own design.

description.en: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.
description.es: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.

sayThis.en: "Revenue, take off direct costs, take off overhead, take off your own time. What's left? Now compare that to what you guessed at the start. Most people guess about double."
sayThis.es: "Revenue, take off direct costs, take off overhead, take off your own time. What's left? Now compare that to what you guessed at the start. Most people guess about double."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows the full subtraction with labor included and the original guess beside it.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows the full subtraction with labor included and the original guess beside it.

watchFor.en: Labor quietly dropped to make the profit look better. That's the exact habit this chapter exists to break.
watchFor.es: Labor quietly dropped to make the profit look better. That's the exact habit this chapter exists to break.

description.en: Calculate final profit: Revenue − Direct Costs − Overhead − Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?
description.es: Calculate final profit: Revenue − Direct Costs − Overhead − Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between overhead and material costs?
Why do we need a RESERVE jar for future tool replacement?
How does bulk buying change your true cost over time?
What happens to businesses that don't count hidden costs?
Is it 'bad' to discover hidden costs? Or is it helpful to know the truth?
How much overhead should we add to our prices? 10%? 20%? How do we decide?
extensionIdeas: Track a week of classroom hidden costs (markers that dry out, paper waste, electricity for lights)
Research real business overhead percentages by industry (restaurants 30-40%, retail 20-30%)
Create a "Reserve Fund Calculator" for different business scenarios
Visit a local business and interview owner about their overhead costs
Calculate true cost of a school fundraiser (bake sale, car wash, etc.)

beforeClass.en: Print the price sheet and check every item on it has a number; a missing price stalls a whole pair. This is a costing exercise on paper — no drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.
beforeClass.es: Print the price sheet and check every item on it has a number; a missing price stalls a whole pair. This is a costing exercise on paper — no drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: do the bulk-buying comparison as one whole-class example. Short: add a second scenario with a rainy day and half the customers.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: do the bulk-buying comparison as one whole-class example. Short: add a second scenario with a rainy day and half the customers.

description.es: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.

description.en: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.

description.es: Return task cards and materials. Share one takeaway with a partner.

description.en: Explain 'pivot': when a business changes its product or approach because original plan isn't working. Discuss real examples: lemonade stand switches to hot chocolate when it's cold. Introduce challenge scenario.
description.es: Explain 'pivot': when a business changes its product or approach because original plan isn't working. Discuss real examples: lemonade stand switches to hot chocolate when it's cold. Introduce challenge scenario.

description.en: Students start simple classroom business: selling bookmarks, offering helper services, or making cards. Set up, create product, prepare to sell. Begin initial sales or service.
description.es: Students start simple classroom business: selling bookmarks, offering helper services, or making cards. Set up, create product, prepare to sell. Begin initial sales or service.

description.en: Teacher announces a problem: 'No one wants bookmarks today!' or 'We ran out of key materials!' Students must pivot: What could you sell instead with materials you have? What different service could you offer? Quick brainstorm.
description.es: Teacher announces a problem: 'No one wants bookmarks today!' or 'We ran out of key materials!' Students must pivot: What could you sell instead with materials you have? What different service could you offer? Quick brainstorm.

description.es: Students quickly change their business: create new product, switch to different service, or modify original offering. Adapt with available resources. Resume sales or service with new approach.

description.es: Divide into groups of 3-4. Each group gets a different failing business scenario (ice cream shop in winter, toy store where nobody buys dolls, pizza place with too many menu items nobody orders).

description.es: Groups identify WHY the business is failing. Write or draw the problem.

description.es: What could they change? Product? Location? Target customers? Time of day? Groups list 3-5 possible pivots.

description.es: Select ONE pivot and create a "Before → After" chart showing what changes.

description.es: Each group shares their pivot. Class discusses: "Would this work? Why or why not?"

description.es: Teams complete "Pivot Plan" worksheet: What we're STOPPING (like journals) What we're FOCUSING ON (like pottery) Why this will work (evidence from data) What we'll lose (emotional cost, like Layla missing her journals) What we'll gain (predicted new revenue and profit) Create visual presentation: "Before Pivot" vs. "After Pivot" comparison
