description.en: Pairs share their partnership agreements with another pair or whole class. Explain: How did you divide responsibilities? Why? Discuss: What makes a good partnership? What could go wrong? How does agreement help? Why is it important to decide these things before starting?
description.es: Pairs share their partnership agreements with another pair or whole class. Explain: How did you divide responsibilities? Why? Discuss: What makes a good partnership? What could go wrong? How does agreement help? Why is it important to decide these things before starting?

discussionQuestions: What business did you and your partner create?
What job will each person do?
Why did you decide to split the money that way?

30.label: 30 Minutes

30.activityName: Negotiated Partnership Agreement with "What If" Clauses
materials: Partnership agreement template with sections for roles, profit split, and problems

description.en: Discuss business partnerships: examples from real world, why people partner up, potential benefits and challenges. Review what makes partnerships succeed or fail. Introduce partnership agreement project.
description.es: Discuss business partnerships: examples from real world, why people partner up, potential benefits and challenges. Review what makes partnerships succeed or fail. Introduce partnership agreement project.

description.en: Students form pairs based on complementary skills or interests. Partners interview each other: What are your strengths? What do you like doing? What business could we run together? Brainstorm business ideas. Choose one business concept both partners agree on.
description.es: Students form pairs based on complementary skills or interests. Partners interview each other: What are your strengths? What do you like doing? What business could we run together? Brainstorm business ideas. Choose one business concept both partners agree on.

description.en: Partners discuss and negotiate responsibilities: Who will handle which tasks? How to divide the work fairly? What if someone doesn't do their part? How to make big decisions together? Practice compromise and clear communication.
description.es: Partners discuss and negotiate responsibilities: Who will handle which tasks? How to divide the work fairly? What if someone doesn't do their part? How to make big decisions together? Practice compromise and clear communication.

description.en: Partners create comprehensive written partnership agreement: business description, each partner's specific responsibilities, decision-making process, work schedule, how to handle disagreements, exit plan if partnership doesn't work. Both sign and date.
description.es: Partners create comprehensive written partnership agreement: business description, each partner's specific responsibilities, decision-making process, work schedule, how to handle disagreements, exit plan if partnership doesn't work. Both sign and date.

description.en: Partner pairs present their agreements to class. Explain their business and how they'll work together. Answer questions from classmates. Reflect on partnership planning process.
description.es: Partner pairs present their agreements to class. Explain their business and how they'll work together. Answer questions from classmates. Reflect on partnership planning process.

discussionQuestions: How did you decide who does which job?
Was it easy or hard to agree on how to split the money?
What happens if one partner does all the work but the other partner wants half the money?
Why is it important to have a written agreement?
What did Benny do in the story when he thought 40¢ was too much?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Partnership Contract with Negotiation & Legal Review
materials: Colored pencils or pens for signing
Sample real-world partnership agreements (simplified for kids)

sayThis.en: "A partnership is two people agreeing who owns what and who does what. When it goes wrong it's almost never about the work. It's about a thing nobody wrote down at the start."
sayThis.es: "A partnership is two people agreeing who owns what and who does what. When it goes wrong it's almost never about the work. It's about a thing nobody wrote down at the start."

doneWhen.en: At least three things a partnership agreement must cover are listed on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least three things a partnership agreement must cover are listed on the board.

watchFor.en: Partnership heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends split lunch, partners split money.
watchFor.es: Partnership heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends split lunch, partners split money.

description.en: Explore business partnerships in depth: legal structures, real partnership agreements, famous successful and failed partnerships. Discuss equity (who owns what percentage), profit sharing, and legal responsibilities. Set ambitious partnership project goals.
description.es: Explore business partnerships in depth: legal structures, real partnership agreements, famous successful and failed partnerships. Discuss equity (who owns what percentage), profit sharing, and legal responsibilities. Set ambitious partnership project goals.

sayThis.en: "Fill in what you're good at and what you want to build. Then find someone whose list is different from yours. Two people who are good at the same thing leave half the business undone."
sayThis.es: "Fill in what you're good at and what you want to build. Then find someone whose list is different from yours. Two people who are good at the same thing leave half the business undone."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a partner and both have completed skills inventories on the table.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a partner and both have completed skills inventories on the table.

watchFor.en: Everyone pairing with their best friend. Say it out loud: pick for the skills, and check the fit by talking first.
watchFor.es: Everyone pairing with their best friend. Say it out loud: pick for the skills, and check the fit by talking first.

description.en: Students complete skills inventory and business interest survey. Use results to find strategically compatible partners: matching skills to business needs. Partners conduct formal business discussion: visions for business, commitment level, long-term goals. Negotiate and form partnerships based on strategic fit.
description.es: Students complete skills inventory and business interest survey. Use results to find strategically compatible partners: matching skills to business needs. Partners conduct formal business discussion: visions for business, commitment level, long-term goals. Negotiate and form partnerships based on strategic fit.

sayThis.en: "Five answers, together. What you sell. Who buys it. How you make it. What it costs. How you make money. Then draw it as boxes and arrows so you can see where the money goes."
sayThis.es: "Five answers, together. What you sell. Who buys it. How you make it. What it costs. How you make money. Then draw it as boxes and arrows so you can see where the money goes."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has a drawn model with all five parts labeled.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has a drawn model with all five parts labeled.

watchFor.en: One partner writing while the other watches. Both hands on the paper.
watchFor.es: One partner writing while the other watches. Both hands on the paper.

description.en: Partners collaboratively develop detailed business model: What will we sell/provide? Who are customers? How will we produce it? What are costs? How will we make profit? Create business model diagram showing all components and how they connect.
description.es: Partners collaboratively develop detailed business model: What will we sell/provide? Who are customers? How will we produce it? What are costs? How will we make profit? Create business model diagram showing all components and how they connect.

sayThis.en: "Now the real thing. Who owns what percentage. What each of you put in. Who does which jobs. Who decides when you disagree. And the awkward one — what happens if one of you wants out."
sayThis.es: "Now the real thing. Who owns what percentage. What each of you put in. Who does which jobs. Who decides when you disagree. And the awkward one — what happens if one of you wants out."

doneWhen.en: Every agreement has all the required sections filled, including the exit clause.
doneWhen.es: Every agreement has all the required sections filled, including the exit clause.

watchFor.en: Fifty-fifty written everywhere without discussion. Ask if the contributions were actually equal.
watchFor.es: Fifty-fifty written everywhere without discussion. Ask if the contributions were actually equal.

description.en: Partners create detailed partnership agreement covering: ownership percentage, capital contributions (what each brings to business), specific role definitions, daily responsibilities, decision-making protocols, conflict resolution process, financial arrangements, performance expectations, exit strategies.
description.es: Partners create detailed partnership agreement covering: ownership percentage, capital contributions (what each brings to business), specific role definitions, daily responsibilities, decision-making protocols, conflict resolution process, financial arrangements, performance expectations, exit strategies.

sayThis.en: "Swap with another pair. Read it like you're about to sign it. Is anything unclear? Is one person doing more? What happens when they argue?"
sayThis.es: "Swap with another pair. Read it like you're about to sign it. Is anything unclear? Is one person doing more? What happens when they argue?"

doneWhen.en: Every agreement carries written feedback from another pair.
doneWhen.es: Every agreement carries written feedback from another pair.

watchFor.en: Reviews that just say it's fine. Require one written question per reviewer.
watchFor.es: Reviews that just say it's fine. Require one written question per reviewer.

description.en: Partners exchange agreements with another pair for peer review. Check: Is everything clear? Are responsibilities balanced? Is conflict resolution specified? Provide feedback. Revise agreements based on input.
description.es: Partners exchange agreements with another pair for peer review. Check: Is everything clear? Are responsibilities balanced? Is conflict resolution specified? Provide feedback. Revise agreements based on input.

sayThis.en: "Make your changes and sign it. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."
sayThis.es: "Make your changes and sign it. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."

doneWhen.en: Every agreement is signed by both partners with at least one visible revision.
doneWhen.es: Every agreement is signed by both partners with at least one visible revision.

watchFor.en: Signing without making the revisions. Check for a change before the signature.
watchFor.es: Signing without making the revisions. Check for a change before the signature.

description.en: Partners finalize and sign their partnership agreements. Discuss: What surprised you about creating an agreement? What might be hard in real partnerships? Why do written agreements matter? How does your partnership agreement protect both partners?
description.es: Partners finalize and sign their partnership agreements. Discuss: What surprised you about creating an agreement? What might be hard in real partnerships? Why do written agreements matter? How does your partnership agreement protect both partners?

discussionQuestions: What negotiation strategies worked best for reaching agreement?
Did any partnership split money unevenly? Why was that fair?
What's the difference between a fair split and an equal split?
Why do real businesses write contracts instead of just making promises?
What clause in your agreement do you think will be most important?
In the story, what would have happened if Ellen and the friends DIDN'T write everything down?
extensionIdeas: Compare to real-world business partnerships (research famous business partnerships)
Create a class "Partnership Law Firm" that reviews all agreements for fairness
Role-play dispute scenarios and use the agreements to resolve them
Calculate actual profit splits with sample revenue numbers
Research consignment vs. other partnership types (joint venture, LLC, etc.)

beforeClass.en: Print the skills inventory and the agreement template. Decide in advance what you'll do with an odd number of students — a group of three needs a three-way split, and it's better to plan it than improvise it.
beforeClass.es: Print the skills inventory and the agreement template. Decide in advance what you'll do with an odd number of students — a group of three needs a three-way split, and it's better to plan it than improvise it.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: 20 craft items (pom-poms, beads, or paper squares) representing "products"

description.en: Students become store owners. Teacher announces: 'It's almost winter holiday!' Students must predict demand and 'buy' inventory. Each student gets 10 tickets to spend on products (pencils, erasers, bookmarks).
description.es: Students become store owners. Teacher announces: 'It's almost winter holiday!' Students must predict demand and 'buy' inventory. Each student gets 10 tickets to spend on products (pencils, erasers, bookmarks).

description.en: Students decide how many of each item to stock. Write predictions on paper. Teacher collects ticket 'payment' for their inventory. Students can't change once purchased.
description.es: Students decide how many of each item to stock. Write predictions on paper. Teacher collects ticket 'payment' for their inventory. Students can't change once purchased.

description.en: Teacher reveals: 'Customers want bookmarks for holiday gifts!' Roll die or draw card to show demand: 8 bookmark customers, 1 pencil customer, 0 eraser customers. Students compare to their inventory.
description.es: Teacher reveals: 'Customers want bookmarks for holiday gifts!' Roll die or draw card to show demand: 8 bookmark customers, 1 pencil customer, 0 eraser customers. Students compare to their inventory.

description.en: Students calculate: How many items did you sell? How many left over? Did you run out? Discuss: What happens if you over-order? Under-order? What clues could help predict demand?
description.es: Students calculate: How many items did you sell? How many left over? Did you run out? Discuss: What happens if you over-order? Under-order? What clues could help predict demand?

discussionQuestions: Was it easy or hard to guess how many people would want?
What happens if you make too many?
Why should you save money from busy weeks?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: "Order form" cards (15-20 cards with customer orders)
Scrap-paper budget card showing $200, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent

description.en: You're a store manager before the holidays. Show product cards with varying demand levels. Introduce the problem: you must order products NOW for customers who will shop LATER. Order too much = waste money. Order too little = miss sales.
description.es: You're a store manager before the holidays. Show product cards with varying demand levels. Introduce the problem: you must order products NOW for customers who will shop LATER. Order too much = waste money. Order too little = miss sales.

description.en: Students review last year's sales data (simplified cards) and make ordering decisions for 5-6 products. Write predictions: how many of each item will sell this holiday season?
description.es: Students review last year's sales data (simplified cards) and make ordering decisions for 5-6 products. Write predictions: how many of each item will sell this holiday season?

description.en: Reveal actual demand (draw customer cards). Students check if they had enough inventory. Calculate: items sold, items left over (wasted money), customers turned away (lost sales).
description.es: Reveal actual demand (draw customer cards). Students check if they had enough inventory. Calculate: items sold, items left over (wasted money), customers turned away (lost sales).

description.en: Calculate profit: revenue from sales minus cost of all inventory ordered (including unsold items). Compare results across the class. Who was the best store manager? What strategy did they use?
description.es: Calculate profit: revenue from sales minus cost of all inventory ordered (including unsold items). Compare results across the class. Who was the best store manager? What strategy did they use?

description.en: Why is predicting hard? What clues help stores prepare? (Weather, trends, past data.) How do real stores handle leftover holiday inventory? (Sales, clearance, donations.)
description.es: Why is predicting hard? What clues help stores prepare? (Weather, trends, past data.) How do real stores handle leftover holiday inventory? (Sales, clearance, donations.)

discussionQuestions: Which week was hardest to predict? Why?
Did anyone run out of inventory? How did that feel?
Did anyone make too many and have leftovers? What's the cost of that?
Why do businesses save money during busy seasons?
How could you use last year's data to predict this year better?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Complete Retail Simulation with Forecasting, Batch Production & Cash Flow
materials: Scrap-paper budget card per team showing $500, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent

sayThis.en: "You run a shop for a year. Three seasons, and you order stock before you know what sells. Order too little and you lose sales. Order too much and it sits there costing you. Nobody gets this perfectly right."
sayThis.es: "You run a shop for a year. Three seasons, and you order stock before you know what sells. Order too little and you lose sales. Order too much and it sits there costing you. Nobody gets this perfectly right."

doneWhen.en: The three seasons and last year's chart are up where everyone can read them.
doneWhen.es: The three seasons and last year's chart are up where everyone can read them.

watchFor.en: The assumption that more stock is always safer. Name the cost of what doesn't sell.
watchFor.es: The assumption that more stock is always safer. Name the cost of what doesn't sell.

description.en: Introduce the retail challenge: managing a store through three seasons (back-to-school, holiday, summer). Each season has different demand patterns. Show historical sales data charts.
description.es: Introduce the retail challenge: managing a store through three seasons (back-to-school, holiday, summer). Each season has different demand patterns. Show historical sales data charts.

sayThis.en: "Look at last September before you order anything. What do children need in the first week of school? Write your order and commit to it."
sayThis.es: "Look at last September before you order anything. What do children need in the first week of school? Write your order and commit to it."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a written, committed order for all products.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a written, committed order for all products.

watchFor.en: Orders written without looking at the historical chart. Send them back to it once.
watchFor.es: Orders written without looking at the historical chart. Send them back to it once.

description.en: Review last year's back-to-school data. Teams decide how much of each product to order. Consider: What do students need in September? How much should you stock?
description.es: Review last year's back-to-school data. Teams decide how much of each product to order. Consider: What do students need in September? How much should you stock?

sayThis.en: "Here's what actually sold. Work out your profit or your loss. Then say out loud what you'd change — that sentence is your strategy for the next round."
sayThis.es: "Here's what actually sold. Work out your profit or your loss. Then say out loud what you'd change — that sentence is your strategy for the next round."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a profit or loss figure and a written change for next round.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a profit or loss figure and a written change for next round.

watchFor.en: Blame on bad luck. Point at the historical chart they had in front of them.
watchFor.es: Blame on bad luck. Point at the historical chart they had in front of them.

description.en: Reveal actual sales. Calculate profit/loss. What did you learn? Teams adjust strategy for the next round based on results.
description.es: Reveal actual sales. Calculate profit/loss. What did you learn? Teams adjust strategy for the next round based on results.

sayThis.en: "Biggest season, hardest to call. New option: buy in bulk and each item costs less — but if it doesn't sell, you've lost more. Cheaper per item is not the same as cheaper."
sayThis.es: "Biggest season, hardest to call. New option: buy in bulk and each item costs less — but if it doesn't sell, you've lost more. Cheaper per item is not the same as cheaper."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a holiday order with a written yes or no on the bulk deal.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a holiday order with a written yes or no on the bulk deal.

watchFor.en: Every team taking the bulk deal automatically. Ask what happens if the season is quiet.
watchFor.es: Every team taking the bulk deal automatically. Ask what happens if the season is quiet.

description.en: Holiday demand is highest but hardest to predict. Teams make ordering decisions with higher stakes. Introduce bulk discount option: order more at lower cost per item, but risk more waste.
description.es: Holiday demand is highest but hardest to predict. Teams make ordering decisions with higher stakes. Introduce bulk discount option: order more at lower cost per item, but risk more waste.

sayThis.en: "Sales drop. Two choices. Order less and stay safe, or discount the leftover holiday stock and pull in bargain hunters. Selling at a discount still beats selling nothing."
sayThis.es: "Sales drop. Two choices. Order less and stay safe, or discount the leftover holiday stock and pull in bargain hunters. Selling at a discount still beats selling nothing."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a summer order and a decision on clearing old stock.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a summer order and a decision on clearing old stock.

watchFor.en: Refusal to mark anything down. Ask what unsold stock is worth in a year.
watchFor.es: Refusal to mark anything down. Ask what unsold stock is worth in a year.

description.en: Demand drops. Teams must decide: order less (safe), or stock sale items to attract bargain hunters? Introduce clearance pricing for leftover holiday inventory.
description.es: Demand drops. Teams must decide: order less (safe), or stock sale items to attract bargain hunters? Introduce clearance pricing for leftover holiday inventory.

sayThis.en: "Add all three seasons. Revenue, costs, profit, each season as its own bar. The winner isn't whoever had the best season — it's whoever survived the worst one."
sayThis.es: "Add all three seasons. Revenue, costs, profit, each season as its own bar. The winner isn't whoever had the best season — it's whoever survived the worst one."

doneWhen.en: Every team's chart shows revenue, cost and profit for all three seasons.
doneWhen.es: Every team's chart shows revenue, cost and profit for all three seasons.

watchFor.en: Charts with revenue only. Costs have to be on there or the bars lie.
watchFor.es: Charts with revenue only. Costs have to be on there or the bars lie.

description.en: Calculate total yearly profit across all three seasons. Create a simple bar chart showing revenue, costs, and profit by season. Compare across teams. Crown the best retail manager.
description.es: Calculate total yearly profit across all three seasons. Create a simple bar chart showing revenue, costs, and profit by season. Compare across teams. Crown the best retail manager.

sayThis.en: "Which season was hardest to predict, and why? Then one forecasting tip you'd give someone doing this next year."
sayThis.es: "Which season was hardest to predict, and why? Then one forecasting tip you'd give someone doing this next year."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written one forecasting tip.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written one forecasting tip.

watchFor.en: Tips that are just try harder. Ask what they'd actually look at first.
watchFor.es: Tips that are just try harder. Ask what they'd actually look at first.

description.en: Discuss: Which season was hardest to predict? What would you do differently next year? How do real stores use data to make these decisions? Write one forecasting tip you learned.
description.es: Discuss: Which season was hardest to predict? What would you do differently next year? How do real stores use data to make these decisions? Write one forecasting tip you learned.

discussionQuestions: How accurate were your predictions compared to actual demand?
What strategy worked best: ordering all supplies upfront, or weekly?
When did batch production help the most?
What was the cost of having leftover inventory? What was the cost of running out?
Why does saving 30% during busy season make business sense?
How could you use this year's data to plan for next year?
What real businesses face seasonal rushes like this?" (Toy stores at Christmas, ice cream shops in summer, ski resorts in winter)
extensionIdeas: Graph revenue across all 4 weeks to visualize the seasonal curve
Calculate "opportunity cost" of missed sales when inventory ran out
Research real retail businesses and their seasonal patterns
Create a "Year 2 Plan" incorporating lessons learned from Year 1
Explore "just-in-time inventory" vs. "bulk ordering" trade-offs
Calculate break-even point and profit margins

description.en: Discuss business seasons: busy times (holidays, summer) and slow times (after holidays, bad weather). Ask: What do businesses do when customers don't come? Introduce slow season strategy challenge.
description.es: Discuss business seasons: busy times (holidays, summer) and slow times (after holidays, bad weather). Ask: What do businesses do when customers don't come? Introduce slow season strategy challenge.

description.en: Present scenario: classroom business had busy fall but now it's winter break and sales dropped. Students brainstorm strategies: What could business do? Lower prices? New products? Save money? Advertise? Work on improvements? List all ideas on board.
description.es: Present scenario: classroom business had busy fall but now it's winter break and sales dropped. Students brainstorm strategies: What could business do? Lower prices? New products? Save money? Advertise? Work on improvements? List all ideas on board.

description.en: Students choose their top 3 strategies from brainstorm. For each, explain: How would this help? What would it cost? When would you do it? Rank strategies: best to worst.
description.es: Students choose their top 3 strategies from brainstorm. For each, explain: How would this help? What would it cost? When would you do it? Rank strategies: best to worst.

description.en: Students share their slow season strategies. Discuss: Which strategies cost money vs. save money? Which are short-term vs. long-term? What do real businesses do in slow seasons? Why is it important to plan for slow times when business is busy?
description.es: Students share their slow season strategies. Discuss: Which strategies cost money vs. save money? Which are short-term vs. long-term? What do real businesses do in slow seasons? Why is it important to plan for slow times when business is busy?

description.es: Discuss how businesses experience seasonal changes: ice cream sells more in summer, hot chocolate in winter, school supplies in fall. Graph simple seasonal business pattern on board. Explain slow season challenges and opportunities.

description.en: Students run classroom business through simulated seasons: busy period (many customers, high sales), then sudden slow period (few customers). Track sales data. Experience the problem firsthand: What happens to money? To inventory? To workers? How does it feel when business is slow?
description.es: Students run classroom business through simulated seasons: busy period (many customers, high sales), then sudden slow period (few customers). Track sales data. Experience the problem firsthand: What happens to money? To inventory? To workers? How does it feel when business is slow?

description.en: In groups, students research different slow season strategies: cutting costs, introducing new products, saving during busy times, finding new customers, improving business during downtime. Each group becomes expert on one strategy.
description.es: In groups, students research different slow season strategies: cutting costs, introducing new products, saving during busy times, finding new customers, improving business during downtime. Each group becomes expert on one strategy.

description.en: Groups present their strategies to class. Compare approaches: Which costs money? Which saves money? Which is risky? Which is safe? Students individually choose which strategies they'd use and create simple slow season survival plan.
description.es: Groups present their strategies to class. Compare approaches: Which costs money? Which saves money? Which is risky? Which is safe? Students individually choose which strategies they'd use and create simple slow season survival plan.

description.en: Discuss: Why do all businesses have busy and slow times? How can planning ahead help? What's the connection between slow seasons and savings? Why might slow season be good time for improvements?
description.es: Discuss: Why do all businesses have busy and slow times? How can planning ahead help? What's the connection between slow seasons and savings? Why might slow season be good time for improvements?

discussionQuestions: Why do some businesses have slow seasons?
Is it smart to give up during slow times? What should you do instead?
How does saving money during good times help during slow times?
What did Frances's garden teach the team about slow seasons?
How did being nice to Mrs. Torres help the team in January?

materials: "Business Scenario" cards (6-8 different slow season scenarios)
Tokens (paper clips) for the budgeting activity, or figures written straight onto the plan sheet

sayThis.en: "A ski resort in July. A pumpkin farm in March. They don't close. So what do they do? Some of you already know one — the landscaper who plows snow, the ice cream shop selling hot chocolate."
sayThis.es: "A ski resort in July. A pumpkin farm in March. They don't close. So what do they do? Some of you already know one — the landscaper who plows snow, the ice cream shop selling hot chocolate."

doneWhen.es: At least four real seasonal businesses and what they do off-season are on the board.

watchFor.en: The assumption that slow means shut. Ask what the staff do on those days.

sayThis.en: "One card per team. It tells you what you sell, how long your quiet spell is, and exactly how much money you have. Read all the numbers before you plan anything."
sayThis.es: "One card per team. It tells you what you sell, how long your quiet spell is, and exactly how much money you have. Read all the numbers before you plan anything."

doneWhen.en: Every team can point to its reserve figure and the length of its slow season.
doneWhen.es: Every team can point to its reserve figure and the length of its slow season.

description.en: Divide class into teams of 3-4 Each team receives a "Business Scenario" card: Beach equipment rental shop in October-March (6 slow months) Wedding photographer in January-February (2 slow months) School supply store in June-July (2 slow months) Pool cleaning service in November-February (4 slow months) Pumpkin farm in January-August (8 slow months) Snow removal service in May-October (6 slow months) Each scenario includes: what they sell, busy season revenue, slow season revenue, money saved, upcoming expenses
description.es: Divide class into teams of 3-4 Each team receives a "Business Scenario" card: Beach equipment rental shop in October-March (6 slow months) Wedding photographer in January-February (2 slow months) School supply store in June-July (2 slow months) Pool cleaning service in November-February (4 slow months) Pumpkin farm in January-August (8 slow months) Snow removal service in May-October (6 slow months) Each scenario includes: what they sell, busy season revenue, slow season revenue, money saved, upcoming expenses

sayThis.en: "Three parts. First, how bad is it — money coming in, how long it lasts, what you've got saved. Second, five moves: prepare, improve, learn, strengthen relationships, or offer something different. Third, the budget — what you spend from reserves and what waits."
sayThis.es: "Three parts. First, how bad is it — money coming in, how long it lasts, what you've got saved. Second, five moves: prepare, improve, learn, strengthen relationships, or offer something different. Third, the budget — what you spend from reserves and what waits."

doneWhen.en: Every team's plan has all three parts filled and at least three named strategies.
doneWhen.es: Every team's plan has all three parts filled and at least three named strategies.

watchFor.en: Plans that are all cutting and no investing. Ask what they'll be ready to sell when it picks up.
watchFor.es: Plans that are all cutting and no investing. Ask what they'll be ready to sell when it picks up.

description.en: Teams complete comprehensive "Slow Season Action Plan": **PART 1: Understanding the Problem** Current situation (how much money coming in now vs. busy season?) How long will slow season last? Do we have reserve funds? How much? **PART 2: Survival Strategies** What can we PREPARE for next busy season? (build inventory, make products, plan marketing) What can we IMPROVE right now? (fix equipment, reorganize, train skills) What can we LEARN to get better? (take classes, practice, research) What RELATIONSHIPS can we strengthen? (call past customers, thank people, ask for referrals) Can we offer a DIFFERENT product for this season? (pivot: pool company offers hot tub service, pumpkin farm hosts winter events) **PART 3: Budget Planning** Use reserve funds: Yes or No? How much? Cut expenses: What can wait? Investments worth making: What will help later?
description.es: Teams complete comprehensive "Slow Season Action Plan": **PART 1: Understanding the Problem** Current situation (how much money coming in now vs. busy season?) Investments worth making: What will help later?

sayThis.es: "Two minutes. Your business, your problem, your best three moves, your budget. The class gets one question each."

doneWhen.en: Every team has presented all four parts and taken a question.

sayThis.en: "The Maplewood team did five different things. Ellis improved the workspace. Layla invested in packaging. Riley built spring stock. Benny called old customers. And they used the money they'd saved. Then a hundred-and-eighty-dollar order came in — because Mrs. Torres recommended them."
sayThis.es: "The Maplewood team did five different things. Ellis improved the workspace. Layla invested in packaging. Riley built spring stock. Benny called old customers. And they used the money they'd saved. Then a hundred-and-eighty-dollar order came in — because Mrs. Torres recommended them."

doneWhen.en: All five strategies from the story are matched to a team's plan on the board.
doneWhen.es: All five strategies from the story are matched to a team's plan on the board.

watchFor.en: The recommendation being read as luck. It came from a relationship somebody kept up on purpose.
watchFor.es: The recommendation being read as luck. It came from a relationship somebody kept up on purpose.

description.en: "What strategies did the Maplewood Makers team use?" Ellis: IMPROVED workspace (better workbench) Layla: INVESTED in future (better packaging) Riley: PREPARED inventory (spring pottery) Benny: CONNECTED with customers (signs, calls, outreach) Team: USED RESERVES ($73 saved from December) Result: Ms. Rivera's $180 wedding order came because they MAINTAINED RELATIONSHIPS (Mrs. Torres recommended them)
description.es: "What strategies did the Maplewood Makers team use?" Ellis: IMPROVED workspace (better workbench) Layla: INVESTED in future (better packaging) Riley: PREPARED inventory (spring pottery) Benny: CONNECTED with customers (signs, calls, outreach) Team: USED RESERVES ($73 saved from December) Result: Ms. Rivera's $180 wedding order came because they MAINTAINED RELATIONSHIPS (Mrs. Torres recommended them)

sayThis.en: "Businesses save in the good months so the quiet ones don't kill them. Now you — when's your slow season? Summer? Rainy days? What could you prepare then that pays off later?"
sayThis.es: "Businesses save in the good months so the quiet ones don't kill them. Now you — when's your slow season? Summer? Rainy days? What could you prepare then that pays off later?"

doneWhen.en: The class anchor chart is built and every student has written a personal answer.
doneWhen.es: The class anchor chart is built and every student has written a personal answer.

watchFor.en: The personal question skipped as silly. It's the one they'll remember.
watchFor.es: The personal question skipped as silly. It's the one they'll remember.

description.en: Create class anchor chart: "Smart Slow Season Strategies" Personal reflection: "When is YOUR slow season? (Summer break from school? Rainy days when you can't play outside?) What can you prepare or improve during that time?" Financial literacy connection: "This is why businesses save money during good times — to survive slow times and invest in getting better"
description.es: Create class anchor chart: "Smart Slow Season Strategies" Personal reflection: "When is YOUR slow season? (Summer break from school? Rainy days when you can't play outside?) What can you prepare or improve during that time?" Financial literacy connection: "This is why businesses save money during good times — to survive slow times and invest in getting better"

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between a failing business and a business in slow season?
Why is giving up during slow season a bad idea?
How can slow times actually be GOOD for a business?
What does 'the roots are growing underground' mean for business? (Frances's garden metaphor)
Why did Ms. Rivera call? How did something the team did in November help them in January? (relationship building)
What's an emergency fund and why do businesses need one?
Can you think of businesses in our community that have slow seasons? What do they do?
How is 'slow season' different from 'no one wants your product'?
extensionIdeas: Research actual businesses in your community and interview owners about their slow seasons
Track a year-long calendar of business cycles (when are different businesses busy/slow)
Create a "Slow Season Survival Guide" booklet for young entrepreneurs
Calculate: if you make $200 in December and $20 in January, how much should you save from December to survive January?
Compare to personal finances: "Sometimes your family has busy expensive months (back to school, holidays) and quiet months. Why might families save during good months?"

beforeClass.en: Cut the six scenario cards and check each one carries busy-season revenue, slow-season revenue, savings and upcoming costs. A card missing its numbers turns the budget section into guesswork.
beforeClass.es: Cut the six scenario cards and check each one carries busy-season revenue, slow-season revenue, savings and upcoming costs. A card missing its numbers turns the budget section into guesswork.

description.es: Students practice quick business presentations: What's your business? What did you learn? What was challenging? What are you proud of? Keep it brief (30-60 seconds).

discussionQuestions: **Financial Analysis:** Which business made the most profit? Why do you think that happened?
